passages.title: Honour your contracts and the sanctities of pilgrimage
passages.tafsir:
# The Contracts That Hold Life Together (5:1–2)

These two ayat open Sūrat al-Māʾidah with a single sweeping command — *fulfil the contracts* — and then immediately show what fulfilling them looks like in practice: honouring what Allah has made lawful and unlawful in food, guarding the sanctities of pilgrimage, and refusing to let old grievances pull the believer into injustice. What binds the passage together is the idea of the covenant: everything that follows, from the meat on your table to the pilgrim on the road, is an article of the agreement between the believer and his Lord.

## A sūrah of final, binding commands

Ibn Kathir opens with the standing of this sūrah itself. At-Tirmidhi recorded from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr that the last sūrahs to be revealed were al-Māʾidah and al-Fath — a report At-Tirmidhi himself graded Hasan, Gharib — and Al-Hakim narrated in his Mustadrak that when Jubayr bin Nufayr visited ʿAʾishah after Hajj, she asked him whether he read al-Māʾidah, then told him: it was the last sūrah to be revealed — so whatever you find made permissible in it, treat as permissible, and whatever you find made impermissible, treat as impermissible. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that its injunctions are *muḥkam* — of established meaning, with no possibility of abrogation remaining — and relates from the Musnad of Ahmad that the sūrah came down upon the Prophet ﷺ while he was travelling on his she-camel Adbāʾ, whose back could barely bear the weight of the revelation, on the journey of his Farewell Hajj. These are among the final instructions of the Qurʾan, and they open with a call to keep your word.

The address itself deserves a pause. Ibn Kathir cites a report of Ibn Abi Hatim that a man once came to ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud and asked him for advice, and he replied: whenever you hear *"O you who believe!"*, pay full attention — for it is either a righteous matter being ordained or an evil being forbidden. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this form of address signals that what follows is required by faith itself.

## "Fulfil the contracts" — how far does al-ʿuqūd reach?

The Arabic word *al-ʿuqūd* is the plural of *ʿaqd*, whose root meaning is **to tie**. A contract is literally a knot — something that ties two parties to each other. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and others explained "obligations" here as treaties, and Ibn Jarir reported a consensus of the early exegetes on this. But ʿAli bin Abi Talhah relates a wider reading from Ibn ʿAbbas: it refers to the covenants — what Allah has permitted, prohibited, ordained and set limits for in the Qurʾan — "therefore, do not commit treachery or break the covenants." Ad-Dahhak said similarly that Allah has taken a covenant from everyone who professes faith in the Prophet ﷺ and the Book to fulfil what He has ordered in the permissible and the impermissible.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists these interpretations do not conflict; the word absorbs them all. It cites Imam Raghib al-Isfahani's division of contracts into three kinds:

1. **The covenant with the Creator** — to believe in Him, obey Him, and observe His limits of lawful and unlawful.
2. **The commitment with one's own self** — a vow (*nadhr*) or an oath one binds oneself by.
3. **The contract with other human beings** — marriage, buying and selling, partnership, leasing, alliances, and treaties between groups and governments.

All of these, provided they are permissible in themselves, become binding by this one verse. The sūrah is even called *Sūrat al-ʿUqūd* for this reason, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that when the Prophet ﷺ sent ʿAmr ibn Hazm as governor to Yemen, this verse was written at the head of his decree of appointment — a ruler's commission opened with the command to keep contracts.

## The first article: the lawful and the unlawful in food

Ayah 1 then moves straight to a concrete instance of the covenant: *"Lawful to you are all the beasts of cattle, except what will be announced to you."* The word *bahīmah* denotes animals whose speech remains obscure to us; *al-anʿām* is the grazing livestock — camels, cows and sheep, as Al-Hasan, Qatadah and others explained, a meaning Ibn Jarir confirms matches Arab usage. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes this covers the eight kinds of domestic animals described in Sūrat al-Anʿām, and that some scholars extended "cattle" to their wild counterparts such as gazelle.

Two exceptions frame the permission. First, *"except what will be announced to you"* — which Ibn ʿAbbas explained as carrion, blood and swine-flesh, and which Ibn Kathir connects to the detailed list coming in ayah 3. Second, game is unlawful *"while you are in iḥrām"* — the pilgrim's consecrated state, in which hunting becomes a sin.

A practical ruling hangs on this ayah: Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas and others relied on it to permit eating a fetus found dead in the belly of its slaughtered mother. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, narrated by Abu Saʿid, records that the Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ about exactly this, and he said: "Eat it if you want, because its slaughter was fulfilled when its mother was slaughtered." At-Tirmidhi graded it Hasan.

The ayah closes: *"Verily, Allah commands that which He wills."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the posture this demands — the believer neither follows the fire-worshippers who declared all slaughter unlawful, nor those who eat every animal without restraint. The Creator knows the natures of His creatures and their effects on the human body and character, and He has built the world so that the lower form of life sustains the higher: soil feeds trees, trees feed animals, animals feed man. Receiving the lawful gratefully and stopping at the unlawful is itself an act of covenant-keeping.

## The second article: do not violate the sanctities of Allah

Ayah 2 turns from the table to the sanctuary: *"Do not violate the sanctity of the shaʿāʾir of Allah."* A *shaʿīrah* is a mark or symbol — something perceptible that signifies the religion. Ibn ʿAbbas said the shaʿāʾir here are the rituals of Hajj; Mujahid named as-Safa, al-Marwah and the sacrificial animal. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān prefers the comprehensive statement of Hasan al-Basri and ʿAtāʾ — which Imam al-Jassas called a compendium of all the explanations — that the Marks of Allah are all the obligations whose limits the Shariʿah has set. Violating them can take three forms: abandoning them altogether, obeying selectively and incompletely, or overstepping the appointed limits. The verse forbids all three.

The ayah then lists specific sanctities. **The Sacred Month:** fighting was forbidden in the four sacred months, and Al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih from Abu Bakrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said during the Farewell Hajj that the year is twelve months, four of which are sacred — Dhul-Qaʿdah, Dhul-Hijjah and Muharram in succession, and Rajab of Mudar. Ibn Kathir says this hadith testifies to the continued sanctity of these months until the end of time (while Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the agreed view of the scholars that the prohibition of fighting in them was later abrogated). **The hady and the garlands:** the sacrificial animals brought to the Kaʿbah, marked by garlands on their necks so that no one would harm them. Ibn Kathir describes how the Prophet ﷺ himself, setting out for Hajj from Dhul-Hulayfah, garlanded his hady — more than sixty of the finest camels — and announced his intention aloud. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that violating these animals includes stopping them from reaching the Haram, seizing them, or even using them for riding or milk. **The pilgrims themselves:** those heading for the Sacred House "seeking the bounty and good pleasure of their Lord" — bounty meaning trade, as Mujahid, Qatadah and many others said, and pleasure meaning Allah's pleasure through their Hajj, as Ibn ʿAbbas said — must not be stopped, prevented or frightened away.

Then a small release: *"When you finish the iḥrām, then hunt"* — the earlier prohibition simply lifts, and what was permitted before iḥrām becomes permitted again.

## Hudaybiyyah: the test of an old wound

The heart of ayah 2 lies in a story — or rather, in three linked events that Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out as the background of the verse. In the sixth year of Hijrah the Prophet ﷺ set out with over a thousand Companions in iḥrām, intending only ʿUmrah. At Hudaybiyyah the idolators of Makkah blocked them, imposed humiliating terms, and forced them to remove their iḥrām and turn back — a wound that, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, planted seeds of resentment in the believers' hearts.

Then came the provocation. ʿIkrimah, As-Suddi and Ibn Jarir relate that al-Hutam bin Hind al-Bakri came to Madinah feigning interest in Islam — the Prophet ﷺ had already told his Companions, by revelation, that a man was coming who would speak with the tongue of Satan — and on leaving he drove off the grazing livestock of the people of Madinah. The following year the Companions, travelling for the ʿUmrah they had missed, heard someone in the distance reciting the talbiyah — the chant by which a pilgrim announces aloud that he has set out for the House: it was the same man, going to ʿUmrah with their stolen animals as his sacrificial offerings. They wanted to attack him on the road.

The third event, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, came with the Conquest of Makkah in the eighth year of Hijrah. The Prophet ﷺ set the defeated Makkans free without taking any revenge, and they went about their lives — even continuing their pagan customs of Hajj and ʿUmrah. Some Companions then thought of settling the old score of Hudaybiyyah: these people had stopped us from an ʿUmrah that was permissible and justified on every count — why should we now allow them a Hajj and ʿUmrah that are impermissible and unjustified on every count? Why not attack them and take their animals? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that these events were narrated by Ibn Jarir on the authority of ʿIkrimah and as-Suddi, and that it was on the basis of some of them that the verse came down. And Ibn Abi Hatim records from Zayd bin Aslam that at Hudaybiyyah itself, when idolators passed by intending ʿUmrah, the Companions said: "Let us prevent them just as their fellows prevented us." It was then that Allah sent down: *"Let not the hatred of a people who once stopped you from al-Masjid al-Haram lead you to transgress."*

The word *shanaʾān*, Ibn ʿAbbas and others said, means enmity and hatred. The command is stark: even a thief in pilgrim's garb, even the very people who barred you from the House, may not be wronged in retaliation where the sanctities of Allah are concerned. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the principle plainly: Islam does not answer injustice with counter-injustice; it answers injustice with justice, guarding even the rights of enemies — and Ibn Kathir links this to the coming verse, *"Be just: that is nearer to piety"* (5:8).

## Cooperate in righteousness, never in sin

The passage closes with what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls a verdict on an elemental question of human life: *"Help one another in al-birr and at-taqwā, but do not help one another in sin and transgression."* *Birr*, by consensus of the commentators, means good deeds; *taqwā*, abstinence from evil; *ithm* is sin in the widest sense; *ʿudwān* is crossing the limits — aggression.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on how the whole human world runs on cooperation — no solitary person, however rich, could grow his own food, weave his own cloth and build his own house; the morsel that reaches your mouth is the combined work of countless hands. But cooperation is a two-edged sword: organised for crime, it can destroy the very order it builds. So the Qurʾan sets the criterion. Notice, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, that it does not say "cooperate with Muslims and not with non-Muslims" — the basis of cooperation is righteousness and taqwā themselves, so that even a Muslim brother receives no help when he moves toward injustice.

The Sunnah seals this. In a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Anas bin Malik — and recorded by Al-Bukhari — the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Support your brother whether he was unjust or the victim of injustice." The Companions asked: helping the wronged we understand, but how do we help the wrongdoer? He said: "Prevent and stop him from committing injustice, and this represents giving support to him." And Muslim recorded that whoever calls to guidance earns reward equal to all who follow him until the Day of Resurrection, without diminishing their reward — while whoever calls to misguidance carries the like of their burdens.

## Living it

The passage asks something concrete of the believer. Every knot you tie — the marriage contract, the business deal, the promise, the treaty, and above all the covenant of faith itself — is binding before Allah, and breaking it is treachery. The sanctities of Allah are not to be touched even when the person sheltering under them is your enemy; grievance, however legitimate, never licenses transgression. And every act of help you give is weighed: lend your strength only to what is righteous, and when a brother turns to wrong, the truest help is the hand that holds him back. The ayah ends with the reason to take all of this seriously: *"Have taqwā of Allah. Verily, Allah is severe in punishment."*

passages.title: Forbidden meats, the perfected religion, and lawful food
passages.tafsir:
This passage sets out, in one connected sweep, what a believer may and may not eat — and in the very middle of that legal detail, Allah places one of the most momentous sentences in the whole Qur'an: "This day I have perfected your religion for you." What holds ayat 3–5 together is a single movement from the forbidden to the lawful: ayah 3 lists the impure foods and pagan practices now closed off, ayah 4 answers the Companions' question about what *is* lawful, and ayah 5 completes the circle by permitting the food — and marriage — of the People of the Book. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the underlying principle simply: whatever harms the human being, physically or spiritually, the Qur'an classes as evil and forbids; whatever is pure and beneficial it declares lawful.

## The forbidden things of ayah 3

The ayah names the categories one by one, and the commentators open each of them up.

**Maytah (carrion)** is the animal that dies without proper slaughter. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah forbade it because of the harm it causes — the blood that clogs in the veins of the dead animal — so it is "harmful, religiously and physically." Fish is the exception: the Prophet ﷺ said of the sea, "Its water is pure and its dead are permissible" — a hadith recorded by Malik in his Muwatta, by Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah in their Sunan, and by Ibn Khuzaymah and Ibn Hibban in their Sahihs. Locusts carry the same exemption.

**Blood** means *flowing* blood, as Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id bin Jubayr explained, in light of the parallel verse "blood poured forth" (6:145). That is why the liver and spleen — blood in substance but not flowing — remain lawful. When Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the spleen he said, "Eat it," and when they objected, "It is blood," he answered, "You are only prohibited blood that was poured forth."

**The flesh of swine** — and here the Arabic matters. *Lahm* ("flesh") in Arab usage means the whole animal: its fat, ligaments, everything, wild or domesticated. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith in Muslim that whoever plays Nardshir (a dice game involving gambling) "is just like the one who puts his hand in the flesh and blood of swine" — if merely touching it is spoken of this way, what of eating it? And the Two Sahihs record that Allah made even the *trade* of dead animals, pigs, alcohol and idols unlawful; when people asked about using the fat of dead animals for greasing boats and fueling lamps, the Prophet ﷺ said, "No, it is illegal."

**What is slaughtered for other than Allah** — any animal over which the name of an idol, false deity or monument was invoked — is unlawful by consensus, because Allah made the mention of His Name a condition of slaughter. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a subtle point: even if someone pronounces Allah's Name but actually *offers* the sacrifice for the pleasure of someone other than Allah, the jurists agree it is unlawful.

Then come the deaths of the Jahiliyyah table: the animal **strangled** (even accidentally in a restraint), **beaten to death** with a staff or rock, **killed by a fall** from a height or into a well, **gored** by another animal, and **partly eaten by a wild beast**. The pre-Islamic Arabs ate all of these; Allah closed each door. The Sunnah draws the same line with precision: 'Adi bin Hatim asked about hunting with the miʿrad (a heavy throwing stick), and the Prophet ﷺ replied — as recorded in the Sahih — "If the game is hit by its sharp edge, eat it. But if it is hit by its broad side, do not eat it, for it has been beaten to death." On that principle, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the jurists — Abu Hanifah, Ash-Shafi'i, Malik and others — ruled that game killed by gunshot falls under *mawqudhah* (beaten to death).

**"Unless you slaughter it"** (*illā mā dhakkaytum*) is the saving clause. Ibn 'Abbas explained: if you reach any of these animals while it is still alive and slaughter it properly, it becomes lawful. 'Ali said: if it still moves a foot or a leg, slaughter it and eat. And what counts as valid slaughter? Rafi' bin Khadij asked whether reeds could be used when no knives were at hand, and the Prophet ﷺ answered — in the Two Sahihs — "Use what makes blood flow, and eat what is slaughtered with the Name of Allah," excepting teeth and claws. Two things, then, define lawful meat: the flowing of the blood and the Name of Allah. The commentators note this exception cannot apply to the first four categories — carrion, blood, swine, and what was dedicated to other than Allah — since those are unlawful in themselves.

**The stone altars (nusub)** were the rock slabs around the Ka'bah — three hundred and sixty of them, Ibn Jurayj said — before which the Arabs slaughtered as an act of worship. Meat slaughtered there is forbidden *even if Allah's Name was pronounced*, because the act itself is a form of shirk (associating partners with Allah).

**The divining arrows (azlam)** were how the pagan Arab made decisions, and the commentators describe the practice in more than one form. Ibn Kathir relates that the Arabs would use three arrows — one with "Do" written on it, another with "Do not," and a third left blank; if the blank arrow was drawn, the person kept drawing until a command came out, then obeyed it. Some wrote instead "My Lord commanded me" and "My Lord forbade me." He also relates, from Muhammad bin Ishaq and others, a second account: the major idol of Quraysh was Hubal, erected over a well inside the Ka'bah where gifts were presented and the Ka'bah's treasure was kept, and there the Arabs kept seven arrows which they used to seek a decision in matters of dispute — whatever the chosen arrow told them, they abided by it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that arrows of this kind, marked "yes" and "no," were kept in the custody of the keeper of the Ka'bah; a person wanting his fortune told would present the keeper a gift of money and act on whichever arrow was drawn. The verse brands all of this *fisq* — disobedience and sin. The scholars extend the ruling to every method of divining the future or claiming knowledge of the Ghayb (the unseen): divination through numbers, palm-reading, the taking of omens. And here is the passage's quiet beauty: Islam did not merely abolish the arrows; it replaced them. Ibn Kathir brings the hadith of Jabir — recorded by Imam Ahmad, Al-Bukhari and the collectors of the Sunan — that the Prophet ﷺ taught the Companions Istikharah (the prayer asking Allah to choose for one) "as he taught us the Surahs of the Qur'an": two units of prayer, then a supplication entrusting the matter to the One who alone knows and is able. The believer still seeks a decision — but from Allah, not from an arrow.

## "This day I have perfected your religion for you"

In the middle of these rulings comes the announcement. The setting, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paints it, was without parallel: the Day of 'Arafah in the Farewell Hajj, year ten of the Hijrah — and that 'Arafah fell on a Friday. The place was the plain of 'Arafat near the Mount of Mercy; the time, after 'Asr, the blessed hour of answered prayers. Some one hundred and fifty thousand Companions were present, and the Prophet ﷺ sat on his she-camel Adba' when the revelation descended with such weight that the camel was compelled to sit down. Ibn 'Abbas said this is almost the last verse of the Qur'an: no verse of legal rulings came after it, and the Prophet ﷺ lived only eighty-one days more.

First: "This day, those who disbelieved have given up all hope of your religion." Ibn 'Abbas explained: they despaired of Muslims ever reverting to their old religion. A hadith in the Sahih carries the same meaning: Shaytan has given up hope of being worshipped by those who pray in the Arabian Peninsula — but he will still stir trouble among them. Hence "fear them not, but fear Me": the believers' security is not license for complacency but a redirection of awe toward Allah alone.

Then the perfection itself. Ibn Kathir calls this "the biggest favor from Allah to this Ummah": the religion is complete, so no other prophet is needed after Muhammad ﷺ — the lawful is what he allowed, the unlawful what he forbade. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a fine linguistic distinction from Raghib al-Isfahani: *ikmāl* (perfection), used for the religion, means the purpose has been fully accomplished; *itmām* (completion), used for the favor, means nothing further is needed — Muslims now had the supremacy to live their faith without dependence on anyone. And perfection "today" does not mean earlier revelations were defective; each was perfect *for its time and people*, while Islam alone is perfect for every people and every age until the Last Day.

Two moments capture what the Companions understood. A Jewish man said to 'Umar: had this verse been revealed to us, we would have taken its day as a day of celebration. 'Umar replied, "By Allah! I know when and where this verse was revealed — the evening of the Day of 'Arafah on a Friday" — recorded by Al-Bukhari, Muslim, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i. His answer hints that the day already *was* a double festival — 'Arafah and Jumu'ah. And 'Umar himself wept when the verse came down. Asked why, he said: nothing is perfect but that it is bound to deteriorate — and, in the account Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, he sensed that with the religion perfected, the Prophet's ﷺ remaining time was short. The Prophet ﷺ told him, "You have said the truth."

## Mercy at the edge of necessity

The ayah closes with the concession: whoever is forced by severe hunger, "with no inclination to sin," may eat of these forbidden things — "then surely Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful." The condition is that one eats only what removes the compulsion, not to enjoy or to fill oneself, and the forbidden things remain forbidden in themselves. Ibn Kathir dispels a folk error: one need not wait three days — when the dire need arises, the allowance applies. The Companions of a famine-stricken land asked when they could eat carrion, and the Prophet ﷺ said, in the narration of Imam Ahmad, "When you neither find food for lunch and dinner nor have any produce to eat." And in the Musnad and the Sahih of Ibn Hibban: "Allah likes that His allowance (rukhsah) be used, just as He dislikes that disobedience to Him is committed." The law is firm; the Lawgiver is merciful.

## Ayah 4: the good things, and hunting with trained animals

The Companions had asked the Prophet ﷺ what was lawful for them. The answer: *at-tayyibat* — the good, pure things — and the catch of trained beasts and birds of prey. The word *jawarih* comes from *jarh*, "to earn": these animals earn food for their owners. It covers trained dogs, falcons and the like, as the majority of Companions and Imams held. *Mukallibin* — from the training of hunting animals — signals the discipline required.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distills the conditions: the animal must be genuinely trained (a dog that catches and holds rather than eating; a falcon that returns when called); you must release it deliberately at the game; it must hold the catch for you, not eat from it — "eat of what they catch *for you*"; and you must say *Bismillah* when releasing it. Abu Hanifah adds that the beast must wound the game — a meaning hinted at in the word *jawarih* itself. If these are met, the game is lawful even if found dead. The Two Sahihs record the Prophet's ﷺ words to 'Adi bin Hatim: "If, with mentioning Allah's Name, you let loose your trained dog after a game and it catches it, you may eat what it catches" — even if it kills it, unless another dog joined the hunt, "for you mentioned Allah's Name over your dog, but not the other." But "if the dog eats from the game, do not eat from it, for I fear it has caught it as prey for itself." Even here the ayah ends "and have taqwa of Allah": Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that lawful hunting never licenses neglecting the prayer for the sake of the chase.

## Ayah 5: the food of the People of the Book, and marriage

"This day" returns — the same Day of 'Arafah — and now the door opens outward. "The food of those given the Scripture is lawful to you, and your food is lawful to them." By the consensus of the Companions and their Successors — Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr and many others — *ta'am* (food) here means their *dhabihah*, their properly slaughtered animals. Why? Because in dry goods like grain and fruit there is no difference between any non-Muslims; slaughter alone depends on religion and belief. And the reason for the permission, as Ibn Kathir states, is that the People of the Book — despite beliefs about Allah that do not befit His majesty — hold that slaughtering for other than Allah is prohibited, and they mention Allah's Name over their slaughter. Their scriptures' rulings on slaughter and marriage still track Islam's. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful on the boundaries: Jews and Christians remain "People of the Book" however far astray they have gone, so long as they still claim the faith — 'Umar ruled that even a sect denying the Last Day was still counted among them — but those who have abandoned belief in Allah and His prophets altogether cannot claim the ruling merely because a census lists them as Christians. 'Ali forbade the slaughter of the Christians of Banu Taghlib on the report that "they have taken nothing from the Christian faith except the drinking of wine," though the majority, finding them ordinary Christians, permitted it.

The same logic extends to marriage: chaste believing women, and chaste women of the People of the Book, are lawful — with the mahr (dower) given fully and with a good heart, "desiring chastity, not illegal sexual intercourse, nor taking them as lovers." Chastity is demanded of the man no less than of the woman. Ibn 'Umar personally advised against marrying Christian women — "I do not know of a worse case of shirk than her saying that 'Isa is her lord" — but other Companions married women of the People of the Book, understanding this ayah as an exception to the general prohibition of marrying idolatresses in 2:221.

The passage that began with carrion and altars ends with a warning that lifts the whole discussion above the plate and the contract: "Whoever rejects faith, his work is fruitless, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers." Food law, in the end, is faith made daily. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses this home: what enters the body shapes the soul — "without eating halal, righteous deeds cannot be imagined." And it explains why the Name of Allah at the moment of slaughter was made obligatory (wajib) rather than merely recommended, as it is for other food: the lives of all living beings are, in one respect, equal, so the taking of an animal's life could never simply be assumed as a right; where Allah has permitted it, that permission is a major reward from Him, and He made the acknowledgment of this blessing — gratitude expressed at the very moment of slaughter — a binding duty.

passages.title: Purification, justice, and remembering Allah's covenant
passages.tafsir:
# Purification, Justice, and the Covenant (5:6–11)

This passage gathers three commands that at first seem unrelated — purify yourselves for prayer, remember the pledge you gave to Allah, and be unswervingly just even with your enemies — and binds them with a single golden thread: **Allah's favor (niʿmah) upon the believers**. The word recurs like a refrain: ayah 6 ends with Allah completing "His favor upon you," ayah 7 opens "remember Allah's favor upon you and His covenant," and ayah 11 opens again "remember Allah's favor upon you" when enemy hands were stretched out and Allah held them back. Law, loyalty, and protection are all presented as one continuous gift — and each command closes by turning the heart back to Allah: be thankful (ayah 6), have taqwa — a vigilant, protective consciousness of Allah, guarding oneself against His displeasure — for He knows what the breasts conceal (ayat 7–8), and let the believers put their trust in Him (ayah 11). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the transition: earlier verses of the sūrah dealt with worldly life, marriage, and food; here the sūrah turns to acts of worship — ṣalāh, wuḍūʼ, ghusl, tayammum, and purity (ṭahārah).

## Ayah 6: the verse of purification

This single ayah carries the essentials of ritual purity: wuḍūʼ (the minor ablution) for prayer, ghusl (the full bath) for major impurity (janābah), and tayammum (purification with clean earth) when water cannot be used.

**When is wuḍūʼ actually required?** The ayah says "when you stand for prayer, wash…" — yet the Prophet ﷺ did not always renew his ablution. Ibn Kathir explains: the command is an obligation for the one in a state of impurity, and a recommendation for the one already pure. It was said that in the beginning of Islam Muslims performed wuḍūʼ for every prayer, and this was later abrogated. Imam Ahmad records from Buraydah that the Prophet ﷺ used to perform wuḍūʼ before every prayer, but on the Day of Victory he prayed all five prayers with one wuḍūʼ, telling ʿUmar, "I did that intentionally, O ʿUmar." Muslim and the collectors of the Sunan also recorded this, and At-Tirmidhi called it "Hasan Sahih." Abu Dawud records that when food was brought to the Prophet ﷺ after he had relieved himself and he was offered water, he said, "I was commanded to perform wuḍūʼ when I stand up for prayer" — not for eating. Still, renewing wuḍūʼ for each prayer remains a virtue: Ibn ʿUmar kept the earlier, harder practice until he died, and the majority of scholars hold it is encouraged, not obligatory.

**Intention, hidden in the grammar.** Ibn Kathir draws the obligation of intention (niyyah) from the ayah's own structure: "when you stand for prayer, then wash" is like the Arabs' saying "when you see the leader, stand" — meaning stand *for him*. The washing is *for* the prayer, which requires intending it. He seals the point with the hadith of the Two Sahihs: "Actions are judged by their intentions, and each person will earn what he intended." It is also recommended to mention Allah's Name at the start — a report narrated by several Companions states there is no wuḍūʼ for one who does not mention Allah's Name over it — and to wash the hands before dipping them into the vessel, especially on waking, for the Two Sahihs record: "one of you does not know where his hand spent the night."

**How the Prophet ﷺ washed.** The Companions preserved his wuḍūʼ limb by limb. In the report of Ḥumrān, ʿUthmān washed his hands thrice, rinsed his mouth and nose, washed his face thrice, then each forearm to the elbow thrice, wiped his head, then washed each foot thrice — and said, "I saw the Prophet ﷺ performing wuḍūʼ like this," adding his words: "If anyone performs wuḍūʼ like this of mine and offers a two-rakʿah prayer during which he does not think of anything else, his past sins will be forgiven" (recorded in the Two Sahihs). Notice how the ayah's wording settles the details the schools discuss:

- **"Your hands up to (ilā) the elbows"** — *ilā* here means *including* the elbows, as in the parallel Qurʼanic usage about not devouring the orphans' wealth "to" your own (i.e., adding it in). Washing part of the upper arm is even recommended, because of the hadith in Al-Bukhari and Muslim that on the Day of Resurrection this community will be called "those with the radiant appendages" from the traces of wuḍūʼ — "whoever can increase the area of his radiance should do so."
- **"Wipe your heads"** — the Two Sahihs record ʿAbdullah bin Zayd demonstrating the Prophet's ﷺ wuḍūʼ: he passed his wet hands over the whole head, front to nape and back again. These narrations indicate wiping the entire head.
- **"And your feet up to the ankles"** — the feet are *washed*, not merely wiped. Ibn Kathir cites Ibn ʿAbbās and a long line of the Salaf (Ibn Masʿūd, ʿUrwah, Mujāhid, Al-Ḥasan and others) for this, then the decisive scene from the Two Sahihs: Companions rushing wuḍūʼ on a journey were wiping their feet, and the Prophet ﷺ shouted at the top of his voice, "Perform wuḍūʼ thoroughly! Save your heels from the Fire." Muslim also records that a man who left a dry spot the size of a fingernail on his foot was told, "Go back and perform proper wuḍūʼ." Thoroughness extends to washing between the fingers and toes, as in the hadith of Laqīṭ bin Ṣabrah recorded by the collectors of the Sunan.
- **Wiping over the khuffs** (leather footwear worn over feet washed in a previous wuḍūʼ) is an established sunnah — Ibn Kathir says the reports reach the mutawātir grade (so massively transmitted that error is inconceivable). The hadith of Jarīr al-Bajalī was especially beloved to the early scholars: since Jarīr embraced Islam *after* al-Māʼidah was revealed and still saw the Prophet ﷺ wipe over his khuffs, the practice could not have been abrogated by this ayah (recorded in the Two Sahihs).

**The necklace in the desert — how tayammum came down.** Al-Bukhari records the occasion from ʿĀʼishah herself: returning toward Al-Madīnah, her necklace broke and was lost at Al-Baydāʼ. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed there and went to sleep with his head on her lap. Abu Bakr, her father, came and hit her on her flank — "You have detained the people because of a necklace?" — and she could not move because the Prophet ﷺ was sleeping on her lap. He rose when dawn broke and there was no water. Then Allah revealed this ayah. Usayd bin Al-Ḥuḍayr exclaimed, "O family of Abu Bakr! Allah has blessed the people because of you — you are only a blessing for the people." What began as an ordeal ended as a mercy for the entire Ummah: the ill and the traveler who find no water simply strike clean earth once and wipe the face and hands.

**"Allah does not want to place you in difficulty."** The ayah closes by revealing the spirit behind all these rulings: not burden but purification, the completion of favor, and gratitude. And the Sunnah unveils what the water is really doing. Malik and Muslim record: when the believing servant washes his face, every sin his eyes looked at departs with the water or with its last drop; when he washes his hands, every sin they committed departs; when he washes his feet, every sin they walked to departs — "until he ends up sinless." Muslim records: "Purity is half of faith," and "The radiance of the believer reaches where the water of his wuḍūʼ reaches." Muslim also records that Allah accepts no prayer without purity — so this ayah is the doorway to every prayer a believer will ever offer. The Sunnah adds a seal: whoever completes his wuḍūʼ and testifies that none is worthy of worship but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, "the eight doors of Paradise will be opened for him so that he can enter from any door he wishes" (Muslim, from ʿUqbah bin ʿĀmir).

## Ayah 7: the covenant of "we hear and we obey"

Having legislated, Allah reminds the believers *why* they obey: His favor in sending this religion and this Messenger ﷺ, and "His covenant with which He bound you when you said: We hear and we obey." Ibn Kathir explains this is the pledge the Companions used to give to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when they embraced Islam — in their own words, "to hear and obey, in times when we are active and otherwise, even if we were passed over for our rights, and not to dispute leadership with its rightful people." A second view, reported by ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah from Ibn ʿAbbās, is that the ayah reminds the Jews of the pledges Allah took from them to follow Muhammad ﷺ. On either reading the point stands: obedience is not a mood but a standing commitment. And because commitments can be kept outwardly while betrayed inwardly, the ayah ends: "Verily, Allah is All-Knower of what is in the breasts."

## Ayah 8: justice that hatred cannot bend

"Stand out firmly for Allah as just witnesses" — for Allah, says Ibn Kathir, not for people or for fame — "and let not the enmity and hatred of a people make you swerve from justice. Be just: that is nearer to taqwa." The command is at its most demanding precisely here: be just with everyone, friend or enemy. Ibn Kathir notes that "nearer to taqwa" does not imply a permissible lesser option — since no other course exists, "nearer" here means "is."

**A precision of word order.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits a subtle observation from Abu Hayyan's tafsir *Al-Bahr al-Muhit*. This ayah's near-twin in Sūrah al-Nisāʼ (4:135) says "be upholders of *justice*, witnesses *for Allah*," while our ayah reverses it: "be steadfast *for Allah*, witnesses *for justice*." Why? Two forces corrupt justice: love and hatred. Al-Nisāʼ addresses love — bias for oneself, parents, kin — so *justice* leads, cutting off the excuse that favoring one's relatives might somehow be "for Allah." Al-Māʼidah addresses hatred — so *for Allah* leads: when you stand for Allah alone, sentiment against an enemy loses its grip, and the inevitable outcome is equal justice even with those you oppose.

**Justice begins at home.** The Two Sahihs record that the father of An-Nuʿmān bin Bashīr asked the Prophet ﷺ to witness a gift he was giving this one son. The Prophet ﷺ asked, "Have you given the like of it to every one of your children?" He said no. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Have taqwa of Allah and treat your children equally," and "I shall not be witness to injustice." The father took the gift back.

**Testimony is wider than a courtroom.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the word shahādah (testimony) into daily life: a medical certificate that misstates a patient's condition is false testimony; marking examination papers unfairly is false testimony; signing a certificate for an incapable graduate is false attestation. Even **casting a vote** is threefold in the Sharīʿah's eyes: a testimony (shahādah) that the candidate is worthy and honest, a recommendation (shafāʿah) whose good or evil fruit returns to the voter (citing 4:85), and an agency (wakālah) over rights the whole nation shares — so voting for the undeserving out of money, pressure, or friendship places a share of every wrong they later commit in the voter's record. Concealing true testimony is itself a grave sin (citing 2:283), and the Qurʼan equally commands that no scribe or witness be made to suffer for testifying (2:282).

## Ayat 9–10: the two destinations

The passage now grounds the commands in the Hereafter. Ayah 9 promises those who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward — Paradise. Ibn Kathir adds a point of creed here: no one *earns* Paradise by deeds alone; it is attained by Allah's mercy and favor, while He, out of pure grace, made righteous deeds the cause and path leading to that mercy — so all thanks return to Him alone. Ayah 10 gives the opposite: those who disbelieve and deny His signs are the dwellers of the Fire, and this, says Ibn Kathir, only demonstrates Allah's perfect justice — He is never wrong.

## Ayah 11: the hands that were held back

The passage closes with a favor the believers could see: "Remember Allah's favor upon you when a people planned to stretch out their hands against you, and He withheld their hands from you." Ibn Kathir relates two occasions. ʿAbdur-Razzāq records from Jābir: the Prophet ﷺ once stayed at an area, and the people spread out seeking shade under the trees. The Prophet ﷺ hung his weapon on a tree. A bedouin man came and took possession of the Prophet's ﷺ weapon, held it aloft, came toward him and demanded, "Who can protect you from me?" He replied, "Allah, the Exalted, Most Honored." The bedouin repeated his question twice or thrice, and each time the Prophet ﷺ answered him, "Allah." The bedouin then lowered the sword, and the Prophet ﷺ called his Companions and told them what had happened while the man sat beside him — for the Prophet ﷺ did not punish him. Maʿmar said that Qatādah used to mention that some Arabs wanted to have the Prophet ﷺ killed and sent that bedouin; Qatādah would then recite this very ayah. The man, Ghawrath bin Al-Ḥārith, is mentioned in the Sahih. The second account, from Ibn Isḥāq, Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah: the Jews of Banū An-Naḍīr plotted to drop a stone on the Prophet ﷺ as he sat beneath their wall, having come to them for help with a blood-money payment. Allah informed him of the plot; he rose and returned to Al-Madīnah, and Banū An-Naḍīr were later expelled.

Hence the closing command: "And in Allah let the believers put their trust." Whoever does, says Ibn Kathir, Allah suffices him and shields him from the plots of people.

## The thread pulled tight

Read as one movement, the passage teaches that every layer of the believer's life is covenant: the water on your limbs, the pledge on your tongue, the justice in your testimony, and the safety of your neck are all His favor. The response He asks is the one each ayah names in turn — gratitude, taqwa, and trust.

passages.title: Broken covenants of Israel and the Christians
passages.tafsir:
# The Covenant Taken, the Covenant Broken (5:12–14)

Having just reminded the Muslims of the pledge *they* gave — "We have listened and obeyed" (5:7) — the sūrah now turns to history's warning label. These three ayat tell the story of two earlier communities who were given covenants very much like ours: the Children of Israel in ayah 12–13, and the Christians in ayah 14. Both were bound by solemn terms, both broke them, and each suffered a distinct punishment. What holds the passage together is a single word repeated through all three ayat: **mīthāq** — the solemn covenant — taken, then breached, then answered.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the placement: pledge-taking is not something special to Muslims. Similar pledges were taken from the communities before us, and they failed to fulfil them. The passage is therefore not merely a history lesson about others; it is a mirror held up to the community that has just been reminded of its own pledge — which, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, is the pledge of obedience contained in the kalimah itself: *lā ilāha illa Allāh, Muḥammadur-Rasūlullāh*. Every Muslim who says it is bound by it.

## The twelve naqībs: a covenant with representatives

Ayah 12 opens with Allah taking the covenant from the Children of Israel and appointing among them **twelve naqībs** — leaders or representatives. Ibn Kathir, citing Muhammad bin Ishaq and Ibn ʿAbbas, places this at the moment Mūsā (peace be upon him) went to fight the mighty enemy in Palestine, when Allah commanded him to choose a leader from every tribe. Each of the twelve chiefs pledged, on his own behalf and on behalf of his entire tribe, to listen and obey Allah, His Messenger, and His Book — taking responsibility both to keep the covenant himself and to make his people keep it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over the wisdom of this arrangement. Islam recognises no dividing line of lineage, colour, or caste — the Prophet ﷺ declared this plainly in his address at the Last Hajj. Yet family and tribal structure may still be harnessed for order and administration: people naturally trust a known member of their own group, and such a leader understands his people's temperament in detail. The twelve-tribe structure of Banī Isrāʼīl appears elsewhere in the Qurʼan too — the twelve springs that gushed from the rock, one for each tribe (7:160).

**The night of ʿAqabah.** Ibn Kathir then draws a striking parallel from the sīrah: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took the pledge from the Ansar at ʿAqabah, there were likewise twelve leaders — three from Aws and nine from Khazraj, men such as Usayd bin Al-Hudayr, Asʿad bin Zurarah, ʿAbdullah bin Rawahah, ʿUbadah bin As-Samit and Saʿd bin ʿUbadah — who gave the pledge of allegiance and obedience to the Prophet ﷺ on behalf of their people, just as the naqībs of Banī Isrāʼīl once had. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a further resonance: the narration of Jabir ibn Samurah in al-Bukhari and Muslim, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that people's affairs will remain well-ordered while twelve Khulafāʼ lead them. Ibn Kathir comments that nothing in this hadith requires the twelve to rule continuously one after another; they may appear with gaps — the four rightly-guided Khulafāʼ, and later ʿUmar ibn ʿAbdul-ʿAzīz accepted by consensus as the fifth righteous Khalīfah.

## "I am with you" — the terms of the covenant

Before listing the articles of the pledge, Allah says: **innī maʿakum** — "I am with you." Ibn Kathir reads this as a promise of protection, support and aid. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān hears two things in it at once: a promise — keep the pledge and you will witness Divine support at every step — and a warning — Allah is with you everywhere, watching over this pledge; nothing you conceal, intend or plan escapes His knowledge, and no one slips His grip by breaking it.

The covenant's articles then follow in ayah 12:

- **Establishing the Ṣalāh and giving the Zakāh.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes what this reveals: the people of Mūsā (peace be upon him) were obligated with prayer and zakāh long before Islam — these duties have been enjoined by every prophet and every Sharīʿah.
- **Believing in Allah's messengers and supporting them.** Since many messengers were still to come to Banī Isrāʼīl, they were particularly charged with honouring and assisting them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes a subtlety in the word order: though faith normally precedes deeds, here ṣalāh and zakāh come first because they were to be acted on immediately, while the messengers in question were yet to arrive.
- **Lending Allah a "goodly loan" (qarḍ ḥasan).** Ibn Kathir explains this as spending in Allah's cause seeking His pleasure. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the metaphor: spending is called a *loan* because a loan's return is due — legally, customarily, morally — so one should give believing the return is certain, giving what one holds dear rather than the spare and the worthless. And since zakāh has already been named, the qarḍ ḥasan points to charity *beyond* zakāh: building a masjid where one is needed, sustaining religious education when no one else will. Zakāh is farḍ ʿayn — binding on every individual — while these further duties are farḍ kifāyah: if some of the community carry them, the rest are released; if no one does, all are sinners. Muslims are not done with their financial responsibilities simply by paying zakāh.

The reward for keeping these terms is total: sins remitted, and Gardens under which rivers flow. But the ayah closes on the hinge of the whole passage: whoever disbelieves *after this* — after pledging, after such clear terms — "has indeed gone astray from the straight way."

## Ayah 13: what breaking the covenant did to their hearts

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes two kinds of punishment that visited Banī Isrāʼīl: the manifest and perceptible — such as the hail of stones mentioned elsewhere in the Qurʼan — and the **intellectual and spiritual**, in which their very minds and hearts were transformed. Ayah 13 describes the second kind, and it is the more terrifying.

**"We cursed them"** — laʿnah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, transmitting the explanation of Hadrat Thanavi, defines the curse precisely: to be made far-removed from Allah's mercy and its effects. Ibn Kathir adds: deviated from truth, expelled from guidance.

**"And made their hearts hard"** — so hard, says Ibn Kathir, that no word of advice they hear penetrates. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connects this to the Qurʼan's image of *rān* — the stain or rust upon hearts in Sūrah al-Muṭaffifīn — and relates a teaching of the Prophet ﷺ: when a person first sins, a black dot is stamped on his heart, and it troubles him like a stain on white cloth. If he repents, it is erased; if he sins carelessly on, dot is added to dot until the heart turns jet black — like a pot placed upside down, into which nothing good can settle. At that stage the person's judgment itself inverts: he takes defect as merit, vice as virtue, sin as reward. As some of the elders said, the immediate reward of a good deed is the ability (tawfīq) to do another, and the immediate punishment of a sin is the pull towards the next one. Hard-heartedness, in other words, is not an arbitrary penalty; it is sin's own compounding interest.

From that hardened state flowed the rest: **"they change the words from their places"** — taḥrīf, tampering with revelation. Ibn Kathir explains that as their comprehension became corrupt they altered Allah's Book from its apparent meanings and attributed to Allah what He did not say — "we seek refuge with Allah from such behavior." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this alteration touched words, meanings, and recitation alike. They also "abandoned a good part of the Message" — by not implementing it and ignoring it: abandonment by neglect, not only by editing.

**"You will not cease to discover deceit in them, except a few."** The Prophet ﷺ would keep uncovering their plots — Mujahid said this ayah refers to their plot to kill the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The "few" excepted, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, are people like ʿAbdullah ibn Salām — those from the People of the Book who became true Muslims.

## "But forgive them and overlook"

After such an indictment, the ayah's ending is astonishing: **fa-ʿfu ʿanhum wa-ṣfaḥ** — forgive them and overlook. Ibn Kathir calls this "the ultimate victory and triumph," and preserves a saying of the Salaf: "You would never treat those who disobey Allah with you better than obeying Allah with them." Meet their disobedience with your obedience — this way hearts may gather around the truth, and Allah may lead them to guidance. Hence the closing words: "Verily, Allah loves the doers of good (al-muḥsinīn)."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the psychology of the command. Everything just described would naturally lead the Prophet ﷺ to hold such people in contempt — and the ayah instructs the opposite. Even granting that hard-hearted people are unlikely to respond to counsel, toleration and civility are "wonder virtues" that may yet probe out some sense from insensate people; and even if the effort fails, keeping one's own conduct and character correct remains worth doing in itself, and brings a Muslim closer to Allah.

It should be noted that Ibn Kathir also records the view of Qatadah that this command of forgiveness was abrogated by the later verse, "Fight against those who believe not in Allah, nor in the Last Day."

## Ayah 14: the Christians — and a different punishment

The passage then turns to **"those who say, 'We are Christians.'"** Ibn Kathir hears a pointed reproach in the very phrasing: they *call themselves* Christians and followers of ʿĪsā son of Maryam, "while in fact they are not as they claim." Their covenant included following, aiding and honouring the Prophet ﷺ, and believing in every prophet Allah sends. But "they imitated the Jews and broke the promises and the pledges" — the same abandonment of "a good part of the Message."

Yet their punishment differs. Where the Jews' breach brought curse and hardened hearts, for the Christians it brought **mutual dissension**: "We planted amongst them enmity and hatred till the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Kathir describes the fulfilment: the numerous Christian sects have always been enemies and adversaries of each other, accusing one another of heresy, cursing and excommunicating one another, barring each other from their places of worship — the Monarchist sect against the Jacobites, and such is the case with the Nestorians and the Arians. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites, from the Taysīr in the marginal notes on al-Baydawi, the three original sects: the Nestorians, who took ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) to be a divine son; the Jacobites, who believed him one with the Divine Being; and the Malkites, who held him one of the Trinity. With divisions of belief that fundamental, mutual malice was inevitable.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also answers the modern objection — don't Christians today seem rather united? The ayah, he explains, describes those who genuinely profess and *practise* the religion; those who have drifted into secular or non-religious identity are, for practical purposes, outside its scope, for the conflict was a religious one, and where the religion is not held, the conflict need not appear. Among observant Christians, the division remains well-known.

The ayah — and the passage — closes on deferred judgment: "and Allah will inform them of what they used to do." Ibn Kathir reads this as warning and threat over their claims about Allah — attributing to Him a companion and a son, while He is the One and Only, the All-Sufficient, Who neither begets nor was begotten, and there is none like unto Him.

## What this asks of us

The passage is addressed to Muslims who have just been reminded of their own mīthāq. Its logic, as the sources present it, is sobering in three ways. First, the terms of the earlier covenants — prayer, zakāh, faith in the messengers, sincere spending — are recognisably the terms of ours; the pledge is not a formality but a live contract with "I am with you" written over it. Second, the punishments were tailored to the crime and largely *internal*: hearts that stop absorbing truth, communities that cannot stop fighting themselves. Breaking covenant with Allah does not always look like lightning from the sky; it can look like slowly becoming unable to hear advice. Third — and most unexpectedly — the believer's stance towards those who broke their covenants is not contempt but iḥsān: "forgive them and overlook," for Allah loves the doers of good, and good conduct may open a heart that argument never could.

passages.title: The Messenger's light offered to the People of the Book
passages.tafsir:
# The Messenger's Light Offered to the People of the Book (5:15–19)

This passage is a direct, sustained address to the Jews and Christians — twice opened with the call "O People of the Book!" (ayat 15 and 19) — in which Allah presents Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an as a light sent to them, corrects the two gravest errors in their creed, and closes off every excuse they might offer on the Day of Judgment. What binds the five ayat together is a single movement: the offer of light (15–16), the removal of the claims that block that light (17–18), and the announcement that this Messenger has arrived at the precise moment in history when he was needed most (19).

## A light and a clear Book (ayat 15–16)

Ibn Kathir opens by stating the scope of the mission: Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ "with the guidance and the religion of truth to all the people of the earth, the Arabs and non-Arabs, lettered and unlettered" — with clear evidences and the distinction between truth and falsehood. But ayah 15 speaks to the People of the Book in particular, and it describes the Prophet ﷺ doing something remarkable: "explaining to you much of that which you used to hide from the Scripture and passing over much."

Notice the balance in that sentence. The Prophet ﷺ exposed the places where, in Ibn Kathir's words, "they altered, distorted, changed and lied about Allah" — but he also *ignored* much of what they had changed, "since it would not bring about any benefit if it was explained." Revelation is not an exercise in humiliation; it corrects what needs correcting and mercifully passes over the rest.

What kind of thing had been hidden? Ibn Kathir gives a concrete example: in his Mustadrak, Al-Hakim recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said, "He who disbelieves in stoning (the adulterer to death) will have inadvertently disbelieved in the Qur'an," citing this very ayah — "and stoning was among the things that they used to hide." Al-Hakim said, "Its chain is Sahih, and they did not record it." The ruling of stoning stood in their own Scripture; concealing it was exactly the kind of suppression ayah 15 describes.

Then Allah names what has come: "a light and a plain Book." Ayah 16 unfolds what this light does, and Ibn Kathir traces its three movements as one continuous rescue. Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to "ways of peace" — meaning, ways of safety and righteousness. He brings them "out of darkness... unto light" by His permission. And He sets them on "a straight path." Ibn Kathir sums it up beautifully: Allah "saves them from destruction and explains to them the best, most clear path. Therefore, He protects them from what they fear, and brings about the best of what they long for, all the while ridding them of misguidance and directing them to the best, most righteous state of being." Guidance, in other words, is not only information — it is protection from what you fear and delivery of what you long for.

Note also the condition in ayah 16: this guidance is for those who *seek His pleasure*. The light has come to everyone; it illuminates those who turn toward it.

## "Allah is the Messiah, son of Maryam" (ayah 17)

Having offered the light, the passage now confronts what blocks it. Ayah 17 declares plainly that those who say "Allah is the Messiah, son of Maryam" have fallen into disbelief — for they have taken 'Isa, "one of Allah's servants and creatures," to be Allah Himself. As Ibn Kathir says, "Allah is holier than what they attribute to Him."

The refutation that follows is an argument from power. "Say: Who then has the least power against Allah, if He were to destroy the Messiah, son of Maryam, his mother, and all those who are on the earth together?" If Allah willed that, who could stop Him? Whatever can be overtaken by its Lord's decree cannot *be* that Lord.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out several subtleties here. First, although the verse refutes the belief of one sect among the Christians — that the Masih is divine — the argument it uses "virtually covers the false beliefs of all sects" against Tauhid, the Oneness of Allah: whether the claim is a divine son or one of three gods, the same reasoning demolishes it.

Second, why are the Masih and his blessed mother mentioned *together*? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two wisdoms. One: it reflects the humility of 'Isa (peace be upon him) before Allah — he could never think of saving himself against Allah's will, nor his mother, whose care a good son holds dearer than his own life. Two: it simultaneously refutes the sect that took Sayyidah Maryam herself as one of three Gods.

Third, the verse speaks of their death as a *supposition* ("if He were to destroy...") even though Maryam had in fact already passed away by the time of revelation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains this either as *taghlib* — a superimposition, where the real intent concerns 'Isa (whose death lay in the future) and his mother is mentioned as a corollary — or as meaning: just as We made death take Maryam, it lies within Our power to make it overtake the Masih and all creation.

Finally, the clause "He creates what He wills" answers the deepest root of the error. Christians reasoned that because 'Isa was born without a father, against the operative laws of nature, he must be more than human. This one sentence replies that Allah's power to create is perfect and comprehensive — He creates what He wills, how He wills. The Qur'an makes the same point elsewhere: "Surely, the case of 'Isa, in the sight of Allah, is like the case of Adam" (3:59) — for Allah created Adam (peace be upon him) without father *or* mother. A miraculous birth proves the power of the Creator, not the divinity of the created. "He is the Creator and the Master and the most worthy of worship. No one else can be associated with His Divinity as a partner or sharer."

## "We are the children of Allah and His loved ones" (ayah 18)

The second claim is subtler: not deifying a man, but presuming a privileged status. The Jews and Christians said, "We are the children of Allah and His loved ones" — meaning, as Ibn Kathir explains, "We are the followers of Allah's Prophets, who are His children, whom He takes care of. He also loves us."

Ibn Kathir traces where this language came from and how it was twisted. The People of the Book had in their Book that Allah said to His servant Isra'il, "You are my firstborn" — "but they explained this statement in an improper manner and altered its meaning." Some of the People of the Book who later became Muslims clarified that such wording "only indicates honor and respect, as is common in their speech at that time." Likewise the Christians report that 'Isa said, "I will go back to my father and your father" — meaning, *my Lord and your Lord*; and tellingly, they never claimed sonship for themselves in the sense they claimed it for 'Isa. Expressions of nearness had been hardened into a doctrine of lineage and entitlement.

The Qur'an's reply is devastatingly simple: "Say: Why then does He punish you for your sins?" If you were truly Allah's children and beloved, why the punishment your own scriptures and history record — why, as Ibn Kathir puts it, would the Fire be prepared for disbelief and false claims? A beloved child is not dealt with as a sinner is dealt with. Then the verdict: "Nay, you are but human beings of those He has created" — you are like the rest of the children of Adam, and Allah is the Lord of all His creation. "He forgives whom He wills and He punishes whom He wills": no ancestry, label, or communal identity overrides His judgment. The ayah closes as ayah 17 did — dominion belongs to Allah, "and to Him is the return," where, in Ibn Kathir's words, He will judge as "the Most Just Who is never wrong in His judgment."

## After a break in the messengers (ayah 19)

The passage now returns to its opening call — "O People of the Book! Our Messenger has indeed come to you" — but adds a phrase that sets this moment in history: *'ala fatratin min ar-rusul*, "after a break in (the series of) Messengers."

**The word.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *fatrah* literally means to slacken, become dormant, or suspend an activity. Here it signifies the suspension of prophethood in the interval between 'Isa (peace be upon him) and the Last of the Prophets, Muhammad ﷺ.

**How long was the gap?** Ibn Kathir records a range of reports: Abu 'Uthman An-Nahdi and Qatadah said six hundred years — and Al-Bukhari recorded this from Salman Al-Farisi; Qatadah (in another report) said five hundred and sixty; Ma'mar said five hundred and forty; others said six hundred and twenty. Ibn Kathir harmonizes them: some counted solar years and others lunar, and roughly three years' difference accrues per century between the two calendars — just as the Qur'an says of the People of the Cave, "they stayed in their Cave three hundred years, adding nine" (18:25), the nine being the lunar adjustment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds perspective from Qurtubi: Ibn 'Abbas related that in the seventeen hundred years between Musa and 'Isa (peace be upon them), prophets came *without any gap* — a thousand prophets to Bani Isra'il alone, besides those sent to other peoples. Never before had so long a stretch gone unvisited by a prophet. The silence before Muhammad ﷺ was historically unprecedented.

**Was there really no prophet in between?** In the Sahih collected by Al-Bukhari, Abu Hurayrah reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I, among all people, have the most right to the son of Maryam, for there was no Prophet between him and I." Ibn Kathir notes this hadith refutes the claim of Al-Quda'i and others that a prophet named Khalid bin Sinan came after 'Isa; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds (citing Ruh al-Ma'ani) that Khalid ibn Sinan's prophethood may be accepted, but he came *before* 'Isa, not after. And the three "messengers" of Surah Ya Sin were envoys sent by 'Isa himself — messengers only in the literal sense of bearers of a message.

**The state of the world.** Ibn Kathir paints the scene into which the Prophet ﷺ was sent: "no Prophet, clear path, or unchanged religions. Idol worshipping, fire worshipping and cross worshipping flourished... Evil had filled the earth by then, and tyranny and ignorance had touched all the servants, except a few of those who remained loyal to the true teachings of previous Prophets, such as some Jewish rabbis, Christian priests and Sabian monks." He cites the long hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from 'Iyad bin Himar Al-Mujash'i, in which the Prophet ﷺ related that Allah said: "I created all My servants Hunafa (monotheists). But the devils came to them and deviated them from their religion..." and that Allah "looked at the people of the earth and disliked them all, the Arabs and non-Arabs among them, except a few from among the Children of Israel" — or, as Muslim recorded it, a few among the People of the Book. Against that darkness, Ibn Kathir says, "the bounty of sending Muhammad ﷺ was the perfect bounty at a time when he was needed the most."

**The excuse removed.** The ayah gives the reason for this timing: "lest you say: 'There came to us no bringer of glad tidings and no warner.'" No one can now stand before Allah claiming they were left without guidance — "But now has come unto you a bringer of glad tidings and a warner." On the closing words, "And Allah is able to do all things," Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Jarir: it means, "I am able to punish those who disobey Me and to reward those who obey Me."

**Who is excused for the gap?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a juristic point from the verse: people who lived in the fatrah, unreached by any prophet or preserved law, may be excusable — on the condition that they did not fall into Shirk, associating partners with Allah, since Tauhid "needs no reported proof": any human being who ponders can reason his way to the Oneness of Allah. The majority of jurists incline to the hope that such people will be forgiven if they adhered to whatever survived of the religion of Musa or 'Isa and were not hostile to Tauhid. But then a question: the Jews and Christians *had* the Torah and the Evangel and their scholars — how could they plead ignorance? The answer given is that by the Prophet's ﷺ time the original Torah and Evangel had gone extinct in practice; what circulated was altered text and false narrative, "no better than its extinction" — though some scholars, including Ibn Taymiyyah, held that original copies survived in some places.

**The proof hidden in the timing.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with a reflection worth sitting with. The Prophet ﷺ appeared in the notorious Jahiliyyah — the Age of Ignorance — among a people described as spoiled, self-centered and uncompromising, in a land without the light of knowledge or faith. Yet the blessing of his company and the light of his mission transformed that very people, in a very short time, into "role models and teachers for the whole world in all departments of life." The commentary offers an image: imagine a physician who takes a hopeless patient, in a place with no instruments and no medicines, and not only restores him to health but raises him into an expert healer himself — "who can doubt the perfection of the master healer!" The transformation of Arabia is itself a widely witnessed proof of his prophethood ﷺ; of all miracles, this one alone could compel a person to believe in him.

## Taking it in

The passage leaves the reader with three anchors. First, revelation is described as *light* — and light in ayah 16 does something: it guides to ways of peace, pulls people out of layered darknesses, and sets them on one straight path; but it does so for "those who seek His pleasure," so the seeking is ours. Second, no exalted status — not a miraculous birth, not descent from prophets, not the labels "children of Allah and His loved ones" — changes the fundamental relationship of every human being to Allah: "you are but human beings of those He has created," and He "forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills." Third, the argument that silenced the People of the Book silences every later generation too: the bringer of glad tidings and warning has come, the excuse of ignorance is gone, and the only fitting response to a light sent after six centuries of silence is to walk by it.

passages.title: Enter the Holy Land: the command and the two brave men
passages.tafsir:
This passage relives the moment when Mūsā (peace be upon him), fresh from the destruction of Pharaoh, commanded his people to enter the Holy Land that Allah had written for them — and they refused. Four voices hold the ayat together as one scene: the prophet reminding his people of Allah's favours (ayah 20), the divine command with its promise (ayah 21), the fearful excuse of the many (ayah 22), and the brave counsel of two men whom Allah had blessed (ayah 23). It is a study in how gratitude should produce courage, and what happens when it does not.

## First the reminder, then the command (ayah 20)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the order of Mūsā's speech. Before announcing the command to march, he acted "in accordance with his prophetic wisdom so crucial in giving good counsel": he reminded his people of what Allah had already done for them. These were people who had been oppressed slaves of Pharaoh for ages, who then watched their enemy drown and found themselves masters. A people carrying that memory should have found obedience easy.

Three favours are named. **"He made Prophets among you"** — a spiritual honour. Ibn Kathir explains that whenever a prophet died among the Children of Israel, another rose in his place, from the time of their father Ibrāhīm until ʿĪsā, the final prophet from among them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, citing Tafsīr Mazharī, that no other community had so many prophets, and relates a report of Ibn Abī Hātim from Aʿmash that in the period from Mūsā to ʿĪsā alone a thousand prophets were sent.

**"And made you kings"** — but how can a whole people be kings? Notice the shift the commentators observe: Allah says He made prophets *among* you (only some), yet made *you* kings (all of you). Two explanations are given. The first takes *malik* in its broader everyday sense of a man of means. ʿAbdur-Razzāq recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās explained "made you kings" as having "a servant, a wife and a house"; and in his Mustadrak, Al-Hakim recorded a report in which Ibn ʿAbbās said "a wife and a servant," and explained "gave you what He had not given to any other among the nations" as meaning *during their time* — a report Al-Hakim graded "Sahih according to the criteria of the Two Sahihs, but they did not collect it." In that age, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, every man of the Banī Isrāʼīl was like a king of his own castle. Qatādah said they were the first people to take servants. The second explanation, related in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from Maulana Ashraf ʿAlī Thānavī's Bayān al-Qurʼān, is that a nation whose own people rule is itself called sovereign — kingship belonging to a ruler is customarily attributed to his whole people. In this spirit Ibn Kathir also cites a hadith: he among you who wakes up healthy in body, safe in his family, and having the provision for that very day, is as if the world and all that was in it were collected for him. Kingship, in other words, is nearer to each of us than we think.

**"And gave you what He had not given to any other among the nations."** Does this contradict the Qurʼān's declaration that the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ is the best community raised for mankind (3:110)? Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answer: the verse means *the worlds of their own time*. The Children of Israel surpassed the Greeks, the Copts and the rest of mankind of that era; that a later community would be blessed even more does not contradict this.

## "The Holy Land which Allah has written for you" (ayah 21)

Then comes the command: "O my people! Enter the Holy Land which Allah has destined for you, and do not turn back, or you will become losers." Ibn Kathir explains the phrase *allatī kataba Allāhu lakum* — "which Allah has assigned to you" — as a promise conveyed through the words of their father Isrāʼīl that this land would be the inheritance of those among them who believe. Jerusalem had been under their control in the time of their father Yaʿqūb; the family had moved to Egypt in the days of Yūsuf, and their descendants remained there until the exodus with Mūsā. Now they were being sent home — with a guarantee of victory attached, since Allah had already written the land for them. "Do not turn back," Ibn Kathir says, means: do not flee from the fight.

Which land is "the Holy Land"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān surveys the commentators: some say Baytul-Maqdis (Jerusalem) itself; some the city of Quds and Eliah; some Arīhā, between the Jordan river and Baytul-Maqdis, one of the oldest cities of the world; others Damascus and Palestine, or Jordan; and Qatādah said the entire land of Syria. Kaʿb al-Ahbār related that he had seen in the Book of Allah (perhaps, the narration adds, the Torah) that this land is Allah's special treasure on earth, home to His very dear servants; and it is reported that when Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) climbed a mountain in Lebanon, Allah told him: look, and as far as you see, that land We have made holy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes there is no real contradiction — the whole region of Syria is the Holy Land, called "holy" because it was home to the prophets, and each narrator simply named a part or the whole.

## The scouts, the giants, and the collapse of nerve (ayah 22)

The people answered: "O Mūsā! In it are a people of great strength (*jabbārīn* — tyrants, men of enormous power), and we shall never enter it until they leave; if they leave, then we will enter."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the story as reported from the masters of tafsir — Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Ibn Abī Talhah and others. Syria and Baytul-Maqdis were then ruled by the Amalekites, an offshoot of the people of ʿĀd, unusually huge in height and build and ferocious in bearing. When Mūsā marched from Egypt, crossed the Jordan and stopped at Arīhā, he sent the twelve chiefs of the tribes — the same chiefs mentioned earlier in this sūrah — on an intelligence mission. Outside the city gate a single Amalekite man arrested all twelve and carried them to his king, who, after consultation, released them deliberately: let them go home as walking eyewitnesses of our power, so their people never dare to march.

Mūsā, forewarned by revelation of victory, was unmoved when the chiefs reported back. But he saw the danger to morale and ordered the twelve to keep what they had seen secret. Ten of them leaked it privately to their friends; the news spread; and the people collapsed into wailing — saying it would have been better to have drowned in the Nile like the people of Pharaoh than to be brought here to die. Out of that panic came the words of ayah 22.

A note of scholarly honesty belongs here. The books of tafsir at this point carry extravagant Isrāʼīlite tales about a giant named ʿAwj ibn ʿUnuq. Ibn Kathir — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records — rejected them flatly: such tales can neither be accepted by reason nor justified in the Sharīʿah; they are "a bundle of lies." The sober truth is enough: the Amalekites were remnants of ʿĀd, whose formidable stature the Qurʼān itself mentions, and one of their men was strong enough to seize twelve scouts.

## Two men who feared Allah (ayah 23)

Against the panic of a nation, two voices: "Assault them through the gate; for when you are in, victory will be yours. And put your trust in Allah, if you are believers indeed." These were Yūshaʿ (Joshua) son of Nūn and Kālib (Caleb) son of Yūfnā — so said Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ʿAtiyyah, As-Suddī, Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas and many other early and later scholars, as Ibn Kathir records. Most commentators identify them as two of the twelve scouts — the only two who had obeyed Mūsā and kept the secret.

The Qurʼān describes them with exactly two attributes, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a lesson from each. First, *alladhīna yakhāfūn* — "those who fear" — with the object of fear left unnamed. The hint: there is only one Being in all existence who truly deserves fear, Allah, the Absolute Master; no one can bring benefit or harm without His permission, so the object needs no naming. And this is the paradox the ayah embodies: the men who feared Allah were the ones telling their people not to be nervous of the giants. Second, *anʿama Allāhu ʿalayhimā* — "on whom Allah had bestowed His grace." All twelve chiefs had the same eyes, limbs, intelligence, and the company of Mūsā; ten slipped and two stood firm. Real steadfastness, then, is not a product of personal capability but a gift from Allah — though effort and deed are the condition for deserving it. The practical rule Maʿārif ul Qurʼān extracts: a person blessed with intelligence should never grow proud of it, but seek guidance in every matter from Allah alone. (Ibn Kathir also notes that it was said the phrase can be read another way — that the two were men feared and respected by their people.)

Their counsel was precise: not "be brave" in the abstract, but *enter by the gate* — why fear death before it has come? The gate of Baytul-Maqdis is not far; take those few steps, and "when you are in, victory will be yours." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two possibilities for their certainty, either of which could be true: it could have been a close assessment that the Amalekites, huge in body, were weak at heart and would flee before a surprise assault; and it is also possible that it rested on their total faith in the promise of victory Allah had already given as glad tidings through Mūsā. Notice too how they welded strategy to creed: "And put your trust in Allah, if you are believers indeed." Tawakkul — entrusting the outcome to Allah — is not a substitute for walking to the gate; it is what makes walking to the gate possible. Ibn Kathir records the sorrowful sequel in a single line: this advice did not benefit them in the least.

## Living this passage

Ibn Kathir observes the bitter irony at the story's heart: these were people who had just watched Allah drown Pharaoh's army before their eyes — an enemy with many times the power of the Amalekites — yet they could not trust Him for the smaller battle, though the Messenger to whom Allah spoke directly stood among them, promising victory. Remembered blessing is meant to fund present courage; when it does not, the blessing becomes an indictment. The passage teaches that Allah's promise does not exempt us from walking to the gate — the land was *written* for them, yet the writing was for "those among you who believe."
