Hoping the Prophet ﷺ would hand down the lighter sentence, they agreed among themselves: "If he gives a ruling of flogging, then implement his decision... But if he decides that the punishment should be stoning to death, then do not accept his decision." This is precisely the scheming the ayah quotes back at them: *"If you are given this, take it, but if you are not given this, then beware!"* Maʿārif, citing al-Baghawi, adds that the couple were from the Jews of Khaybar and belonged to an influential family, and that the people of Khaybar sent the case to their clansmen of Banu Qurayzah to have it settled by the Prophet ﷺ — with the same instruction: accept the verdict if the punishment is light, reject it otherwise.

## The day the Tawrah was brought

The hadith of this second case is one of the most vivid scenes in the seerah. Malik reported it from Nafi' from 'Abdullah bin 'Umar; Al-Bukhari and Muslim also collected it, and this is Al-Bukhari's wording. The Prophet ﷺ asked the Jews, "What do you find of the ruling about stoning in the Tawrah?" They claimed it prescribed only exposure and flogging. 'Abdullah bin Salam said, "You lie. The Tawrah mentions stoning, so bring the Tawrah." When it was brought, one of them hid the verse of stoning with his hand and recited what came before and after it. "Remove your hand," Ibn Salam said — and there beneath it was the verse of stoning. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ decided that the adulterers be stoned, and Ibn 'Umar says: "I saw that man shading the woman from the stones with his body." In the narration recorded by Muslim, the Jews had described their own custom for adulterers: "We expose them, carry them (on donkeys) backwards and parade them in public" — yet under the reader's hand lay the verse of stoning all along.

Abu Dawud's narration adds a detail of the Prophet's ﷺ reverence for genuine revelation even in the hands of those who betrayed it: when the Tawrah was brought to him, he removed the pillow from under himself, placed the scripture upon it, and said, "I trust you and He Who revealed it to you."

Ibn Kathir draws out the meaning carefully: the Prophet ﷺ did not rule by the Tawrah to honour the Jews in what they believed — "the Jews were commanded to follow the Law of Muhammad ﷺ only." He did so because Allah commanded him, and to make them admit, publicly and from their own Book, what they had collaborated to hide, deny, and exclude from implementing for all that time. Maʿārif preserves the confession itself, on the tongue of Ibn Surya — of whom the Jews themselves said, "Of the learned people among Jews, there is no scholar greater than him on this earth." Put on oath, he admitted the Torah commanded stoning, and explained how the law had died: a prince of theirs committed the crime and was spared; when an ordinary man was later sentenced to stoning, the criminal's supporters demanded the prince be punished first; and rather than apply the law equally, they sat together and invented one light punishment for everyone — some beating, and a procession with the culprits' faces blackened with soot. Law was bent for the powerful, and then broken for all.

## Four traits of the schemers

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the passage as an anatomy of four evil traits, each carrying a warning for Muslims.

**"Listeners of the lie" (sammāʿūn lil-kadhib).** They habitually listened to and accepted falsehood — blind followers of leaders they could see were openly negating the Torah's injunctions. The lesson Maʿārif draws: ordinary people must follow scholars, but they are responsible for *whom* they follow. A person searches out the best physician when sick and the best lawyer when sued, yet hands the reins of his faith to anyone with a confident manner, without investigating his learning or integrity. Whoever does investigate sincerely and is still misled is excused — the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that the sin then falls on the one who gave the wrong ruling — but whoever never bothered to check shares fully in the consequences.

**"Listeners for other people who have not come to you."** Ibn Kathir gives two readings: they listened on behalf of absent people, or conveyed the Prophet's ﷺ words to enemies who never attended his gatherings. Maʿārif is blunter: the deputation were spies for arrogant senders who stayed away, seeking only to learn the verdict so their masters could decide whether to accept it. The warning: whoever asks a scholar for a ruling must intend to follow the command of Allah and His Messenger. Collecting opinions until one matches your desire is "an open demonstration of following one's own desiring self — and Shaytan."

**"They change the words from their places."** Ibn Kathir: altering meanings and knowingly distorting them *after* comprehending them. Maʿārif notes this covers both tampering with the text itself and leaving the words intact while forcing absurd interpretations onto them — the Jews did both. Against this stands Allah's own guarantee for the Qur'an: its wording is secured in countless copies and millions of memories, and for its meaning Allah has arranged that a group in this Ummah will always remain armed with the correct understanding, until the Day of Qiyamah.

**"Devourers of suht" (ayah 42).** Suht here means bribery — so said Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Dahhak among the early authorities. The word's root sense is to uproot or destroy something totally, as in Allah's warning "lest He destroy you (fa-yus-hitakum) with a punishment" (20:61). Bribery earned this name, Maʿārif explains, because it destroys giver and taker alike and then uproots the whole society: when bribery gains currency, law freezes, and when law stands suspended nothing remains safe — life, property, or honour. Maʿārif also relates, citing al-Jassas, a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said that Almighty Allah causes His curse to fall on the giver and taker of a bribe and on the one who acts as broker between them. The juristic definition is precise: taking compensation for what you were already duty-bound to do — the official taking something from the person whose case he is handling, even parents taking "compensation" for marrying off their daughter, whose marriage is already their responsibility. Ibn Kathir adds the spiritual diagnosis: if a person is like this, "how can Allah cleanse his heart and accept his supplication?"

## Judge between them, or turn away

Ayah 42 gives the Prophet ﷺ a striking choice: judge between them, or turn away — and if they are ignored, "they cannot hurt you in the least," for they never sought truth, only a ruling that matched their desires. But if he judges: *"judge with justice between them. Verily, Allah loves those who act justly."* Ibn Kathir underlines the weight of this: justice was owed even to these people — "even if the Jews were unjust and outcasts from the path of fairness." The very people plotting against the court were entitled to perfect fairness in it.

The scholars discussed how this choice relates to the later command, "And judge between them by what Allah has revealed" (5:49). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, As-Suddi, Zayd bin Aslam, 'Ata' Al-Khurasani and others held that the option in ayah 42 was abrogated by that verse. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the reconciliation of Imam Abu Bakr al-Jassas: no abrogation is needed, because the two verses address two situations. The choice concerns non-Muslims like Banu Qurayzah and Banu Nadir at that time — outsiders bound only by a no-war pact, for whom the Islamic authority bore no judicial responsibility. The command concerns dhimmis, non-Muslim citizens of the Islamic state, whose rights the state is duty-bound to protect; their cases cannot simply be turned away. In either case, whenever the Prophet ﷺ did judge, he was to judge by what Allah revealed — his own Shari'ah — not by the parties' wishes. Maʿārif adds a careful distinction from his practice: punishments for crimes like killing and adultery belong to the common law of the land, applied to all alike, but the Prophet ﷺ never interfered in the personal religious law of non-Muslims — he accepted their marriages as valid and left them free in what their religion permitted them.

## The question that unmasks them (ayah 43)

Then comes the passage's piercing irony: *"But how do they come to you for a decision while they have the Tawrah, in which is the decision of Allah; yet even after that they turn away."* Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here chastises the Jews for their false ideas and deviant desires: they abandon what they themselves believe is true in their Book — the Book they claim is their eternal Law, which they are always commanded to adhere to — and prefer other laws over it, "although they believe that these other laws are not correct and do not apply to them." Hence the verdict that closes the ayah: "For they are not believers." Their problem was never lack of knowledge — Ibn Surya knew the ruling to the letter. It was that desire, not revelation, sat on the throne of their hearts.

## Living it

The Qur'an tells this story about others so that we do not repeat it ourselves — Maʿārif states plainly that though the passage describes the Jews, "the message behind it is actually beamed at Muslims." Its tests are perennial. Do I accept Allah's ruling only when it lands in my favour — taking the verdict "if you are given this" and bewaring when I am not? Do I shop between muftis for the answer my desires already chose? Have I verified the learning and integrity of those I take my religion from? Do I touch bribery — that "suht" which uproots hearts and nations alike? And when I hold power over a dispute, do I give even my adversary flawless fairness? The passage closes ayah 42 with the standard and the reward in a single breath: "And if you judge, judge with justice between them. Verily, Allah loves those who act justly."

passages.title: Judging by what Allah has revealed
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the heart of Sūrah al-Māʾidah's third section: Allah surveys the three great revealed Books — the Torah, the Injīl (Gospel), and finally the Qurʼān — and binds all three communities to a single principle: **judge by what Allah has revealed**. What holds ayat 44–50 together is a refrain that falls three times like a hammer: whoever does not judge by what Allah has sent down — "such are the disbelievers" (44), "such are the unjust" (45), "such are the rebellious" (47) — before the passage turns to the Prophet ﷺ himself and closes with the piercing question of ayah 50: "Is it the judgment of ignorance they seek?"

## The story behind the revelation

Ibn Kathir records two occasions, and concludes that both together lie behind these ayat.

**The two adulterers and the hidden verse.** A Jewish man and woman had committed adultery. The Torah's ruling was stoning, but the Jews had changed the law in their own Book from stoning to death to a hundred lashes and making the offenders ride a donkey facing the animal's back, parading them in public. When this case arose after the Hijrah, they said to one another: let us take it to Muhammad — if he rules flogging, accept it and make it a proof before Allah; if he rules stoning, refuse. In the hadith which Al-Bukhari and Muslim both collected from ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked them, "What do you find of the ruling about stoning in the Tawrah?" They claimed it prescribed only exposure and flogging. ʿAbdullah bin Salam said, "You lie. The Tawrah mentions stoning, so bring the Tawrah." When it was brought, the reader hid the verse of stoning with his hand and recited what was before and after it. "Remove your hand," said ʿAbdullah bin Salam — and there was the verse. The Prophet ﷺ ruled that the two be stoned, and Ibn ʿUmar says he saw the man shielding the woman from the stones with his own body. In Abu Dawud's narration, when the Torah was brought, the Prophet ﷺ removed the pillow he was sitting on and placed the scripture upon it, saying, "I trust you and He Who revealed it to you" — an extraordinary gesture of reverence toward the original revelation even while its custodians were betraying it.

Ibn Kathir is careful about what this ruling meant: the Prophet ﷺ did not judge by the Torah to honor the Jews in their religion — they were obliged to follow his Law. He did it because Allah commanded him to, and to make them admit publicly to the very ruling they had collaborated to hide for so long.

**The unequal blood money.** Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas the second occasion: two Jewish tribes — identified in the narration of Ibn Jarir (also recorded by Ahmad, Abu Dawud and An-Nasaʼi) as Banu An-Nadir and Banu Qurayzah — had an old arrangement from the days before Islam. The stronger tribe, having defeated the weaker, imposed a treaty: a victim from the mighty tribe was worth one hundred wasaq of gold in blood money, a victim from the weak tribe only fifty — a wasaq being a unit of weight, each roughly three kilograms. When both became subject to the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah and a new killing occurred, the weaker tribe refused the old terms: "How can two groups of the same religion, one lineage and one land, have a diyah for some that is half that of others? We only agreed because you oppressed us." The stronger tribe sent hypocrites to sound out the Prophet's ﷺ judgment first — accept it if favorable, reject it if not. Allah exposed their plot, and the Prophet ﷺ compelled them to equality: one diyah for both tribes. Ibn ʿAbbas swore: "By Allah, it is because of their problem that Allah sent down these verses."

Both stories share one anatomy: people who possess Allah's ruling, know it is Allah's ruling, and shop for a different one because it suits their power or their desires. That is the disease this whole passage diagnoses.

## Ayah 44: the Torah and its guardians

Allah opens by praising the Torah He sent down: "in it was guidance and light." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a subtle implication: the later abrogation of the Torah's law was never because of any defect in the Torah itself — it is a Book from the same Revealer — but because Divine wisdom changes subsidiary rulings as times change.

By this Torah judged "the Prophets who submitted themselves" — the prophets of the Children of Israel, who, as Ibn Kathir notes, never deviated from it or altered it — and after them two classes of deputies: the **Rabbāniyyūn** and the **Aḥbār**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks these beautifully. *Rabbāniyy* is derived from *Rabb* (Lord) and means a "man of Allah" — one devoted chiefly to worship, remembrance and deeds, with the knowledge his path requires. *Aḥbār* is the plural of *ḥibr*, the Jewish term for a religious scholar — one devoted chiefly to knowledge, teaching and training others. In principle every man of Allah must be learned and every scholar must live his knowledge; the two titles simply name a person by his dominant occupation. From this Maʿārif draws a wider lesson: there is no real dichotomy between the scholars and the people of the spiritual path — ʿulamāʼ and mashāʼikh converge on one purpose, obedience to Allah and His Messenger.

These guardians judged by the Torah "because they were entrusted with the protection of Allah's Book, and they were witnesses thereto." The contemporary Jewish leadership, by contrast, had betrayed that trust — and Maʿārif names the two motives with unsparing clarity: **love of position** (if they followed the Prophet ﷺ they would become ordinary Muslims and lose their leadership over their people) and **love of money** (they had almost made a profession of bending the Torah's provisions to suit influential people in exchange for bribes — the *suḥt*, "ill-gotten gain," that ayah 42 condemned, which Ibn Masʿud explained as bribery). Hence the double command that follows: "So fear not men, but fear Me; and do not sell My verses for a paltry price."

## "Kufr" and "kufr less than kufr": the refrain understood

The verse ends: "And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed — such are the disbelievers (al-kāfirūn)." Who is meant? Ibn Kathir gathers the early authorities. Al-Baraʼ bin ʿAzib, Hudhayfah, Ibn ʿAbbas, Al-Hasan Al-Basri and others said these ayat were revealed about the People of the Book — and Al-Hasan added that they also apply to us; Ibrahim An-Nakhaʿi put it as: "revealed about the Children of Israel, and Allah accepted them for this Ummah."

But is every failure to rule by revelation outright disbelief? Here the Salaf drew a crucial distinction. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Whoever *rejects* what Allah has revealed has committed kufr; and whoever accepts what Allah has revealed but does not rule by it is a ẓālim (unjust) and a fāsiq (rebellious sinner)." Tawus related that when Ibn ʿAbbas was asked about the verse, he answered, "It is an act of kufr" — and Ibn Tawus added, "not like those who disbelieve in Allah, His angels, His Books and His Messengers." ʿAtaʼ put it memorably: "There is kufr and kufr less than kufr; ẓulm and ẓulm less than ẓulm; fisq and fisq less than fisq." And Tawus said of the verse: "This is not the kufr that annuls one's religion." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the same rule as settled doctrine: ruling contrary to what Allah revealed is disbelief when joined to the belief that Allah's ruling is not true; it is injustice and sin when one accepts the ruling as true but violates it in practice. This balanced position — taking the threat with full seriousness while refusing to excommunicate every sinful ruler — is the mainstream understanding of the refrain.

## Ayah 45: a life for a life

Allah then cites what He ordained in the Torah: "a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth — and for wounds, equal retaliation (qiṣāṣ)." The mention is a direct exposure of the blood-money fraud: the equality the tribes were evading was written in their own Book. Their coming to the Prophet ﷺ, as Maʿārif says, was never sincere arbitration — only a ruse to escape a ruling they already possessed.

Ibn Kathir then shows how this Torah ruling lives on in Islam. Imam Abu Nasr bin As-Sabbagh recorded in his book Ash-Shamil the scholars' agreement that this ayah is implemented in our Law, and the Imams agree that a man is killed in retaliation for a woman he kills — supported by the hadith An-Nasaʼi recorded, that the Messenger ﷺ had written in the book he gave ʿAmr bin Hazm: "The man is killed for the woman." Imam Ahmad recorded the moving story that Anas bin Malik told of his aunt Ar-Rabiʿ, who broke a girl's tooth; when the girl's relatives refused to forgive, the Prophet ﷺ ordered retaliation. Ar-Rabiʿ's brother, Anas bin An-Nadr, asked, "O Allah's Messenger! Will the tooth of Ar-Rabiʿ be broken?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ answered, "O Anas! The Book of Allah prescribes retaliation." Anas said, "No, by Him Who has sent you with the Truth, her tooth will not be broken." Then the girl's relatives relented and pardoned her, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "There are some of Allah's servants who, if they take an oath by Allah, Allah fulfils them" — a hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs. The law is firm, yet the door of forgiveness stands open at every step.

Two further rulings from Ibn Kathir: retaliation for a wound waits until the victim's wound heals (Imam Ahmad recorded that a man stabbed in the leg demanded retaliation early despite the Prophet's ﷺ instruction "Not until you heal," was granted it, then limped — and was told his limp carried no compensation, for he had disobeyed). And the crown of the verse: "whoever remits it as charity, it is expiation for him." Ibn ʿAbbas explained: the pardon expiates the aggressor's sin and earns the victim reward with Allah. Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿUbadah bin As-Samit that the Messenger ﷺ said that any man who suffers a bodily wound and forgoes his right of retaliation as charity, Allah pardons him in the measure of what he forgave (also recorded by An-Nasaʼi and Ibn Jarir).

## Ayat 46–47: ʿIsa and the people of the Injīl

"In their footsteps" — the footsteps of Israel's prophets — Allah sent ʿIsa son of Maryam, confirming the Torah before him, and gave him the Injīl, "in which was guidance and light." Ibn Kathir explains: a guidance that directs to truth, a light that removes doubts and settles disputes. ʿIsa adhered to the Torah except in the few matters where he clarified the truth for a differing Israel — as the Qurʼān quotes him saying elsewhere, "to make lawful to you part of what was forbidden to you" (3:50, cited by Ibn Kathir) — so the scholars say the Injīl abrogated some rulings of the Torah. Then the same standard is applied to the second community: "Let the people of the Injīl judge by what Allah revealed in it" — either, says Ibn Kathir, a command binding them in their own era, or a command to follow everything in it, including its good news of Muhammad ﷺ and the obligation to follow him when sent. And the refrain falls a third time: whoever does not judge by what Allah revealed — "such are the fāsiqūn," the rebellious who prefer falsehood and abandon truth. Ibn Kathir notes this third clause was revealed about the Christians, as the context shows.

## Ayah 48: the Qurʼān as Muhaymin

Now the address turns to the Prophet ﷺ. The Qurʼān comes "confirming the Scripture before it and *muhaymin* over it." Ibn Kathir assembles the explanations of Ibn ʿAbbas and the early commentators: *muhaymin* means **trustworthy**, **witness**, and **dominant** — and, he says, the word includes them all. Ibn Jarir gives the practical criterion: whatever in the previous Books agrees with the Qurʼān is true; whatever contradicts it is false. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the historical point: after the people of the Torah and Injīl altered their Books, it is the Qurʼān alone that stands as overseer and protector, exposing the alterations — so that even today the true teachings of those Books survive only through the Qurʼān. And unlike them, this Book is divinely guarded: "Verily We have sent down the Reminder, and surely We will guard it" (15:9).

Then the command: "So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, diverging from the truth that has come to you." Ibn ʿAbbas said the Prophet ﷺ had previously had the choice to judge between the People of the Book or turn away; with this ayah he was commanded to judge between them by our Book.

**"To each of you We have prescribed a law and a way."** Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the passage's deepest question: if all prophets come from the one Allah, why do their Laws differ, and why does one abrogate another? The answer is in the verse itself: "Had Allah willed, He would have made you one nation — but that He may test you in what He has given you." Differing Sharīʿahs are a test of *true servanthood*: the real worshipper obeys the command itself, not his attachment to an inherited form. Prayer at a forbidden time earns sin, not reward; fasting on the two ʿĪds is unlawful; standing at ʿArafāt is the greatest worship on the ninth of Dhul-Ḥijjah and no special act on any other day. Worship is not an end in itself — its whole reality is obedience to Allah's command. Whoever grasps this can let go of a beloved ancestral law the moment Allah sends a new one; whoever misses it clings to habit and custom until, as with the earlier communities, innovation disfigures the religion itself. Maʿārif adds a second wisdom: human temperaments differ across ages, so subsidiary rulings were adjusted for each era — and abrogation (*naskh*) implies no change of the Divine mind, any more than a physician's staged prescription implies the first medicine was a mistake: each was exactly right for its stage, and the Physician knew the whole course from the beginning. Hence the verse's conclusion is not anxiety but energy: "so race one another in good deeds. To Allah is your return, and He will inform you of that over which you used to differ."

## Ayat 49–50: the last temptation, and the judgment of Jāhiliyyah

Ayah 49 repeats the command to judge by revelation and adds a warning: "beware of them lest they tempt you away from *some* of what Allah has sent down to you." Ibn Kathir records the occasion from Ibn ʿAbbas: Kaʿb bin Asad, Ibn Saluba, ʿAbdullah bin Surya and Shas bin Qays — scholars, noblemen and chiefs of the Jews — came to the Prophet ﷺ with an offer: "If we follow you, the Jews will follow us. We have a dispute with some of our people; rule in our favor and we will believe in you." A whole community's conversion, for the price of one bent verdict. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ refused, and these ayat came down. Even a seemingly noble end — mass acceptance of Islam — cannot purchase a single departure from Allah's Law. And if they turn away from a just ruling? "Then know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins" — their rejection is itself, in Allah's wise decree, a punishment drawn by their own past deeds.

Ayah 50 closes the passage with a question that needs no answer: "Is it the judgment of Jāhiliyyah (the pre-Islamic ignorance) they seek? And who is better in judgment than Allah for a people of certain faith?" Ibn Kathir's comment reaches beyond the seventh century: whoever abandons Allah's commandments — which embrace every good and forbid every evil — for opinions, desires and man-made customs has done exactly this. He gives the famous example of the Mongols, who ruled by the *Yāsiq* of Genghis Khan, a code containing rulings derived from various religions — Judaism, Christianity, Islam — and many from the king's own opinion and desires, which his descendants preferred to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ. And he cites the hadith which Al-Hafiz Abu Al-Qasim At-Tabarani recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas — Al-Bukhari recording a similar narration with some addition — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The most hated person to Allah is the Muslim who seeks the ways of the days of ignorance, and he who seeks to shed the blood of a person without justification."

The final clause is the key that turns the whole passage: "for a people who have **certainty** (yūqinūn)." Ibn Kathir asks: who could judge better than Allah — for those certain that He is the best of judges, more merciful to His creation than a mother to her own child, perfect in knowledge, able over all things, just in every matter? The measure of our contentment with Allah's rulings is the measure of our certainty about Allah Himself. Where certainty lives, His judgment is not a burden but a light — the same "guidance and light" that ran through Torah, Injīl and Qurʼān alike.

passages.title: True allegiance: Allah, His Messenger, and the believers
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These eight ayat answer one question from every angle: **where does a believer's deepest loyalty belong?** Ayah 51 forbids taking Jews and Christians as *awliyāʾ* — intimate allies and protectors. Ayat 52–53 expose the hypocrites who rushed to keep such alliances "just in case". Ayah 54 declares that even mass desertion cannot harm this religion, for Allah will simply raise up a people He loves. Then comes the positive answer at the centre of the passage, ayah 55: *"Your only guardian is Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe."* Ayah 56 promises that whoever holds to that allegiance belongs to the party of Allah, and the party of Allah will prevail. Ayat 57–58 close by naming the people with whom intimacy is impossible: those who treat the religion itself — even the call to prayer — as a joke. The passage moves from prohibition, to exposure, to promise, to the true object of loyalty, and back to the reason the prohibition exists at all.

## What the prohibition means — and what it does not

The key term is *muwālāt*, from the same root as *walī* (guardian, protector, close ally). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to define the boundary. Muslims may — indeed should — deal with non-Muslims "in the spirit of tolerance, sympathy, goodwill, equity, justice, favour and kindness". What is forbidden is "the kind of fast friendship and indiscriminating intimacy which may garble the distinctive hallmarks of Islam" — what the scholars call *tark al-muwālāt*, refraining from that deep, identity-dissolving attachment. The ayah itself gives the reasoning: "they are but friends of each other" — such communities reserve their real allegiance for their own, so a Muslim who pours his whole loyalty into them gives what will not be reciprocated, and loses his own footing. Hence the stern warning: *"whoever of you takes them as allies is one of them."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that such a person is, in the sight of Islam, fit to be counted with them rather than with the Muslims.

How seriously the early generation took this is shown in a report Ibn Kathir cites from Ibn Abi Hatim. ʿUmar asked Abu Musa al-Ashʿari for his accounts; the fine work turned out to be that of a Christian scribe. When ʿUmar asked that the scribe read a letter publicly in the masjid and learned why he could not, he admonished Abu Musa and told him to dismiss the man — then recited this very ayah. The issue was not the man's skill, which ʿUmar had just praised, but placing the community's sensitive affairs inside a bond of trust the ayah had closed. Ibn Kathir also relays the piercing words of ʿAbdullah bin ʿUtbah: "Let one of you beware that he might be a Jew or a Christian, while unaware" — understood as a warning about this ayah: loyalty drifts quietly, and a person can cross the line without noticing.

## The occasion: a conspiracy in Madinah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, reporting from ʿIkrimah through Ibn Jarir, gives the moment behind ayat 51–52. After settling in Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ made a treaty with the neighbouring Jews and Christians: neither side would fight the other or aid its enemies; each would defend the other against aggressors. For a time it held. Then the Jews of Banu Qurayzah made a secret pact with the pagans of Makkah, writing to invite them against the Muslims — while at the same time maintaining warm personal "friendships" with many Muslims in Madinah, friendships that served as a front for gathering intelligence. When the Prophet ﷺ learned of the conspiracy, he sent men to confront them, and this ayah came down, cutting the channel through which sensitive information had been leaking. Companions such as ʿUbadah ibn Samit openly renounced their old treaty ties. But the hypocrites hedged. ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul said he saw danger in cutting off these people and would not do it.

That is the scene ayah 52 paints: *"You see those in whose hearts is a disease racing towards them, saying: We fear a misfortune may strike us."* Ibn Kathir defines the disease — doubt, hesitation, hypocrisy — and unpacks the excuse: they feared the disbelievers might yet defeat the Muslims, so they wanted credit banked with the Jews and Christians to cash in on that day. Allah's reply is almost gentle in form and devastating in content: *"Perhaps Allah will bring the victory, or a decision from Himself"* — the victory being, according to As-Suddi (cited by Ibn Kathir), the conquest of Makkah, and the decision the imposition of the jizyah. When that day came, the hypocrites were left *nādimīn* — regretful — over the calculations they had hidden in their hearts, which had bought them nothing but exposure. And in ayah 53 the believers, seeing the pretence collapse, ask in astonishment: *"Are these the ones who swore their strongest oaths by Allah that they were with you?"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the conquest of Makkah and the disgrace of the hypocrites foretold here were witnessed by everyone only a short time later.

## Ayah 54: the religion does not depend on you

Ayah 54 lifts the whole discussion to a higher plane. If anyone abandons this faith, Islam loses nothing: *"Allah will bring a people He loves and who love Him."* Ibn Kathir reads it as a statement of Allah's absolute ability — He will replace deserters with those "better, mightier and more righteous", just as He says elsewhere, "If He wills, He can remove you and bring a new creation." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it memorably: Allah's purposes depend on no individual and no party; "when He so wishes, He can make straws work for beams and logs."

The ayah then describes this beloved people by four qualities, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on each:

**They love Allah and He loves them.** Our love for Allah can be cultivated — by contemplating His majesty, His power, His blessings. And His love for us, seemingly beyond our reach, has a stated means: *"Say: if you love Allah, follow me; Allah shall love you"* (3:31). The road to being loved by Allah is the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ made the pivot of one's life.

**Humble towards the believers, stern towards the disbelievers.** The Arabic repays attention. *Adhillah* can be the plural of *dhalīl* (lowly) or *dhalūl* (soft, tractable, easily led) — and the majority of commentators, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, take the second sense here: with fellow believers these people are yielding, willing to set aside a dispute even when they are in the right. *Aʿizzah*, plural of *ʿazīz*, means the opposite: firm, unyielding — the enemies of the religion cannot bend or manipulate them. Their love and hate are not for themselves but for Allah, His Messenger, and His religion. Ibn Kathir links this to 48:29 — "severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves" — and records the description of the Prophet ﷺ as "the smiling fighter": smiling to his allies, fighting his enemies.

**They strive in the way of Allah**, and — the fourth quality — **they fear no blamer's blame**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a sharp psychological observation here: leaders of a cause can endure prison and torture from the enemy, yet falter before the taunts of their own people. These people do not. Ibn Kathir cites here the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad in which Abu Dharr said his beloved friend ﷺ commanded him seven things — among them to love the poor, to look at those below him and not above, to keep the ties of kinship even when cut, to speak the truth even when bitter, and "not to fear the blame of anyone for the sake of Allah."

And the ayah closes: *"That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills."* These qualities are not self-made achievements but gifts of grace.

**The prophecy fulfilled.** The majority of commentators, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, saw in this ayah a prophecy of the *fitnah* of apostasy that erupted after the Prophet's ﷺ passing — false prophets like Musaylimah the Liar, Aswad al-ʿAnsi, and Tulayhah ibn Khuwaylid, and seven Arabian tribes turning against Islam and refusing the zakah. The promised people who rose to meet it were Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and the Companions with him. ʿAishah said the shock her father bore would have crushed mountains; his counsellors urged caution; yet he declared that even if all jinn and men, trees and rocks combined against him and he had no comrade left, he would wage this struggle alone. ʿAli, Hasan al-Basri, Dahhak, Qatadah and other Imams of tafsir therefore said this ayah was revealed about Abu Bakr — he was the first of the promised people. Yet, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists, the soundest position is that the ayah embraces every Muslim until the Last Day who stands for this religion when others fall away.

## Ayah 55: the only true Guardian

Now the positive centre. *Innamā* — "only, none but" — *"your walī is Allah, and His Messenger, and those who believe."* Ibn Kathir states its force plainly: the Jews are not your allies; your allegiance belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the faithful believers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the reason of the heart: Allah alone is the real friend, guardian and guide of a Muslim at all times and in all conditions — every other bond perishes — and loyalty to the Prophet ﷺ is not a second, separate loyalty but flows from loyalty to Allah Himself.

The believing allies are marked by three signs: they establish the prayer, they give zakah, *wa-hum rākiʿūn* — "and they bow down." On this last phrase the commentators genuinely differed, and both sources lay out the views:

- **Some leading commentators** (Tafsir Mazhari is cited) took *rukūʿ* literally, as the bowing of salah — mentioned separately because it distinguishes the Muslim prayer: the Jews and Christians also pray, but their prayer has no *rukūʿ* in it.
- **The majority** — Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr al-Muhit and al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf among them, followed by Mazhari and Bayan al-Qurʼan — took it in its lexical sense of humility: these people are never proud of their good deeds; modesty is their disposition.
- Some narrations connect the phrase to **ʿAli**, who is said to have given his ring to a beggar while bowing in prayer. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the chain of this narration is debated among the scholars, and that even if sound, the ayah's wording is general: it includes all the Companions and all believers. When Imam Baqir was asked whether "those who believe" here means ʿAli, he answered that ʿAli is included within it as one of the believers. Ibn Kathir, for his part, rejects reading the ayah as praise for paying zakah *while* bowing — no scholar of rulings, he says, holds that giving zakah in that posture is its best form — and understands the phrase to mean they attend the congregational prayer and spend on the needs of the Muslims.

## Ayah 56: the party of Allah prevails

Whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as his allies belongs to *ḥizb Allāh* — the party of Allah — "and the party of Allah, they are the victorious." Ibn Kathir places beside it Allah's decree, "It is I and My Messengers who shall be the victorious," and the ayah declaring that true believers do not love those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, "even though they were their fathers or their sons." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the promise through history: Abu Bakr prevailed over every internal rebellion; when the empires of Caesar and Cyrus marshalled against ʿUmar al-Faruq, Allah effaced them; and so long as Muslims held to this allegiance, they remained winners in the struggle of life.

## Ayat 57–58: no intimacy with mockers

The passage ends where it began, but now the reason is named. Do not take as allies "those who take your religion as mockery and play" — whether from the People of the Book or the disbelievers at large. Abu Hayyan (cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān) asks why the People of the Book are singled out though the word "disbelievers" already covers them: though nearer to Islam in principle, experience showed that fewer of them accepted it — pride in already possessing a divine scripture hardened them, and mockery of the Muslims became their most visible attitude.

Ayah 58 gives the concrete case: *"When you call to the prayer, they take it as mockery and play."* The adhan — in Ibn Kathir's words, the proclamation of "the best action there is" — became their joke. Ibn Kathir sets against this the hadith, which he notes is agreed upon, that when the call to prayer is made Shaytan flees so as not to hear it, returns when it ends, flees again at the iqamah, then whispers to the praying person until he forgets how much he has prayed — and whoever falls into that doubt should make two prostrations before the salam. Mockery of the adhan is thus the mark of Shaytan's own party. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Tafsir Mazhari with reference to Ibn Abi Hatim, recounts the fate of a Christian in Madinah who, on hearing "I testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," would say "May Allah burn the liar" — until a stray spark from his servant's fire, while the household slept, burned him and his family.

The final verdict is the quiet phrase that closes the passage: *"that is because they are a people who do not understand."* Qadi Thanaullah of Panipat observes in Tafsir Mazhari that Allah calls them devoid of understanding despite their well-known worldly intelligence: a mind can be sharp in one direction and simply not work in another. As the Qurʼan says elsewhere, "They know the outward of the worldly life, while of the Hereafter they are heedless" (30:7).

## Living it

The passage does not ask a believer to be harsh, unjust, or withdrawn — justice and kindness towards non-Muslims remain taught duties. It asks for clarity about where the heart's anchor lies. Deep, defining loyalty belongs to Allah, His Messenger ﷺ, and the people of prayer, zakah, and humility; it is never to be traded away for the hedged, fearful calculations of ayah 52 — which history showed to be worthless the moment Allah's help arrived.

passages.title: Resentment, past curses, and the scholars' silence
passages.tafsir:
# Resentment, Past Curses, and the Scholars' Silence (5:59–63)

This passage answers a taunt. Certain People of the Book had taken to mocking the believers' religion, and Allah instructs His Prophet ﷺ to respond — first by exposing the emptiness of their grievance, then by holding up a mirror to their own record, and finally by turning to the deepest sickness in their community: the sins of the ordinary people, and the silence of the scholars who could have stopped them. The five ayat move like a single argument, from the accusation, to the counter-charge, to the diagnosis of how a religious community rots from within.

## Ayah 59: A grievance with nothing in it

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah commands the Prophet ﷺ to say to those among the People of the Scriptures who mock and jest about his religion: *do you have any criticism or cause of blame against us other than that we believe in Allah, in what was sent down to us, and in what was sent down before us?* And this, he says, is by no means a cause of blame at all. The "accusation" is faith itself — which is to say, there is no accusation.

The key verb is **tanqimūn**, rendered "do you resent" or "do you criticize." Ibn Kathir shows that the Qur'an uses this same root elsewhere for exactly this kind of hollow grievance: "And they had no fault (mā naqamū) except that they believed in Allah, the Almighty, Worthy of all praise" (85:8), and "they could not find any cause to do so except that Allah and His Messenger had enriched them of His bounty" (9:74). He also cites the agreed-upon hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said, "What caused Ibn Jamil to *yanqim* (refuse to give Zakah), although he was poor and Allah made him rich?" In every case the word marks a resentment whose stated "cause" is actually a blessing — faith, or enrichment from Allah's bounty. Resentment of this kind indicts the resenter, not the one resented.

A grammatical point from Ibn Kathir sharpens the closing phrase. "And that most of you are rebellious (fāsiqūn)" is not a new sentence; it connects back to "that we believe." So the sense is: *the only things you hold against us are that we believe in Allah and His revelations — and that we also believe most of you have rebelled and deviated from the straight path.* The believers' conviction about the state of their accusers is itself part of what enrages them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the precision of "**most** of you" — not all. Among the People of the Book were those who remained true believers under all conditions: before the Prophet's ﷺ coming they followed the Torah and Injīl sincerely, and when he came and the Qur'an was revealed, they believed in him and followed it. The Qur'an never erases them with a sweeping charge.

## Ayah 60: "Shall I inform you of something worse?"

Having shown the grievance to be empty, the passage turns it around. Ibn Kathir paraphrases: *shall I tell you about a people whose standing with Allah on the Day of Resurrection is worse than what you imagine ours to be? It is you* — those who incurred the curse of Allah, meaning they were expelled from His mercy; who incurred His wrath, after which He will never be pleased with them; some of whom He transformed into monkeys and swine; and who worshipped **Ṭāghūt** — false objects of worship — serving them and becoming their servants. How, Ibn Kathir asks on the ayah's behalf, can people with this record mock a religion that consists of Allah's Tawḥīd, singling Him out in worship without any partner?

Two clarifications from Ibn Kathir guard against misreadings:

**The transformed people left no descendants.** Sufyan ath-Thawri narrated from Ibn Masʿūd that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked whether today's monkeys and swine are the people Allah transformed. He replied: "Allah never destroyed a people by transforming them and making offspring or descendants for them. The monkeys and swine existed before that." Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by Muslim. The transformation was a terminal punishment on a particular people, not the origin of any animal species.

**"Worse in rank and far more astray" is not a comparison of two astray parties.** The Arabic comparative here does not imply that the believers are merely "less" astray; it means the People of the Scriptures are far astray, full stop. Ibn Kathir parallels it with "The dwellers of Paradise will, on that Day, have the best abode, and have the fairest of places for repose" — a form of expression that exalts one side without conceding any deficiency in it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a subtle observation about *how* this counter-charge is worded, under the heading "Consideration of the Addressee: A Principle of Daʿwah." The condition described in ayah 60 applied to these very addressees, and the occasion seemingly demanded that they be charged directly. Instead, the Qur'an shifts into the form of a similitude — "Shall I inform you of those who…" — out of consideration for the listener. This, Maʿārif says, displays a distinctive prophetic method of calling to Allah: never say things in a manner that needlessly enrages the person you are addressing. Even in its severest rebuke, the Qur'an models restraint of form.

## Ayat 61–62: What the eye cannot see, and what it can

Ayah 61 describes the hypocrites among them. They come to the Prophet ﷺ saying "We believe," but — as Ibn Kathir puts it — they enter with disbelief in their hearts and leave with it intact. This is why nothing they hear benefits them: the knowledge, advice, and reminder pass over hearts that were never open. "And Allah knows all that they were hiding" — He knows their secrets perfectly, however convincingly they perform belief before His creatures, and He will recompense them accordingly.

Ayah 62 moves from concealed disbelief to open sin: "You see many of them racing towards sin, transgression, and their devouring of unlawful gain." Ibn Kathir explains the unlawful consumption (**suḥt**) as devouring people's property unjustly through bribes and ribā (usurious gain), alongside transgression against people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out two points of language here:

- **"Many," not all.** As in ayah 59, the word *kathīran* deliberately excludes the good people among them. And though aggression and unlawful eating are already included under "sin," they are named separately — Maʿārif cites Al-Baḥr Al-Muḥīṭ — to stress the ruin these two sins in particular bring on everyone.
- **"Racing" (yusāriʿūna) as diagnosis.** Citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, Maʿārif observes that "racing towards sin" hints that these evils had become fixed, ingrained habits — so second-nature that the person moves toward them automatically, without even deliberate intention. And the same idiom describes the righteous at the opposite pole: "they race towards good deeds" (3:114). A deed repeated becomes character; character then produces deeds effortlessly, for good or for ruin.

## Ayah 63: The verse that frightened the scholars

Then comes the verse of which Ibn ʿAbbās said — as Ibn Jarir recorded — "There is no ayah in the Qur'an that has more severe admonition than this ayah"; and of which Ḍaḥḥāk, a recognized authority in tafsir cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, said: "In my view, this is the most frightening ayah for the Mashāyikh and ʿUlamā." Its terror is aimed not at sinners, but at scholars. "Why do their **Rabbāniyyūn** and **Aḥbār** not forbid them from their sinful speech and their devouring of unlawful gain? Evil indeed is what they have been doing."

Who are these two groups? Ibn Kathir explains the Rabbāniyyūn as the scholars in positions of authority and the Aḥbār as the regular scholars. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the views: Rabbāniyyūn as the devoted men of Allah — those intensely given to worship and detachment from the world — with Aḥbār as the religious scholars of the Jews; and, from other commentators, Rabbāniyyūn as the scholars appointed and authorized by the government, with Aḥbār as the ʿulamā in general. On either reading, the verse fixes the duty of commanding good and forbidding evil upon those with religious knowledge and standing — and on the second reading, upon state authority as well.

**Why so severe?** Ibn Kathir, from ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reporting from Ibn ʿAbbās, notes that the closing censure falls on the Rabbāniyyūn themselves — because they abandoned forbidding evil.

**A change of one word carries the verdict.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān highlights that ayah 62, censuring the common sinners, ends "evil is what they have been doing" with the verb *yaʿmalūna* (from ʿamal — a deed done with intention), while ayah 63, censuring the scholars, ends with *yaṣnaʿūna* (from ṣanaʿa — a thing done by design, with deliberation and settled habit, like a craft). The silent scholars' failing is worded more gravely than the sinners' sins. Maʿārif explains the hint: these leaders knew that if they spoke, their people would likely listen and desist — yet greed for the offerings they received, or fear of losing their followers' devotion, kept them silent. A failure of that kind, the verse implies, is graver than the crimes of the criminals themselves.

**The correction of deeds.** In its commentary on this verse, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over the insight that surfaced in ayah 62 — that deeds, good or bad, flow from ingrained habits which become a person's second nature — and notes that the respected Sufis (spiritual masters) and the men of Allah, the foremost of those who stressed the correction of deeds, deduced from these very Qur'anic sayings their whole method of reforming souls. Rather than correcting each crime separately, they treat the ingrained trait beneath it. For the man whose heart is filled with greed — who therefore takes bribes and devours interest — the prescription is the realization of the world's mortality and the poisoned nature of its luxuries. For the one ruled by pride, arrogance, or anger, it is concern for the life to come and fear of the ultimate accountability before Allah. Once these remain actively in sight, the evil behaviour patterns die out of themselves; correct the root trait, and the deeds that issue from it start coming out right.

**The Sunnah and the Companions confirm it.** Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Yahya bin Ya'mar said that ʿAli bin Abi Talib once gave a speech, which he began by praising and thanking Allah, then said: "O people! Those who were before you were destroyed because they committed sins and the Rabbāniyyūn and Aḥbār did not forbid them from evil. When they persisted in sin, they were overcome by punishment. Therefore, enjoin righteousness and forbid evil before what they suffered also strikes you. Know that enjoining righteousness and forbidding evil does not reduce the provision or shorten the term of life." That last line answers the two excuses that most often silence people — fear for livelihood and fear for safety.

Imam Ahmad recorded from Jarir that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no people among whom there are those who commit sins, while the rest are more powerful and mightier than the sinners, yet they do not stop them, but Allah will send a punishment upon them." Abu Dawud recorded it with the wording that Allah will punish them all before they die, and Ibn Majah also recorded this hadith. The punishment for tolerated evil, in other words, does not confine itself to the evildoers.

Maʿārif relates further narrations cited from Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ in the same vein: Malik ibn Dinar's account of a devoted worshipper included in a town's punishment "because he never showed his anger against people disobeying Us openly, not even with a sign of it on his face"; and the account of the prophet Yushaʿ ibn Nūn (Joshua), in which the righteous were destroyed alongside the wicked because they befriended them, ate and drank with them, and never frowned on their sins.

## Living it: when speaking out is a duty — and when it remains merely better

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with careful jurisprudence, deduced — it notes — from authentic hadith. Every Muslim who knows something to be sinful is duty-bound to check it to the best of their ability: with the hand, or the tongue, or at the very least with genuine distaste in the heart. But the *obligation* to speak is conditioned on a reasonable likelihood of being heard. Where experience makes it more likely that no one will listen — or that harm will result — the strict obligation lapses; yet even then, the higher and better path is to keep speaking without fear of blame, the quality the surah praised in verse 54: "they fear not the blame of any blamer."

And Maʿārif adds a sobering historical note: as long as Muslims carried this duty themselves, they held distinction in knowledge, deed, and character; once they outsourced the prevention of wrong entirely to governments and withdrew from their own role — even within their own families — the results became plain for all to see.

The passage that opened with the enemies' resentment thus ends facing inward. The taunt of outsiders is easy to answer: faith is no crime. The harder question is the one ayah 63 leaves ringing — Ibn ʿAbbās heard no sterner verse in the whole Qur'an — addressed to everyone who knows better and says nothing.

passages.title: 'Allah's hand is chained' and the missed blessing
passages.tafsir:
This passage records one of the ugliest things ever said about Allah — "Allah's hand is chained," an accusation of divine stinginess — and Allah's majestic answer: "Nay, both His Hands are widely outstretched. He spends as He wills." What binds ayat 64–66 together is a single contrast between two postures toward Allah: the bitterness of a people who, when their worldly means dried up, blamed their Lord rather than themselves; and the open door Allah still holds out to them — *if only* they had believed, *if only* they had upheld their Scriptures, blessing would have poured on them from above and beneath. The passage moves from blasphemy, to refutation, to a missed blessing described in heartbreaking detail.

## The story behind the words

The commentators tell us who said this and why. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates (as in al-Lubāb, from Ibn ʿAbbās, narrated by al-Ṭabarānī and Abū al-Shaykh) that the remark came from particular men — Nabbash son of Qays, and Finhas, the chief of the Jewish tribe of Qaynuqāʿ. Ibn Kathir records from ʿIkrimah that the ayah was revealed about Finhas — the same man who had earlier said, "Truly, Allah is poor and we are rich!", for which Abu Bakr smacked him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the background. The Jews of Madinah had long enjoyed extended means and money. When the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah they heard the call of Islam, but remained unmoved — they were more interested in holding on to their communal hegemony and the income they drew from offerings tied to their self-perpetuating customs. So they turned hostile to the call of truth. As a punishment, Allah turned their affluence into straitened circumstances, and they faced poverty. It was then — frustrated and off guard — that they began to say the divine treasure must be running short, or that Allah — hallowed be He above such a claim — had chosen to become miserly.

This is the psychology the ayah exposes: when a people who resisted truth for the sake of money lose that money, they blame Allah's generosity rather than their own choice.

## What "chained hand" means — and what it does not

In ayah 64, Ibn ʿAbbās explains (as reported by ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah): "They do not mean that Allah's Hand is literally tied up. Rather, they mean that He is a miser and does not spend from what He has. Allah is far holier than what they attribute to Him." The same was reported from Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Qatādah, al-Suddī, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. The "chained hand" was a known Arabic idiom for stinginess — Ibn Kathir points to Surah al-Isrāʼ (17:29), where Allah tells the believer, "let not your hand be tied (like a miser) to your neck, nor stretch it forth to its utmost reach (like a spendthrift)." So the Jews' words were a metaphor — but a metaphor of contempt, calling the Lord of all treasures a miser.

Allah's answer comes in three strokes:

**First, the curse turns back on the speakers.** "May their hands be tied up, and may they be accursed for what they uttered." Ibn Kathir observes that what Allah said came to pass — they became known for miserliness, envy, and humiliation, and he cites 3:112, "Indignity is put over them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the curse reaches them in this world as disgrace and in the Hereafter as punishment.

**Second, the affirmation:** "Nay, both His Hands are widely outstretched. He spends as He wills." As Ibn ʿAbbās's comment shows, the point of the verse is Allah's boundless generosity — and, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, the hands of Allah are always open and well-extended, and His generosity has been there since ever and shall remain forever. His favors are ample, His bounty unlimited; He owns the treasures of everything, and any good that reaches His servants is from Him alone. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a crucial nuance: Allah's giving is not indiscriminate. He is Independent and free of need, yet He is also Wise — He extends means for whom He wills in His Wisdom and straitens them for whom He wills in His Wisdom. Tight circumstances are never evidence that the treasury has run dry.

**Third, a prophetic image of that generosity.** Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Abu Hurayrah — recorded, he notes, in the Two Sahihs — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah's Right Hand is perfectly full, and no amount of spending can decrease what He has, even though He spends by night and by day. Do you see how much Allah has spent since He created the heavens and earth? Yet surely it has not decreased what He has in His Right Hand. His Throne is over the water and in His Other Hand is the hold by which He raises and lowers." And: "Allah said, 'Spend and I will spend on you.'" Every raindrop, every harvest, every provision since creation began — and nothing has diminished. That is the reality the words "chained hand" slandered.

## When revelation hardens instead of heals

Ayah 64 then says something sobering: the revelation sent to the Prophet ﷺ "makes many of them increase in rebellion and disbelief." Ibn Kathir explains the word *tughyān* — rebellion — as exceeding the ordained limits of things. The same Qurʼan that increases believers in faith, good works, and beneficial knowledge increases these opponents in envy and denial; Ibn Kathir compares 17:82, where the Qurʼan is "a healing and a mercy to those who believe, and it increases wrongdoers in nothing but loss." Light does not change; hearts differ in how they receive it.

The ayah continues: "We have put enmity and hatred among them till the Day of Resurrection." Their hearts are never united, Ibn Kathir says, because they do not agree on the truth. And "every time they kindled the fire of war, Allah extinguished it" — their plots turn back against them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads these two clauses as a protection granted to the Muslims: because of the differences Allah cast within their own ranks, they could neither dare an open war nor bring any conspiracy to success — the first failure named in "whenever they lit the flames of war, Allah puts it out," the second in "they run about on the earth spreading mischief" (mischief-making being all their striving amounts to). And the passage closes its indictment simply: "Allah does not like the mischief-makers."

## The missed blessing — ayat 65 and 66

Then the tone turns, remarkably, from curse to invitation. Two conditional sentences — "if only…" — describe what was, and still could be, theirs.

**Ayah 65:** "Had the People of the Book believed and had taqwa (been mindful of Allah), We would have expiated for them their sins and admitted them to Gardens of pleasure." Ibn Kathir: had they believed in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and avoided the sins they committed, Allah would have removed the dangers from them and granted them their objectives. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that this door was not closed — if they were to take to faith and godliness *even now*, Allah could forgive their past sins.

**Ayah 66** goes further: "Had they upheld the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been sent down to them from their Lord" — meaning the Qurʼan, as Ibn ʿAbbās and others said — "they would surely have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on one word here, and it repays attention. The verse does not say "had they *acted according to*" the Torah and Injil; it uses *iqāmah* — to establish, to make something stand upright and straight. Scripture is upheld only when it stands whole: no additions, no omissions, no self-invented things equated with established religion. What is meant to stand straight must stand perfectly straight — established, not tilting. This was aimed precisely at a community whose characteristic sin, the commentary notes, was altering and distorting Scripture.

And the promise? "Provision from above them and from beneath their feet" — rain and blessing descending from the sky, crops and sustenance growing from the earth, as Ibn Kathir explains, citing the parallel in 7:96: "And if the people of the towns had believed and had taqwa, We should have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Tafsīr Kabīr) adds that "above and beneath" signifies sustenance available easily and constantly.

**Why promise worldly wealth at all?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices that ayah 65 promises the Hereafter, while ayah 66 extends the promise to worldly comfort — and offers a moving explanation. What kept these people from Islam, despite the clear signs they had seen, was fear of loss: loss of leadership, loss of the offerings and gifts they received as religious high-priests. So Allah answered the fear itself: if you believe truly and act righteously, nothing of your worldly wealth will decrease — it will increase. The very thing they clutched at was the thing Allah promised to multiply for them, if only they would let go of it for His sake.

**A necessary caution.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to head off a misreading: this was a promise made to a particular group under particular conditions — the Jews of the Prophet's ﷺ own time — and those of them who did believe received it in full, like Najāshī (the Negus), the king of Ethiopia, and ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām. It is *not* a universal rule that faith always brings extended sustenance and disbelief always brings poverty. What faith and good deeds universally bring is the blessing of a good and pure life — which may come with extended means or with outwardly constricted ones, as with the prophets and the men of Allah, not all of whom had ample sustenance all the time, yet all of whom had the purest of lives.

## "Among them is a moderate community"

The passage refuses to end in blanket condemnation. "Among them is a *muqtaṣid* community — but most of them, evil is what they do." *Muqtaṣid* means one who follows a balanced, middle course. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies them concretely: people who were first Jews and Christians, then believed in the Qurʼan and the Prophet ﷺ and entered Islam — justice required that the evil described in these verses not be pinned on all of them. Ibn Kathir links the phrase to 7:159, "of the people of Musa there is a community who lead with truth and establish justice therewith," and to 57:27 on the believing followers of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. He then adds a subtle point of rank from 35:32–33: *iqtiṣād*, the middle course, is the *highest* grade Allah mentions for them — whereas in this Ummah there is a grade above it, the *sābiqūn*, those foremost in good deeds by Allah's permission.

## Living it

The passage's warnings were addressed to others, but its mirror faces everyone.

- **Never read hardship as divine stinginess.** The root sin here was interpreting straitened circumstances as a defect in Allah's generosity. The believer's creed is the opposite: His Hands are outstretched, and His giving and His withholding are both Wisdom.
- **Spend, trusting the One whose treasure never decreases.** The hadith pairs the fullness of Allah's Right Hand with a direct promise: "Spend and I will spend on you." Nothing given for His sake diminishes what is with Him.
- **Uphold revelation whole.** The lesson of *iqāmah* is that Scripture is not a menu. Trimming it to protect income, position, or custom is precisely the failure this passage mourns.
- **Watch what greed does to religion.** What stood between these people and a blessing "from above them and from beneath their feet" was attachment to status and offerings — and to the very people who feared that loss, Allah promised that true faith and righteous action would not decrease their worldly portion but increase it.
- **Speak of groups the way the Qurʼan does.** Even in its severest passage, the Qurʼan pauses to honor the muqtaṣid minority. Blanket judgment of a people is not the Qurʼan's way.

passages.title: Convey the message; salvation is by faith and deeds
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the hinge of the sūrah's long engagement with the People of the Book. First Allah turns to His Messenger ﷺ with a command and a promise: convey *everything* revealed to you, and Allah Himself will shield you from the people (ayah 67). Then the Messenger ﷺ is told what to say to the Jews and Christians: your religion counts for nothing until you actually uphold what Allah revealed (ayah 68). Finally comes the universal principle that resolves it all: with Allah, no lineage or label saves anyone — only faith in Allah and the Last Day, joined to righteous deeds (ayah 69). Command, confrontation, and criterion: the three ayat hold together as one movement from the duty of conveying the message to the terms on which it must be received.

## Why this command came when it did

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The preceding sections of the sūrah had described, at length, the obstinacy and hostility of the Jews and Christians toward Islam. That sustained opposition could have had two natural effects on the Prophet ﷺ — for he was human. He might feel disheartened, and the work of *tablīgh* (conveying the message) might slow or fall short somewhere; or, if he pressed on regardless, he stood to suffer the worst hardships at the hands of his enemies. Ayah 67 answers both dangers at once: it emphatically commands him to convey all that was revealed — whether people like it or reject it should not concern him — and it gives him the good news that his enemies will be unable to harm him, for Allah will Himself protect him.

The severity of the wording is worth pausing over: "And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His Message." Ibn Kathir cites Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, as reported by ʿAlī bin Abī Talḥah: "If you hide only one āyah that was revealed to you from your Lord, then you have not conveyed His Message." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same conclusion — concealing even a single divine command would leave the Prophet ﷺ unabsolved of the responsibility of prophethood. This is why he strove with his full strength, all his life, to discharge this weighty trust.

## The testimony that he conveyed it all

Did he fulfil it? The sources answer with two great witnesses.

The first is ʿĀʼishah, may Allah be pleased with her. Al-Bukhari recorded her saying: "Whoever says to you that Muhammad hid any part of what Allah revealed to him, then he is uttering a lie" — and she recited this very ayah as her proof. (Muslim, At-Tirmidhi, and An-Nasa'i also collected this hadith.) The Two Sahihs record her further remark that *if* Muhammad ﷺ were ever going to hide anything of the Qur'an, he would have hidden the ayah "But you did hide in yourself that which Allah will make manifest, you did fear the people while Allah had a better right that you should fear Him" — an ayah that mentions something to his own discomfort, yet he conveyed it. Al-Bukhari also recorded the words of Az-Zuhri, which distil the whole ayah: "From Allah comes the Message, for the Messenger is its deliverance, and for us is submission to it."

The second witness is the entire Ummah at the Farewell Hajj — Ibn Kathir calls it the biggest gathering, with over forty thousand Companions present. Muslim recorded from Jābir bin ʿAbdullāh, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked them in his speech: "O people! You shall be asked about me, so what are you going to reply?" They said: "We bear witness that you have conveyed, fulfilled, and offered sincere advice." He kept raising his finger toward the sky and pointing at them, saying: "O Allah! Did I convey? O Allah! Did I convey?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a detail from that Khutbah with lasting consequences: he instructed that those present should convey his message to those absent — including those not yet born. The Companions took this so seriously that they treated every word and deed of his as a trust from Allah, determined that not a single sentence from his blessed tongue should go un-conveyed. If a Companion had, for some reason, withheld a particular hadith, he would recite it before his death so as to be relieved of the burden. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the case reported in the Sahih of al-Bukhari of Muʿādh, may Allah be pleased with him, who recited such a hadith on his deathbed lest he sin by carrying the trust to his grave.

## "Allah will protect you from mankind"

The promise in the second half of ayah 67 was not abstract; it visibly changed the Prophet's ﷺ daily life. Before its revelation, he was guarded. Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿĀʼishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that one night the Prophet ﷺ was vigilant and said, "Would that a pious man from my companions guard me tonight!" — whereupon they heard the clatter of arms, and Saʿd bin Abī Waqqāṣ, may Allah be pleased with him, announced he had come to guard him. Only then did the Prophet ﷺ sleep. This hadith is recorded in the Two Sahihs.

Then the ayah came down. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from ʿĀʼishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet ﷺ had been under guard until "Allah will protect you from mankind" was revealed — and he raised his head from the room and said, "O people! Go away, for Allah will protect me." At-Tirmidhi recorded this and called it *Gharīb*; Ibn Jarir also recorded it, and Al-Hakim in his Mustadrak said, "Its chain is Sahih, but they did not record it" — that is, despite his grading, the narration does not appear in the Two Sahihs. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān confirms the picture: Companions had guarded him in the city and on journeys; after this ayah he relieved them all, for Allah had taken the responsibility Himself. The commentary also relates — citing Tafsir Kabir, and identifying the narrator only as Ḥasan — a report in which the Prophet ﷺ is said to have described how, when he was first charged with conveying Allah's message, the charge felt frightening, since people were bound to reject and oppose him; but when this ayah was revealed, he was at peace. The commentary gives no hadith collection for this report, so it should be received as it is transmitted there: a note of comfort from the tafsir literature, not a narration of the Sahih collections. And so it proved: no one thereafter succeeded in harming him in his mission (injuries received in battle being another matter, not contrary to the promise).

The closing clause — "Verily, Allah guides not the people who disbelieve" — draws the boundary of the Prophet's ﷺ task. Ibn Kathir explains: you convey, and Allah guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills, citing "Not upon you is their guidance, but Allah guides whom He wills" (2:272) and "Your duty is only to convey, and on Us is the reckoning" (13:40). Delivery is his charge; hearts are Allah's.

## "You have nothing to stand on" — the message itself

Ayah 68 is the message being conveyed, and it is uncompromising: "O People of the Book! You have nothing" — Ibn Kathir glosses this: no real religion — "until you uphold the Torah, the Injil, and what has been sent down to you from your Lord." And since those very Books command following Muhammad ﷺ and believing in his prophethood, upholding them honestly leads straight to Islam. Hence Ibn Kathir's heading for the passage: there is no salvation except through faith in the Qur'an.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point about what the People of the Book *did* have. They had the privilege of descent from prophets, the intellectual excellence of the Torah and Injil, and many devoted men who undertook rigorous spiritual exertions in search of truth. None of it, the ayah declares, carries weight without adherence to the divine Sharīʿah (revealed law). And the lesson is turned toward Muslims too, in a striking application: no path of spiritual discipline — no *sulūk* or *ṭarīqat* (paths of spiritual wayfaring), no *mujāhadah* (spiritual striving), no *kashf* (unveiling) or *ilhām* (inspiration) — can be a source of salvation with Allah without full adherence to the Sharīʿah. Experiences and exertions do not substitute for obedience.

**Why "what has been revealed to you" and not simply "the Qur'an"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers on this wording. The Torah and Injil are named by name; the third Book is described by a whole clause. One possible wisdom: the clause is wider than the muṣḥaf. The commentary cites the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: "Remember! I have been given the Qur'an and, with it, (many fields of knowledge) like it — lest, in times to come, some sated man reclining on his couch were to say: For you this Qur'an is sufficient... although what the Messenger of Allah has declared to be Haram is like what Allah has declared to be Haram" (Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Darimi and others). The Qur'an itself testifies that the Prophet ﷺ "does not speak from desire; it is only revelation revealed." So the commands binding on the Ummah are of three kinds: those stated plainly in the Qur'an; those given through separate revelation not recited as Qur'an (*waḥy ghayr matlū*); and those the Prophet ﷺ gave by his own considered judgment (*ijtihād* and *qiyās*) which Allah did not correct — these too take the force of revealed injunctions. All three fall within "what has been revealed to you from your Lord," and all three are obligatory to follow.

**But how can one follow three Books that abrogate one another?** The Injil abrogated some rulings of the Torah, and the Qur'an abrogated many rulings of both. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers: since each incoming Book itself changed rulings of the previous one, following the *replacement* is precisely how one acts on both Books at once — while clinging to an abrogated ruling violates the requirement of both.

The ayah ends with consolation. Revelation would, perversely, make many of them "increase in rebellion and disbelief" — grace spurned hardens the heart. "So do not grieve for the people who disbelieve": the Prophet ﷺ is told not to be saddened or shaken by their refusal, nor to carry sympathetic sorrow for those who choose it.

## Ayah 69: the one door of salvation, open to all

Now the criterion. Allah addresses four communities — the believers (Muslims), the Jews, the Sabians, and the Christians — and promises: whoever among them believes in Allah and the Last Day and works righteousness, "on them shall be no fear, nor shall they grieve." The wording almost exactly parallels 2:62, as both commentaries note.

Who were the Sabians? The sources record genuine scholarly difference, and it should be left as such. Ibn Kathir cites Mujahid, that they were a sect from the Christians and Magians who did not follow any particular religion. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Qatādah through Ibn Kathir, reports that they worshipped angels, prayed facing away from the Qiblah, and recited the Zabūr revealed to Dāwūd, peace be upon him — and observes that the Qur'anic context supports this, since the four communities would then correspond to the believers in the four Scriptures the Qur'an names: Torah, Zabūr, Injil, and Qur'an. No community by this name exists today.

**The point of the verse.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly: distinctions of lineage, homeland, and nationality do not matter in the sight of Allah. Whoever takes to obedience, faith, and good deeds — no matter what he was before — is acceptable to Allah. And after the revelation of the Qur'an and the coming of the last of the Prophets ﷺ, total obedience *means* being a Muslim; it is not valid to follow the Torah, Injil, or Zabūr without faith in the Qur'an and its Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir says the same: the good deeds the ayah accepts "must conform to Muhammad's Law, after Muhammad ﷺ was sent to all mankind and the Jinns." For those who do enter — and this answers a natural anxiety — all past sins, disbelief, and even former hostility to Islam stand forgiven, and in the life to come they shall have no fear or grief.

**Why mention Muslims at all**, when they already stand where the verse calls people to stand? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains this as a mode of Qur'anic eloquence: like a law promulgated for everyone, rewarding the compliant and punishing the violator. Its subtlety is that the believers are told they are appreciated not for any personal or group excellence, but purely for their obedience to their Creator — and the dissenter is thereby told that the same grace awaits him on the same terms.

## Does this verse open salvation without the Prophet ﷺ?

Some have theorized, from the absence of an explicit mention of prophethood here, that anyone — Jew, Christian, even an idol-worshipper — attains salvation by mere belief in Allah and the Last Day plus good deeds, without entering Islam. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refutes this at length.

First, a verse mentioning some articles of faith is not obliged to list them all; the whole Qur'an brims with clear statements that there is no salvation without believing in the Messenger. The commentary cites 2:285, where faith is detailed as belief in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His Messengers, "We make no difference between any of His Messengers" — so rejecting even one Messenger invalidates faith; and 4:150–151, which brands those who say "We believe in some and disbelieve in some" as "the disbelievers in reality." It also cites the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Had Mūsā been alive, he would have had no choice but to follow me."

Second, the pluralist theory collapses under its own weight. If every community's existing religion sufficed in every age, the sending of the final Prophet ﷺ and the revelation of the Qur'an would be meaningless, and the succession of Sharīʿahs — "For each of you We have made a way and a method" (5:48) — redundant.
