And most piercingly: why then is Iblīs accursed? He believed in Allah, and even in his rage confirmed the resurrection — "till the Day they are raised." Belief in Allah and the Last Day, detached from submission, saved him nothing.

Finally, the verse itself hints at prophethood. In the Qur'an's own terminology, only that "belief in Allah" is valid which believes everything Allah has said — "So, if they believe in the like of what you believe in, they have certainly found the right path" (2:137), the faith of the Companions, of which faith in the Messenger ﷺ was a great pillar. So "whoever believes in Allah" already includes belief in His Messenger ﷺ.

## Living the passage

The duty of *tablīgh* did not end with the Prophet ﷺ; his own instruction at the Farewell Hajj — let those present convey to those absent, including generations unborn — made the spreading of Allah's Dīn the inherited work of the Sahabah, the Tābiʿīn, and those after them. And the passage sets the manner as well as the matter: convey without concealment and without fear of people's reaction, leave guidance to Allah, and do not let grief over those who refuse consume you. Toward non-Muslims, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the Qur'an itself commands relations of tolerance, sympathy, favour, charity, and mercy — while keeping the frontiers of the religion fully guarded: kindness without compromise, and the door of ayah 69 always open to whoever walks through it with faith and righteous deeds.

passages.title: Israel's covenant and the killing of messengers
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are a compressed history of the Children of Israel's relationship with Allah: a solemn covenant taken, messengers sent, and a repeating cycle of rejection, punishment, forgiveness, and relapse. What binds them as a unit is that ayah 70 states the crime — breaking the covenant to the point of denying and even killing the messengers — and ayah 71 diagnoses the delusion behind it: they assumed no consequences would ever come.

## The covenant and how it was broken

In ayah 70, Allah reminds us that He took a covenant (mīthāq) from the Children of Israel and sent them messenger after messenger. Ibn Kathir explains that this covenant was a pledge to hear and obey Allah and His Messenger. Yet, as he puts it, they broke these pledges and followed their lusts and desires instead of the law — and their treatment of revelation became selective: whichever part of the law agreed with them, they took; whatever did not conform to their desires, they abandoned.

The ayah's own wording exposes the mechanism. The messengers were rejected not because their message was doubtful, but because it came "with what they themselves desired not" (bimā lā tahwā anfusuhum). The measuring stick was no longer "Is this from Allah?" but "Does this suit us?" And the ayah states what followed: "a group of them they called liars, and others among them they killed." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that they were commanded to believe in Allah and act righteously — and this was their response: betraying Allah to the limit of falsifying His messengers and killing some of them.

## "They thought there would be no fitnah"

Ayah 71 turns from the deed to the mindset that made it possible: "They thought there will be no fitnah" — no trial or punishment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān links this to the other half of what they had been commanded: belief in the Last Day. Having committed such oppressive acts, they became totally carefree, as if they would never have to pay for what they had done and as if the consequences of their injustice and rebellion would never come out into the open.

The result is described in two devastating words: fa-ʿamū wa-ṣammū — "so they became blind and deaf." Ibn Kathir is careful to spell out what this blindness and deafness mean: they were blinded from the truth and became deaf, incapable of hearing it, and for that reason they could no longer be guided by it. Their eyes and ears still worked; what died, as Ibn Kathir describes it, was their capacity to receive the truth and be guided by it.

## The cycle: punishment, forgiveness, relapse

Then comes the astonishing turn in the middle of ayah 71: "after that, Allah turned to them" — thumma tāba, He relented and accepted their repentance. And then, just as astonishingly: "yet again many of them became blind and deaf."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (drawing on the notes of Tafsir Usmani) fills in the history behind this cycle. After they went on killing some prophets and imprisoning others, Allah imposed on them the mastery of Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylonia (605–562 BC), who took them as slaves to Babylon — the episode recorded in the Old Testament book of Daniel. After a long time they were returned to Jerusalem, released from that disgrace through the help of Persian kings. They repented and set about making amends, and Allah accepted their repentance. But with the passage of time they slid back into their old ways and became blind and deaf once again — so much so that they dared to kill Sayyidna Zakariyyah (Zechariah) and Sayyidna Yahya (John), peace be upon them, and were fully prepared to kill Sayyidna ʿIsa (Jesus), peace be upon him.

## "And Allah is the All-Seer of what they do"

The passage closes with a name of Allah that answers the delusion it began with. They imagined their deeds would carry no consequence — and the ayah ends: "And Allah is the All-Seer (Baṣīr) of what they do." Ibn Kathir comments that He has perfect knowledge of what they do, and of who among them deserves guidance and who deserves misguidance. Nothing in the long history just narrated — the betrayals, the killings, the repentance and the relapse — was ever outside His sight. The blindness was entirely on one side.

## Living it

Though the passage narrates the history of a particular nation, every element of the cycle is a mirror. The selective religion Ibn Kathir describes — taking the parts of the law we agree with and quietly shelving the rest — is not a temptation unique to the Children of Israel. Nor is the false security of ayah 71: sinning grows easy precisely when a person becomes "carefree," acting as though no reckoning is coming. And the passage teaches something sobering about relapse: Allah's acceptance of repentance is real — He turned to them — but forgiveness received and then squandered leads back to the same blindness and deafness as before. The believer's task is to keep desire under revelation rather than over it, to live with the Last Day in view, and to guard a repentance once it has been granted.

passages.title: Refuting the deification of the Messiah
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is doing

These six ayat are the Qur'an's direct answer to the central claim of Christian doctrine: that ʿĪsā (Jesus), son of Maryam — peace be upon them both — is divine. The passage names the claims plainly (ayat 72–73), lets the Messiah himself refute them in his own words (ayah 72), opens a door of repentance (ayah 74), then dismantles the doctrine with an argument so simple a child can follow it (ayah 75), and finally diagnoses the disease beneath the doctrine — *ghuluww*, religious excess (ayah 77). What holds the ayat together is that single movement: from the claim, to its refutation, to the root cause that produced it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene by connecting this passage to what came just before. Earlier verses described how the Banī Isrāʾīl broke their pledge, falsified some messengers and killed others. These verses now expose the opposite failure of the same people: not content with degrading Allah's messengers, a section of them swung to the other extreme and raised a messenger to godhood itself. Both errors, the Qur'an will show, come from the same abandonment of the middle path.

## The two claims, named without euphemism (ayat 72–73)

Ayah 72 begins: *"Those who say, 'Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,' have certainly disbelieved."* Ibn Kathir explains that this refers to the Christian sects — he names the Monarchite, Jacobite and Nestorite among them — who said that ʿĪsā is Allah. Allah is far holier than what they attribute to Him.

Ayah 73 addresses the second formulation: *"Those who say, 'Allah is the third of three,' have certainly disbelieved."* Who are the "three"? Ibn Kathir records two views from the early authorities. Mujahid and several others said the ayah was revealed about the Christians in particular. As-Suddi and others said it concerns taking ʿĪsā and his mother as gods besides Allah, making Allah the third in a trinity — and As-Suddi connected this to Allah's question at the end of the sūrah: *"O ʿĪsā, son of Maryam! Did you say unto men: 'Worship me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?'"* (5:116).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Shabbir Ahmad Usmani) explains the phrase *thālithu thalāthah* — "the third of three" — as referring either to the Messiah, the Holy Spirit (Rūḥul-Quds) and Allah, or to the Messiah, Maryam and Allah, all three taken as divine. Allah becomes a one-third partner; then the three are declared one, and that one is three. This "unity in trinity," he observes, is supported by neither reason nor revelation, and is explained in language deliberately kept circuitous and ambiguous — and when it cannot be understood, it is declared a reality beyond comprehension. Against all of this the Qur'an sets one sentence: *"And there is no god but the One"* — there are not many worthy of worship; there is only One, without partners, the Lord of all creation.

## The Messiah's own testimony (ayah 72)

The most striking feature of ayah 72 is that the refutation is placed in the mouth of ʿĪsā himself: *"But the Messiah said: 'O Children of Israel! Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.'"* Ibn Kathir draws out the force of this. The very first words ʿĪsā uttered, while still a baby in the cradle, were "I am ʿAbdullāh" — the servant of Allah. He did not say "I am Allah," or "I am the son of Allah." Rather: *"Verily, I am a servant of Allah; He has given me the Scripture and made me a Prophet"* (19:30), and: *"Verily Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him alone. That is the straight path"* (19:36). And when he was sent as a Prophet in manhood, he commanded the worship of "my Lord and your Lord" — one Lord over prophet and people alike, alone, without partners. Those who deify him are therefore contradicting the very man they claim to exalt.

The ayah then carries the Messiah's warning: *"Whosoever sets up partners with Allah, then Allah has forbidden Paradise for him, and the Fire will be his abode."* Shirk — associating partners with Allah in worship — is the one sin that locks the gate of Paradise. Ibn Kathir supports this with Allah's words, *"Verily, Allah forgives not that partners should be set up with Him, but He forgives what is less than that to whom He wills"* (4:48), and with the scene where the people of the Fire beg the people of Paradise for water and are told, *"Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers."* He also cites what is recorded in the Sahih: the Prophet ﷺ had someone proclaim to the people, "Only a Muslim soul shall enter Paradise" — and in another narration, "Only a believing soul." The ayah closes: *"And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers"* — on that Day there is no help from Allah, and no one to shield them from the state they will be in.

## The astonishing mercy of ayah 74

After a warning of painful torment for those who persist (end of ayah 73), the tone turns with a question full of tenderness: *"Will they not turn to Allah in repentance and seek His forgiveness? For Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."*

Ibn Kathir pauses over this. The people being addressed have just been described as inventing the gravest lie against Allah — and yet Allah does not simply condemn them; He *invites* them. This, he writes, demonstrates Allah's generosity, kindness and mercy toward His creatures: despite this grave sin and false allegation, He calls them to repent so that He may forgive them, for Allah forgives whoever sincerely repents to Him. Even the door out of shirk is opened by mercy. No one reading this passage — Christian or Muslim — is left facing the warning without also facing the invitation.

## The argument from a plate of food (ayah 75)

Ayah 75 is the intellectual heart of the passage, and its method is remarkable: it refutes an elaborate theology with two everyday observations.

**First: messengers pass away.** *"The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger; messengers have passed away before him."* Ibn Kathir says ʿĪsā is just like the previous prophets — one of Allah's servants and one of His honourable messengers, as Allah says elsewhere: *"He was not more than a servant; We granted Our favour to him, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel"* (43:59). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the logic: prophets came, completed their mission, and were gone. They were not eternal — and eternity is the mark of godhood. The Messiah, human like them, cannot be what the Divine Being is.

**Second: "They both used to eat food."** His mother was a *ṣiddīqah* — a truthful, saintly believer — and both mother and son ate. Ibn Kathir notes what eating entails: needing nourishment, and relieving the call of nature. They were servants like other servants. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (from Tafsir Usmani) unfolds this into a full argument. Whoever needs to eat depends, in the end, on almost everything in the world — the earth, the air, the water, the sun, the animals; the whole chain of causes that brings a grain of food into existence and carries it through digestion. By mentioning that ʿĪsā and his pious mother ate — a fact proved by observation and by narrations not denied even by Christians — the Qur'an points to this endless chain of needs. One who cannot free himself from the need to eat cannot be free of dependence on anything in the world; and a being enmeshed in the chain of causation for his very survival cannot be divine. It is, as the commentary says, a proof the educated and the uneducated can grasp alike. (And the argument does not cut the other way: *not* eating is no proof of godhood — otherwise all the angels would be gods.)

**Was Maryam a prophet?** The word *ṣiddīqah* opens a question the scholars genuinely debated. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (abridging Rūḥ al-Maʿānī) reasons that on an occasion of praise, the *higher* rank is the one mentioned; had Maryam held prophethood, the ayah would have called her *nabiyyah*. That it calls her *ṣiddīqah* — the station of sainthood — indicates she was a godly woman, not a prophet. This accords with the position of the majority of Muslim scholars that prophethood was given only to men, as in *"And We have not sent before you any but men to whom We revealed, from among the peoples of the towns"* (12:109). Ibn Kathir reads the ayah the same way: her being named ṣiddīqah is the highest rank she was given, which shows she was not a prophet. Notice, though, what both agree on: this is the language of honour. The Qur'an denies Maryam's divinity while affirming her as one of the truthful — refutation without a word of disrespect toward her.

The ayah ends by turning to us, the readers: *"Look how We make the signs clear to them; yet look how they are deluded away."* Ibn Kathir: marvel first at how plain and unequivocal the clarification is — then marvel at the opinions and misguided claims they still cling to after it.

## Worshipping what cannot harm or help (ayah 76)

Ayah 76 widens the lens from the Messiah to every object of worship besides Allah: *"Say: how can you worship besides Allah that which has no power either to harm or to benefit you? But it is Allah Who is the All-Hearer, the All-Knower."* Ibn Kathir explains the contrast: these deities can neither ward off harm from their worshippers nor bring them benefit — while Allah hears what His servants say and knows all things. How, then, worship what does not hear, see or know, and cannot help even itself — instead of the One Who hears and knows everything?

## The root of it all: ghuluww (ayah 77)

Ayah 77 gives the diagnosis: *"Say: O People of the Book! Do not go to extremes in your faith beyond the truth."* The key word is *ghuluww*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines as crossing the limits drawn by religion in belief and deed. There is a limit to honouring prophets: the farthest one may go is to hold them the best of Allah's creation. To go beyond that — to call a prophet divine, or a divine son — is ghuluww in belief. Ibn Kathir puts it memorably: you were commanded to honour him, and you exaggerated that honour until you elevated him from the rank of prophet to the rank of a god.

**The cycle of excess and deficiency.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the Banī Isrāʾīl swung between opposites: irreverent enough to falsify and even kill prophets, yet excessive enough to ascribe divinity or divine sonship to prophets — and the Jews too were censured for saying "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah" (as the Christians said it of the Messiah). He cites the Arab saying that the ignorant person never stays on moderation: he falls either into *ifrāṭ* (excess, crossing the limit) or *tafrīṭ* (deficiency, falling short of one's duty). Perhaps different groups took the two extremes; perhaps one group treated different prophets in the two opposite ways.

**Why this matters for every generation.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this ayah as a standing principle for the People of the Book and for all who come after, to the Last Day. Allah has appointed two sources through which people know Him: His Books, and His chosen men — the messengers and prophets who are the living models and practical keys to those Books — for a book alone can never complete the grooming of a human being; it takes a person to nurture a person. And it is precisely about these "men of Allah" that people have always fallen into excess and deficiency. At one extreme, messengers — and later even pīrs and faqīrs — were treated as knowers of the unseen and possessors of Allah's own attributes, until people slid from venerating living saints into worshipping their graves. At the other extreme, some reduced even a messenger of Allah to a mere courier, hiding behind the slogan "the Book of Allah is enough for us" — true words twisted to negate the standing of the prophets. The ayah teaches that dīn is, in reality, a set of limits: it is a crime to fall short of them, and a crime to overrun them; a grave sin to insult Allah's messengers, and a graver one to make them sharers in Allah's attributes.

**"Beyond the truth."** The ayah says "do not go to extremes in your faith *ghayr al-ḥaqq*" — beyond the truth. The investigative scholars of tafsir, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, read this as emphasis: excess in religion is *always* unjust; a "just excess" does not exist. Al-Zamakhshari distinguished two kinds — the false excess forbidden here, and deep intellectual research of the kind pursued by the theologians and jurists of Islam, which he called a permissible "excess"; the majority reply that such rigour simply is not ghuluww at all, so long as it stays within the limits proved from the Prophet ﷺ and from the Companions and their successors. Careful scholarship is not extremism; leaving the revealed limits is.

**The straight path is the middle path.** The ayah closes by warning the People of the Book not to follow the desires of a people who went astray before them, misled many, and *"strayed from the right path"* — teachers and advocates of misguidance, as Ibn Kathir says, whose error the later generations inherited. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the final lesson: the "right path" they lost is precisely the path of moderation between the two extremes. The ayah both exposes the fatal error of overshooting or undershooting the norm, and commands firmness on the straight middle way.

## Living it

For the believer, this passage is not only about others' history. It sets the permanent measure of how to love the beloved of Allah: honour the prophets and the righteous as the best of creation — and not one step further. Reverence that crosses the revealed limit does not increase in piety; it changes religion itself. And the passage models something else: even while carrying the Messiah's warning that Allah has forbidden Paradise to whoever sets up partners with Him, its very next breath is *"Will they not turn to Allah in repentance?"* Firmness about the truth and warmth toward the person are not opposites here — they stand side by side in a single passage.

passages.title: Cursed by David and Jesus for tolerated evil
passages.tafsir:
# Cursed by Dawud and ʿIsa for Tolerated Evil (5:78–81)

This passage is one of the most sobering in the Qur'an: Allah declares that disbelievers among the Children of Israel were cursed on the tongues of two of their own prophets — Dawud and ʿIsa, son of Maryam (peace be upon them) — and then tells us exactly why. The four ayat form a single argument. Ayah 78 announces the curse; ayah 79 names the sin that earned it — they stopped forbidding one another's evil; ayah 80 shows where that decay ended — open loyalty to the enemies of faith; and ayah 81 delivers the verdict — real faith would have made such loyalty impossible. The passage is history, but it is told as a warning: Ibn Kathir notes that Allah chastised them for this behaviour precisely "so that their behaviour would not be imitated."

## A curse pronounced by prophets (ayah 78)

Allah states that He cursed the disbelievers among the Children of Israel long ago, and revealed this to His Prophets Dawud and ʿIsa, son of Maryam. Part of the gravity of this curse is that it was not pronounced by an enemy but came, in the ayah's own words, "by the tongue of Dawud and ʿIsa, son of Maryam" — the very prophets sent among them.

Ibn Kathir records the report of al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas: "They were cursed in the Tawrah, the Injil, the Zabur (Psalms) and the Furqan (Qur'an)." In other words, every major scripture carries the record of this condemnation.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds detail and breadth. It relates that the curse through Sayyidna Dawud resulted in their transformation into swine, and the curse through Sayyidna ʿIsa in their transformation into monkeys. It also notes that some commentators observed that only two prophets are named here because the context requires it — in reality, the cursing began with Sayyidna Musa and ended with the Last of the Prophets ﷺ, so that four prophets, one after another, verbally invoked the curse. Maʿārif describes those who were overtaken by it as a people caught in an "error of excess and deficiency": some were hostile to the prophets, while others went to the opposite extreme of making prophets sharers in the Divine attributes.

Why were they cursed? Ayah 78 itself answers: "because they disobeyed and were ever transgressing." Ibn Kathir spells out the two dimensions: they disobeyed Allah, and they transgressed against His creatures. Rebellion against heaven and wrongdoing against people went together.

## The sin of silence (ayah 79)

Then comes the ayah on which the whole passage pivots: "They used not to forbid one another from the evil they committed. Vile indeed was what they used to do." Their society's fatal habit, Ibn Kathir explains, was that they did not forbid each other from sins and prohibited things. Notice what the ayah condemns: not only the doing of evil, but the *tolerating* of it. The curse fell on a community in which wrongdoing had become unremarkable — witnessed, known, and left unchallenged.

## From the Sunnah: the duty of forbidding evil

At this point Ibn Kathir gathers a remarkable cluster of hadith, noting that there are many hadiths that order enjoining righteousness and forbidding evil.

**The warning.** Imam Ahmad recorded from Hudhayfah bin al-Yaman that the Prophet ﷺ said: "By He in Whose Hand is my soul! You will enjoin righteousness and forbid evil, or Allah will send a punishment on you from Him. Then, you will supplicate to Him, but He will not accept your supplication." At-Tirmidhi also recorded it and graded it Hasan. The stakes could not be stated more starkly: abandoning this duty invites punishment from Allah, to the point that supplication itself goes unanswered.

**The method.** Muslim recorded from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "He among you who witnesses an evil, let him change it with his hand; if he cannot do that, then by his tongue; if he cannot do even that, then with his heart — and this is the weakest faith." Objection to evil is graded by ability — action, speech, or at the very least the heart's rejection — but even that last station is described as faith, the weakest of it. Indifference appears nowhere on the scale.

**The heart's stance is what counts.** Abu Dawud recorded that al-ʿUrs ibn ʿAmirah related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When sin is committed on the earth, then whoever witnesses it and hates it — once he said: forbids it — will be like those who did not witness it. Whoever was absent from it, but agreed with it, will be like those who witness it." This is a piercing standard: physical distance from a sin does not clear you if your heart approves of it, and physical presence does not stain you if your heart rejects it.

**Courage in speaking.** Ibn Majah recorded that Abu Saʿid al-Khudri heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say in a speech: "Behold! Fear of people should not prevent one from saying the truth if he knows it." Abu Saʿid then wept and said, "By Allah! We have seen some errors, but we feared (the people)." If a Companion of that rank wept over falling short here, none of us can consider ourselves above this struggle. In the same vein, Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah recorded from Abu Saʿid that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The best Jihad is a word of truth proclaimed before an unjust ruler" — at-Tirmidhi grading it Hasan Gharib from that route. And Abu Dawud recorded from one of the Companions that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The people will not perish until they do not leave — or — have any excuse for themselves."

**The balance.** Yet the duty is not a command to recklessness. Imam Ahmad recorded from Hudhayfah that the Prophet ﷺ said: "It is not required of the Muslim that he humiliate himself." They asked how one humiliates himself, and he replied: "He takes on trials that he is not capable of enduring." (Also recorded by at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah; at-Tirmidhi graded it Hasan Sahih Gharib.) Forbidding evil is measured against capacity — the earlier hadith of Muslim already built that grading in.

## Where silence leads: misplaced loyalty (ayah 80)

Ayah 80 moves from their silence to its fruit: "You see many of them taking the disbelievers as their friends." Mujahid said that this ayah refers to the hypocrites.

The ayah's language is striking: "Evil indeed is that which they have sent forward before themselves." Loyalty is treated as something *dispatched ahead* to the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir explains the chain of consequences: by giving loyalty and support to the disbelievers instead of the believers, this evil act caused hypocrisy to settle in their hearts and brought upon them the anger of Allah — an anger, he says, that will remain with them until the Day of Return. Hence the ayah's ending: "for that reason Allah is wrath with them, and in torment they will abide" — abiding in punishment, Ibn Kathir notes, on the Day of Resurrection.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the two halves of the passage together with a penetrating diagnosis: deep friendship with disbelievers is prohibited because its outcome is disastrous, and the sequence of the ayat may itself indicate that the very deviation of Bani Isra'il *began* with close friendly collaboration with disbelievers, which adversely affected their ways and finally became the cause of their fall into the abyss. On this reading, misplaced loyalty was not just the symptom of their corruption — it was the doorway to it.

## The verdict of faith (ayah 81)

Ayah 81 closes the argument with a simple conditional: "Had they believed in Allah, and in the Prophet, and in what has been revealed to him, never would they have taken them as friends." Ibn Kathir's comment: had they sincerely believed in Allah, His Messenger and the Qur'an, they would not have committed the evil act of supporting the disbelievers in secret while being enemies to those who believe. The loyalty of the heart is thus presented as a *test* of faith — where a person's allegiance actually rests reveals what he actually believes. The ayah ends soberly: "but many of them are rebellious (fasiqun)" — disobedient, as Ibn Kathir puts it, to Allah and His Messenger and defiant of the ayat He sent down.

## Living it

The passage was preserved so that, in Ibn Kathir's words, this behaviour "would not be imitated." Its demands on a believer are concrete:

- **Never make peace with evil.** Do what you can — hand, tongue, or at minimum the heart's firm rejection. The one thing the passage forbids absolutely is comfortable approval of wrong.
- **Do not let fear of people silence known truth** — while also not hurling yourself into trials beyond your capacity; the Sunnah commands courage, not self-destruction.
- **Guard the heart's loyalties.** The Children of Israel's fall, on Maʿārif's reading, began with close collaboration that adversely affected their ways — and what we send forward ahead of ourselves, we will meet.

passages.title: The humble Christians nearest in affection
passages.tafsir:
This passage answers a question the surah has been circling for many verses: are all the People of the Book the same? The preceding verses, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, had spoken of the friendliness of the Jews with the disbelievers; now their hostility toward the Muslims, hand in hand with those disbelievers, is named — and against it Allah draws a careful distinction. On one side stand the fiercest enemies of the believers; on the other, a particular kind of Christian: humble, learned, tender-hearted, who weeps at the truth and embraces it. Ayat 82–86 form one connected movement: the contrast is stated (82), the sincere response is pictured (83), its inner logic is voiced (84), and the eternal outcomes of both responses are sealed (85–86).

## The story behind these verses: Ethiopia

Both of our sources agree that this passage came down in connection with real people and a real moment in the seerah — and the story is worth telling in full, because it makes every phrase of the passage concrete.

When the Muslims of Makkah were worn down by the persecution of the Quraysh, the Prophet ﷺ advised them to migrate to Ethiopia (Abyssinia). As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, he had heard that its king, the Najashi (Negus), "was no oppressor of people, nor did he allow anyone to oppress others." A first group of eleven set out — among them Sayyidna ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan and his wife Sayyidah Ruqaiyyah, the Prophet's ﷺ own daughter. Later a much larger caravan, eighty-two men besides women, arrived under the leadership of Sayyidna Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib. The king and his people received them gently, and they lived there in peace.

The Quraysh could not bear this. They sent a delegation to the Najashi with the customary gifts, demanding that the Muslims be expelled. But the king refused to act without investigating. He questioned Jaʿfar and his companions about Islam and its Prophet — and what he heard matched the glad tidings in the Injil (the Gospel) of the coming of the Last of the Prophets: his teachings, his description, even the features of his Companions. Convinced, the Najashi returned the gifts of the Quraysh and told them plainly he would never order such people out of his country.

The story does not end there. When the Prophet ﷺ later settled in Madinah, the Najashi sent a delegation of his own scholars and religious men, dressed in the coarse robes of monks. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives its size differently in different places — in one passage a deputation of thirty men, in another seventy persons, of whom sixty were from Ethiopia itself and eight from Syria — so the exact number should not be pressed; what matters, and what both accounts agree on, is what happened next. The Prophet ﷺ recited Surah Yasin to them. As they listened, tears flowed from their eyes, and they said: how like this is to what was revealed to Sayyidna ʿIsa (peace be upon him)! All of them embraced Islam. When word reached Ethiopia, the Najashi himself embraced Islam, and even sent his son at the head of another delegation with a letter to the Prophet ﷺ — though the boat carrying them was tragically lost at sea.

Ibn Kathir records the same background from the early authorities: Saʿid bin Jubayr, As-Suddi and others said these ayat were revealed concerning the delegation the Najashi sent to hear the Prophet's ﷺ words; when he recited the Qurʼan to them they embraced Islam, cried, and were humbled. ʿAtaʼ bin Abi Rabah said they were Ethiopians who accepted Islam when the Muslim emigrants lived among them; Qatadah said they were followers of the religion of ʿIsa, son of Maryam, who became Muslims without hesitation on seeing the Muslims and hearing the Qurʼan. And Ibn Jarir added the key interpretive point: the ayat were revealed concerning *anyone who fits this description*, "whether they were from Ethiopia or otherwise." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the same principle: though revealed about the Najashi and his delegation, the wording is general, so its force covers every Christian of this truth-loving type, in any age.

Read ayah 83 again with this scene in mind — "when they listen to what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized" — and it stops being an abstraction. It is a portrait of that delegation in monks' robes, weeping in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ as Surah Yasin is recited.

## Why the two ends of the spectrum?

Ayah 82 does not merely observe the difference; it explains it, and both commentators dwell on the explanation.

**The enmity.** Ibn Kathir writes that the disbelief of the Jews described here was one of "rebellion, defiance, opposing the truth, belittling people and degrading the scholars." He recalls their history: they killed many of their own Prophets, attempted the life of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ more than once, worked magic against him and poisoned him, and incited the polytheists against him. This is why the ayah pairs them with "those who commit shirk": Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the preceding verses had already described the Jews' friendship with the disbelievers, and this verse names the real glue of that alliance — shared hostility toward the believers ("the enemy of my enemy is my friend").

**The nearness.** The ayah's praise attaches to "those who *say*: We are Christians" — which Ibn Kathir explains as those who follow the religion of the Messiah and the teachings of his Injil. Such people, he says, are generally more tolerant of Islam and its adherents "because of the mercy and kindness that their hearts acquired through part of the Messiah's religion." He connects this to Allah's words elsewhere: "And We ordained in the hearts of those who followed him compassion, mercy, and monasticism" (57:27), and notes that their own book contains the teaching, "he who strikes you on the right cheek, then turn the left cheek for him," and that fighting was prohibited in their creed.

**The diagnosis itself.** The ayah gives its own reason in three phrases: "because among them are *qissisin* (priests) and *ruhban* (monks), and they are not proud." Ibn Kathir explains that *ruhban* refers to one dedicated to worship, and that the verse is describing a combination of "knowledge, worship and humbleness, along with following the truth and fairness." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the contrast sharply: the scholars and rabbis of the Jews had harnessed their learning as a means of accumulating worldly gain, until the lust for the mundane left them unwilling to distinguish true from false or lawful from unlawful — whereas these Christian priests and monks had renounced worldly pleasure for the sake of knowledge and religion, and were "not arrogant (which could make them unwilling to listen and think)."

Notice what the ayah itself is identifying. The decisive variable it names is not ethnicity or even religious label — it is pride versus its absence: "and they are not proud." Knowledge plus worship plus freedom from pride leaves a heart able to recognize truth when it arrives; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's gloss makes the mechanism explicit — arrogance is what "could make them unwilling to listen and think." That is the engine of the whole passage.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a further lesson from this: the ʿulamaʼ and mashaikh — the scholars and spiritual guides — are the real movers and spirit of any community. So long as a society contains genuine scholars who act from the fear of Allah and the sense of answerability before Him rather than from worldly desire, that community will never be deprived of real good and blessing.

## The anatomy of a sincere response (ayat 83–84)

Ayah 83 paints recognition before it records profession: first the eyes overflow with tears "because of the truth they have recognized" — Ibn Kathir links this to the good news they already possessed about the advent of Muhammad ﷺ; they were not learning something foreign but meeting something long awaited — and only then comes the prayer: "Our Lord! We believe; so write us down among the witnesses," that is, among those who testify to the truth and believe in it.

Ayah 84 then lets us hear their reasoning from the inside, and it is disarmingly simple: "Why should we not believe in Allah and in the truth that has come to us, when we long for our Lord to admit us among the righteous people?" For the humble heart, faith is not a leap demanded against the evidence; it is the obvious step, and the only question worth asking is why one would refuse. Ibn Kathir places these Christians alongside those praised elsewhere in the Qurʼan: the People of the Scripture who believe in what was revealed to you and to them, humbling themselves before Allah (3:199), and those who, when the Qurʼan is recited to them, say "We believe in it; verily it is the truth from our Lord — indeed even before it we were Muslims" (28:52–53).

## The two destinies (ayat 85–86)

Ayah 85 opens with a striking phrase: "So Allah rewarded them *for what they said*" — Ibn Kathir explains that their words of faith, spoken from recognition of the truth, earned them "Gardens under which rivers flow," in which, he stresses, they will remain forever and ever, never to be removed. And the ayah names them *muhsinin*, good-doers — defined by Ibn Kathir in a sentence worth memorizing: those "who follow the truth and obey it wherever, whenever and with whomever they find it." Truth-following is not loyalty to a tribe; it is loyalty to the truth itself, wherever it surfaces.

Ayah 86 closes the passage with the mirror image: those who disbelieved and denied Allah's ayat — defied and opposed them, in Ibn Kathir's words — are the dwellers of the Fire. The pairing is deliberate. The passage that began by ranking people's attitudes toward the believers ends by ranking only two responses to the truth: humble acceptance and arrogant denial, each with its everlasting abode.

## What this passage does — and does not — say

Because ayah 82 is often quoted alone, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān devotes a section to the "limits of interpretation," and it deserves careful attention.

The praise here is for a *particular kind* of Christian — fearing Allah, upright, devoted to truth and justice like the people of Ethiopia — including any who share those qualities in times to come. It is not a blanket declaration that Christians as such are the friends of Muslims regardless of how hostile they may become. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Imam Abu Bakr al-Jassas, who wrote in his Ahkam al-Qurʼan that taking this verse as absolute praise of Christians — or as proof that they are better than the Jews in an absolute sense — is "open ignorance": in creed, he argued, Christian doctrine is more pronounced in shirk (ascribing partners to Allah), and in conduct, hostility toward Islam has by no means been confined to one community. What the verses establish is a real and observable difference of *disposition*: among the Christians there existed, in significant numbers, humble and truth-loving souls — and it was precisely this quality that gave them the tawfiq (the divinely granted enablement) to recognize Islam and enter it, as the Najashi and his people finally did. Indeed, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the people praised here did not remain where they were: they were followers of the Injil before Islam, and when Islam came, they followed it.

The enduring lesson, then, cuts toward the reader. The passage is ultimately a study in what makes a heart receptive: knowledge joined to worship, and above all the absence of *istikbar* — the pride that, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, could make a person unwilling to listen and think. The tears of the Ethiopian delegation flowed because nothing in them stood between the truth and its recognition. That is the state every believer is meant to guard: to be, in the words of ayah 85, among the muhsinin who follow the truth wherever, whenever, and with whomever they find it.

passages.title: Do not forbid the good things; expiating oaths
passages.tafsir:
# Do Not Forbid What Allah Has Made Lawful — and How to Undo a Rash Oath

This passage sets out one of the defining balances of Islam: piety is not achieved by banning yourself from the good things Allah has permitted, and if you have sworn yourself into such a ban — or into any oath better broken — Allah Himself has legislated the way out. Ayat 87–88 forbid self-imposed prohibition and command the grateful enjoyment of lawful provision; ayah 89 then deals with the oath, the most common instrument by which people lock themselves into such prohibitions, and prescribes its expiation. The three ayat are one connected legislation: the principle, the correct attitude, and the legal remedy.

## Why here? The thread from the previous passage

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (drawing on Bayān al-Qurʼān of Mawlānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānavī) notes that up to this point the sūrah has been addressing the People of the Book, and that a few ayat earlier (5:82) monasticism was mentioned in a complimentary light — but only in respect of one feature of it, the abandonment of worldly desires. Since someone might take from that praise that the *whole* monastic project is praiseworthy, it was fitting to follow immediately with a prohibition of making unlawful what Allah has made lawful. The sequence into ayah 89 is equally deliberate: declarations of \"I will never touch such-and-such\" are often sworn, so the ruling on oaths follows naturally from the ruling on self-prohibition.

## The occasion: Companions who wanted to live like monks

Ibn Kathir relates, through ʿAli bin Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas, that ayah 87 was revealed about some Companions of the Prophet ﷺ who said, \"We should cut off our male organs, abandon the desires of this life and travel in the land, just as the Ruhban (monks) do.\" When the Prophet ﷺ heard of this, he summoned them, and when they confirmed it, he said: \"I fast and break my fast, pray and sleep, and marry women. Whoever follows my Sunnah is of me, and whoever abandons my Sunnah is not of me.\" Ibn Abi Hatim also collected this hadith, and Ibn Marduwyah recorded a similar narration from Ibn ʿAbbas through al-ʿAwfi.

Ibn Kathir adds the famous parallel account recorded in the Two Sahihs from ʿAʼishah: some Companions asked the wives of the Prophet ﷺ about his private worship, and — apparently concluding they must go further — one said, \"I will not eat meat,\" another, \"I will not marry women,\" a third, \"I will not sleep on the bed.\" The Prophet ﷺ responded: \"What is the matter with some people who said such and such? I fast and break the fast, sleep and wake to stand to pray, eat meat, and marry women. He who is not pleased with my Sunnah is not of me.\"

Notice what these men wanted. Not sin — *extra devotion*. The passage's first lesson is that even devotion has limits set by Allah, and the Prophet's ﷺ own balanced life is the standard. Ibn Kathir titles this section simply: **there is no monasticism in Islam**.

## \"And do not transgress\" — a limit on both sides

The command in ayah 87 ends: *and transgress not; verily, Allah does not like the transgressors*. Ibn Kathir reads this transgression in two directions at once. First: do not exaggerate and make things hard on yourselves by prohibiting the permissible. Second: do not transgress by *excessively indulging* in the permissible either — take what satisfies your need and do not fall into extravagance. He supports this with Allah's words, \"And eat and drink but waste not by extravagance\" (7:31), and the description of the servants of the Merciful who, when they spend, \"are neither extravagant nor miserly, but hold a medium way between those extremes\" (25:67). In his words, Allah legislated a medium way that allows neither excessive application nor lack of application.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the point on the ascetic side: \"transgressing\" here means abandoning something halal, without valid excuse, *as an act of thawāb* — as if the abstention itself earned reward. An ignorant person mistakes this for taqwa (fear and consciousness of Allah); in Allah's sight it is transgression. That is why ayah 88 does not merely permit but *commands*: \"Eat of the good, lawful things provided to you by Allah, and have taqwa of Allah in Whom you believe.\" Real taqwa, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, lies not in refusing Allah's blessings but in using them *as* blessings and showing gratitude for them — while, as Ibn Kathir puts it, obeying Him and seeking His pleasure in all your affairs and staying away from disobedience.

## The three ways halal is turned into haram

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out three forms in which a person might declare halal to be haram, each with its own ruling:

**1. By belief.** If someone believes a thing to be haram when its being halal is established by absolute proofs, this open contradiction of the divinely ordained law takes the person out of Islam — it is disbelief (kufr).

**2. By word — the oath.** Someone swears, \"By Allah, I will never eat that,\" or says, \"I make this haram for myself.\" Such an oath takes effect legally. Taking such oaths unnecessarily is a sin; once taken, the rule is that one must break the oath and make amends by paying the kaffārah (expiation) — which is exactly what ayah 89 then legislates.

**3. By practice.** Someone neither believes nor declares anything, but resolves to abandon a halal thing forever. If the abandonment is treated as an act of reward, it is bidʿah (innovation in the religion) and rahbāniyyah (monasticism) — a grave sin categorically established in the Qurʼan and Sunnah, such that acting against the self-imposed restriction becomes obligatory. But if a person abstains for some *other* reason — a physical or spiritual harm the thing causes them — there is no sin. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that reports of pious elders and Sufis abandoning certain halal things fall in this category: they left them as treatment and remedy, not as legislation.

This threefold analysis is the hinge of the whole passage: it explains why ayah 89, seemingly a change of subject, follows immediately — the second form, prohibition by sworn word, needs a legal exit.

## Ayah 89: which oaths count, and which do not

The ayah opens: *Allah will not call you to account for your thoughtless oaths, but He will call you to account for your deliberate oaths.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes three kinds of oath in the jurists' terminology:

- **Yamīn ghamūs** — the \"disastrous oath\": knowingly swearing falsely about the past (\"I swear I did not do it,\" knowing full well he did). *Ghamūs* literally means \"that which drowns,\" because this oath drowns a person in sin and its curse in this life and the next. It is a grave major sin. No kaffārah is prescribed for it; what is required is tawbah (repentance) and istighfār (seeking Allah's forgiveness).
- **Yamīn laghw** — the \"ineffectual oath,\" the one \"not counted\": swearing to something about the past believing it true when it turns out false, or an oath-word slipping off the tongue without intention. Ibn Kathir gives the same example: saying \"No, by Allah\" or \"Yes, by Allah\" unintentionally — a subject, he notes, already treated under Sūrat al-Baqarah. This brings neither kaffārah nor sin.
- **Al-yamīn al-munʿaqidah** — the \"binding oath\": swearing that one will or will not do something in the future. If it is broken, kaffārah becomes necessary — and depending on the situation, breaking it may or may not also involve sin.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a subtle harmonisation with the similar wording in 2:225. In al-Baqarah, \"Allah does not hold you accountable for laghw in your oaths, but holds you accountable for what your hearts have designed\" — there the contrast is with the intentional lie (yamīn ghamūs), so the accountability meant is the sin of the Hereafter. Here in al-Māʼidah, laghw is contrasted with \"the oaths you have bound yourselves with\" (mā ʿaqqadtum al-aymān), so the accountability meant is worldly: the obligation of kaffārah. The two ayat address two different consequences of two different contrasts — no contradiction.

## The expiation itself

For a broken binding oath, the ayah gives three options, and Ibn Kathir records the scholars' consensus that whichever one chooses will suffice:

**Feed ten poor persons** \"on a scale of the awsat (average) of that with which you feed your own families.\" Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿīd bin Jubayr and ʿIkrimah explained this as the *average* of what you feed your family; ʿAṭāʼ al-Khurāsānī said \"from the best of what you feed your families.\" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing the Fuqahāʼ (jurists), notes that the word *iṭʿām* allows two modes: either actually feed ten poor persons two full meals of the day from your household's average fare, or give the food into their possession — at the rate of one fitrah per person, 1¾ kilograms of wheat or its cash value.

**Or clothe them.** Ibn Kathir reports the explanations: clothing suitable to pray in for each of the ten, male or female; Ibn ʿAbbas (via al-ʿAwfi) said a robe or garment each; Mujahid said the least is a garment and the most is whatever you wish; al-Hasan, Abu Jaʿfar al-Bāqir, ʿAṭāʼ, Ṭāwūs, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, Ḥammād bin Abī Sulaymān and Abū Mālik all said a garment for each. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it as sufficient proper cover — a garment for the lower body and one for the upper.

**Or free a slave** — a *believing* slave, says Ibn Kathir. Here he cites the lengthy hadith recorded in the Muwaṭṭaʼ of Mālik, the Musnad of al-Shāfiʿī and the Sahih of Muslim: ʿUmar bin al-Ḥakam al-Sulamī had to free a slave and brought a black slave girl before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who asked her, \"Where is Allah?\" She said, \"Above the heavens.\" He asked, \"Who am I?\" She said, \"The Messenger of Allah.\" He said, \"Free her, for she is a believer.\"

Ibn Kathir observes that Allah listed the options from easiest to hardest — feeding is easier than clothing, clothing easier than freeing a slave — and only if a person cannot manage *any* of the three does the fourth apply: **fasting three days**. Ubayy bin Kaʿb, Ibn Masʿūd and his students read the ayah \"then he should fast three *consecutive* days\"; Ibn Kathir says that even if this reading is not Qurʼan by mutawātir (mass) transmission, it stands as a Companion's explanation carrying the ruling of something related from the Prophet ﷺ. On this basis, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, Imam Abū Ḥanīfah and some other Imams hold that the three fasts must be consecutive. Fasting is valid only for one genuinely unable to take any of the three financial options.

## Two closing cautions

The ayah ends with two directives the commentators unpack carefully.

**\"That is the expiation for your oaths when you have sworn.\"** According to Imam Abū Ḥanīfah and other Imams (as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports), the kaffārah is valid only *after* the oath is broken — paying it in advance does not count, because the cause that makes kaffārah necessary is the breaking itself. Just as there is no salah before its time and no Ramadan fast before Ramadan, there is no kaffārah of an oath before the oath breaks.

**\"And protect your oaths.\"** Ibn Kathir gives Ibn Jarīr's reading: do not leave broken oaths unexpiated — pay the kaffārah you owe. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds two further senses from the scholars: do not break an oath you have taken without legal or physical necessity; and — as some scholars said (cited via Mazhari) — do not be quick to swear in the first place. Guard your oath as something kept in reserve, taken only under real compulsion, never casually.

And the passage closes as it began — with grace: *Thus Allah makes clear to you His ayat, that you may be grateful.* The same gratitude that ayah 88 asked of us in enjoying Allah's provision is asked of us here for the clarity of His law, which never leaves a believer trapped, whether by misplaced asceticism or by a rash word sworn in haste.

## Living it

- Piety is following the Sunnah, not out-performing it. The Prophet ﷺ fasted *and* broke his fast, prayed at night *and* slept, ate meat and married — and declared that whoever turns away from his Sunnah is not of him.
- Taqwa is gratitude in enjoyment, not self-denial for its own sake. Giving up a halal thing \"for reward\" is transgression, not devotion; giving it up because it genuinely harms you is permitted.
- Do not swear casually. If you have sworn a harmful or foolish oath, the way out is to break it and pay the kaffārah — feed ten poor, or clothe them, or free a slave; failing all three, fast three days — and pay it only after the oath is broken.

passages.title: The prohibition of intoxicants and gambling
passages.tafsir:
This passage is where the Qurʼān's prohibition of intoxicants and gambling reached its decisive form. The four ayat move as one unit: ayah 90 issues the command, ayah 91 unveils the *reason* behind it, ayah 92 anchors it in the principle of obedience to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and ayah 93 answers the tender question the Companions immediately asked — what about our brothers who died before this came down?

## Three stages to a final verdict

The most illuminating thing about this passage is *how* it arrived. Ibn Kathir relates the narration of Abu Hurayrah, recorded by Imam Ahmad: "There were three stages to prohibiting Khamr." When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ migrated to Madinah, the people were drinking and gambling, and they asked him about it. First came the ayah of Surah al-Baqarah (2:219): "In them is a great sin, and (some) benefit for men." The people reasoned that this was not an outright ban, and continued — until one of the emigrants led the Maghrib prayer and mixed up the ayat in his recitation. Then came the tougher word of Surah an-Nisaʼ (4:43): do not approach the prayer while intoxicated. So people simply timed their drinking around the prayers. Finally a firmer ayah was revealed — this ayah of al-Maʼidah — and the response was immediate: "We abstained, O Lord!"

A separate narration, also recorded by Imam Ahmad, preserves ʿUmar bin al-Khattab's persistent duʿaʼ across those same stages. He prayed, "O Allah! Explain the verdict about Khamr to us clearly." After the ayah of al-Baqarah was revealed and recited to him, he still said, "O Allah! Make the verdict of Khamr clear to us." After the ayah of an-Nisaʼ, he said it again. Then the ayah of al-Maʼidah was revealed and recited to him, and when he reached the words *fa-hal antum muntahun* — "So, will you not then abstain?" — ʿUmar said, "We abstained, we abstained." Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi, and An-Nasaʼi recorded this hadith, and ʿAli bin Al-Madini and At-Tirmidhi graded it Sahih.

**The day the wine was spilled.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Anas said: "I once was giving an alcoholic beverage to Abu ʿUbaydah bin Al-Jarrah, ʿUbayy bin Kaʿb, Suhayl bin Baydaʼ and several of their friends meeting at Abu Talhah's house. When they were almost intoxicated, some Muslims came and said, 'Did you not know that Khamr has been prohibited?' They said, 'We'll wait and ask.' They then said, 'O Anas! Spill the remaining alcohol out of your container.' By Allah! They never drank it again" — and their Khamr at that time was made from unripe and normal dates. This is also recorded in the Two Sahihs. In another narration, Anas relates that he was the butler of the people in Abu Talhah's house when a caller heralded that alcoholic drinks had been prohibited; Abu Talhah ordered him to spill the wine — "I went out and spilled it, and it flowed in the streets of Al-Madinah." And in the narration Ibn Jarir recorded, Anas describes what the gathering did next: they spilled the alcohol and broke its barrels, some performed ablution and others bathed, they put on perfume, and they went out to the mosque — where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was reciting these very ayat. No debate, no phase-out. And note what their wine was made of that day — unripe and normal dates, not grapes; the prohibition was never about one beverage.

## The four things named in ayah 90

**Khamr** is not merely "wine." ʿUmar defined it from the Prophet's ﷺ own minbar, as recorded in the Two Sahihs: Khamr was being extracted from five things — grapes, dates, honey, wheat and barley — and "Khamr is what intoxicates the mind." The Prophet ﷺ said, in a hadith Muslim recorded from Ibn ʿUmar: "Every intoxicant is Khamr, and every intoxicant is unlawful." The ruling follows the *effect* — the clouding of the mind — not the ingredient.

**Maysir** is gambling. Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas both defined it so, and Ibn ʿAbbas added that the people of Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance) gambled habitually until Allah forbade it. The early authorities drew the circle wide: Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from ʿAli bin Abi Talib that chess is a type of gambling, and from ʿAtaʼ, Mujahid and Tawus that *every* type of gambling — even children playing for nuts — is Maysir.

**Al-Ansab** were the altar-stones of Jahiliyyah, beside which sacrifices were offered to idols — so explained Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿAtaʼ, Saʿid bin Jubayr and Al-Hasan. **Al-Azlam** were the divining arrows used for lotteries. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the custom: ten partners would slaughter a camel, then instead of dividing it into ten equal shares, they would draw marked and blank arrows from a quiver — some men walking away with multiple shares, others with nothing. Maʿārif notes this is essentially the same as many lottery-based games and enterprises common today, and it is haram. (It also records the exception: drawing lots is permissible, and proven from the Prophet ﷺ, when rights are already *equal* and lots merely assign identical shares — deciding who gets which portion of a fairly divided house, for instance. What is forbidden is creating winners and losers by chance.)

**Why list drink and gambling next to idols?** This is the rhetorical heart of the ayah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the altar-stones are placed in this list so the listener understands that drinking and gambling are as serious a crime as the worship of idols. It cites a hadith from Ibn Majah in which the Prophet ﷺ said that the one who drinks is like the one who worships idols — in some narrations, "like the one who worships al-Lat and al-ʿUzza."

All four are called **rijs** — a word Maʿārif renders as "filth," something foul and disgusting to sound human taste. Ibn ʿAbbas explained it as "abomination of Shaytan's handiwork," Saʿid bin Jubayr as "sin," and Zayd bin Aslam as "an evil handiwork of Shaytan." And the command is not merely "do not drink" but *fajtanibuhu* — "avoid it": keep away from the whole thing. The ayah closes with encouragement, as Ibn Kathir notes: "in order that you may be successful" — success in this world and the next hangs on the abstaining.

## Ayah 91: why — Shaytan's two-pronged attack

Ayah 91 does something the earlier revelations did not: it opens up the *reason*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the two clauses as the two dimensions of harm.

**The worldly harm: enmity and hatred.** These verses came down against a backdrop of real violence. Al-Bayhaqi recorded the narration of Saʿd — Muslim also recorded this hadith — about a feast before the prohibition: the drinkers began boasting, the Ansar claiming superiority and the Quraysh claiming it, until a man of the Ansar struck Saʿd's nose with a bone and split it open, scarring him for life. Maʿārif comments that such things do not happen by chance: when drunk, a man loses his reason and acts this way compulsively. Gambling works the same poison more slowly — the loser walks away, but malice against his adversary keeps working on him. Qatadah said it was the habit of some Arabs to bet everything they owned, even their families, lose it all, and then live a sorry life.

**The spiritual harm: barred from remembrance and prayer.** "And hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from the Salah." Maʿārif observes that this is mentioned *after* the worldly harms, perhaps as a hint that it is the real harm — for the real life is the eternal life of the Hereafter. A heart cut off from the remembrance of Allah makes even this world a misery: the one who chases wealth and recognition as his ultimate goal is never at peace with or without them, while the one whose heart is lit with the thought of his Creator is unshaken whether fortune comes or goes. And why is Salah named separately, when prayer is itself remembrance of Allah? Maʿārif answers: to signal that Salah is the highest of all forms of *dhikr* (remembrance), important in its own right.

Then the passage turns and asks, not commands: *"So, will you not then abstain?"* Ibn Kathir calls this a threat and a warning; Maʿārif calls the manner of asking "disarming and heart-winning." Both are true — it is a question that leaves the believer nowhere to hide, and it was answered out loud: "We abstained, we abstained."

## Ayah 92: whose loss is it?

"And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the quiet logic of the ayah's ending — "if you turn away, know that Our Messenger's duty is only to convey clearly." Obedience is commanded in *your* interest. If people refuse, Allah loses nothing — that much is obvious — but one might imagine the Messenger's ﷺ standing or reward is diminished by being disobeyed. The ayah removes that thought: his mission was to convey the commands of Allah openly and clearly, and he accomplished it. Whoever turns away after that brings loss only upon himself.

## Ayah 93: mercy for those who died before the ruling

Almost at once, a question rose from grieving hearts. Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas: "When Khamr was prohibited, some people said, 'O Allah's Messenger! What about our brethren who died while still drinking Khamr?'" Allah sent down ayah 93: "Those who believe and do righteous good deeds, there is no sin on them for what they ate…" In the same narration, Ibn Kathir pairs this with the identical anxiety after the Qiblah changed — "what about our brethren who died while still praying toward Jerusalem?" — answered by "And Allah would never make your faith to be lost" (2:143). The same worry echoes through the other narrations of that day: in one of Anas's narrations, people said, "Some people were killed and wine was still in their stomachs"; and in the narration of Abu Hurayrah that Ahmad recorded, people said, "Some people died in the cause of Allah, while some others died in their beds, but they used to drink alcohol and indulge in gambling." In that narration, after ayah 93 came down, the Prophet ﷺ said of those who died: "Had they been made impermissible for them, they would have abandoned them as you have abandoned them." The principle is one of Allah's mercy: no one is blamed for what was permitted when he did it.

The ayah's strange, beautiful repetition — *taqwa* and faith and good deeds, three times over — drew the scholars' attention. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Tafsir Usmani) explains that taqwa (guarding oneself from what harms the purity of one's faith) and iman have *degrees*: the more one advances in remembrance, concern for this life and the next, good deeds and Jihad in the way of Allah, the more the heart fills with the fear and awe of Allah and the firmer faith becomes. The triple repetition marks the seeker's ascent, station by station, ending at *ihsan* — righteousness at its best — and its reward: the love of Allah, "And Allah loves the good-doers." When this ayah was revealed, ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud reports, the Prophet ﷺ said, "I was told that you are among them" — a narration collected by Muslim, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasaʼi.

## The full weight of the prohibition

The Sunnah left no loophole around this passage. Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Ten matters related to Khamr were cursed. Khamr itself was cursed, whoever drinks it, its server, seller, buyer, brewer, who asks for it to be brewed, whoever carries it, whomever it is carried to and whoever consumes its price" — Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah recorded this hadith. The curse covers the entire economy of intoxicants, not just the glass; profiting from it, transporting it, serving it are all inside the circle of "avoid it."

And the stakes reach into the Hereafter. Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded from Ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever drinks Khamr in the life of this world and does not repent from it, will be deprived of it in the Hereafter." In Muslim's narration from Ibn ʿUmar the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever drinks Khamr and dies while addicted to it, without repenting from drinking it, will not drink it in the Hereafter." Yet the door of repentance stands open in the very wording: the deprivation is for the one who *does not repent*.

ʿUthman bin ʿAffan called Khamr "the mother of all sins," and told of a devout worshipper of earlier times who was lured into a locked house and confronted with three demands — to commit fornication, to kill a servant boy, or to drink a cup of wine. He took the drink, kept asking for more, and, intoxicated, committed the other two as well. "Avoid Khamr," ʿUthman concluded, "because it is never combined with faith, but one of them is bound to expel the other." Al-Bayhaqi recorded this, and the statement has an authentic chain of narration. It is the whole passage in miniature: intoxication is not one sin among many but a gate through which the others walk.

**Living it.** The passage asks of the believer exactly what it asked of the Companions: complete avoidance — of every intoxicant regardless of its source, of every game of winners-and-losers by stakes and chance (including, as Maʿārif notes, the modern lottery), and of the whole trade surrounding them. And it models *how* to obey: the Companions did not finish their cups, ask for a grace period, or renegotiate. They spilled the wine, washed, put on perfume, and went to the mosque. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the whole passage with a larger truth: the universe was created to serve the human being, with one restriction — do not transgress the limits Allah has set in benefiting from it. To use the world under the Creator's instructions is *ʿabdiyyah*, true servanthood, the highest achievement a human being can reach — "in order that you may be successful."

passages.title: Hunting rules during the pilgrim's consecration
passages.tafsir:
# Hunting Rules During the Pilgrim's Consecration (5:94–96)

This passage sets out one of the distinctive laws of the pilgrimage: while a believer is in *ihram* — the state of consecration entered for Hajj or ʿUmrah — land game becomes forbidden to him, even game standing within arm's reach. The three ayat form a single legal and spiritual unit: ayah 94 announces the prohibition as a divine *test*, ayah 95 states the prohibition formally and legislates the penalty for breaking it, and ayah 96 draws the boundary of the rule — the sea remains open, the land is closed — before sealing everything with a reminder of the gathering before Allah.

## A test placed within arm's reach

Ayah 94 does not begin with a command but with a warning: "Allah will certainly make a trial for you with something in the game that is well within reach of your hands and your lances." The wording is deliberate. Ibn Kathir records from Ibn ʿAbbas (through ʿAli bin Abi Talhah) that this refers to weak and young game — animals so close that a pilgrim could simply reach out and take them with his hands, yet Allah commanded that they be left alone. Mujahid read the two phrases as a pairing: "within reach of your hands" is the young game and chicks; "and your lances" is the mature game a hunter would normally spear.

Muqatil bin Hayyan gives the occasion: this ayah was revealed during the ʿUmrah of Al-Hudaybiyyah, when wild animals and birds came streaming into the Muslim camp in numbers the Companions had never seen before — and precisely then, while every man was in ihram, Allah forbade hunting them. The test could hardly have been sharper: abundant, easy game, and a command to hold back.

The ayah itself names the purpose: "that Allah may test who fears Him in the unseen (*bil-ghayb*)." A man could have snatched a bird in his tent with no witness. Ibn Kathir explains that this is how the obedience of those who obey Allah both in public and in secret becomes apparent, and he connects it to Allah's words elsewhere: "Verily, those who fear their Lord in the unseen, theirs will be forgiveness and a great reward" (67:12). The hunting rule, in other words, is not merely game management; it is a device for revealing — and training — the fear of Allah that operates when no one is watching. As for "whoever transgresses thereafter," As-Suddi explained it as meaning after this warning and threat; and the painful torment awaiting such a person, Ibn Kathir continues, is for his defiance of Allah's command and what He has decreed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Bayan al-Qurʼan) also notes how this ayah answers what came before it. In ayah 87 the believers were told not to make lawful things unlawful on their own; now ayah 94 shows the other side of the coin: it is *Allah alone* who has the authority to declare a particular thing unlawful in particular circumstances — even something ordinarily as lawful as hunting.

## The prohibition and its limits

Ayah 95 states the rule: "O you who believe! Kill not game while you are in a state of ihram." Two clarifications from the sources define its scope.

**What counts as "game" (ṣayd)?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines *ṣayd* as wild animals that do not habitually live near human beings. Naturally domesticated animals — sheep, goats, cows, camels — are not game at all, so slaughtering and eating them in ihram is perfectly valid. The prohibition covers game generally, whether the animal is eatable (halal) or uneatable.

**Which animals are exempt?** The Sunnah carves out harmful creatures. In the Two Sahihs, ʿA'ishah narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Five are *fawāsiq* (vicious, harmful creatures); they may be killed while in ihram or not: the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse and the rabid dog." Ibn ʿUmar narrated the same teaching, also recorded in the Two Sahihs. When Ayyub asked Nafiʿ about the snake, he replied, "There is no doubt that killing the snake is allowed." Ibn Kathir extends the ruling on the rabid dog to the wolf, lion, leopard, tiger and their like — either because they are more dangerous, or because the word *kalb* (dog) covers them — adding "Allah knows best." And in a hadith of Abu Saʿid, recorded by Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi (who graded it Hasan) and Ibn Majah, the Prophet ﷺ was asked which animals the *muḥrim* (person in ihram) is allowed to kill, and he answered: "The snake, the scorpion, the mouse, and the crow — which is shot at but not killed — the rabid dog, the kite and wild beasts of prey." Notice the crow's distinctive treatment in this narration: it is not simply killed like the others; it is driven off — shot at — but spared. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a linguistic point from these exemptions: the definite article in *al-ṣayd* is the *lām* of *ʿahd* — it marks a restricted, known referent, not an absolute generality. Not every animal is included in the prohibition; the exempted harmful creatures stand outside it.

## The penalty: tasting the weight of one's deed

The heart of ayah 95 is the expiation (*jazāʼ*) for a muḥrim who kills game. The ayah lays out a graded system, and the sources unfold each element.

**"The penalty is livestock equivalent to the one he killed."** An animal from the flocks and herds matching the killed game must be offered. The Companions themselves established the equivalences: a camel for an ostrich, a cow for wild cattle, a goat for a deer. Where no equivalent exists, Ibn ʿAbbas ruled that its value should be spent in Makkah as charity (recorded by Al-Bayhaqi).

**"As adjudged by two just men among you."** The assessment is not left to the offender. Ibn Jarir records that Abu Jarir Al-Bajali killed a deer in ihram and brought the matter to ʿUmar, who said, "Bring two of your brethren and let them judge you" — ʿAbdur-Rahman and Saʿd ruled he should offer a male sheep. In another report, when Arbad killed a deer and came to ʿUmar, ʿUmar said "Let us both judge," and the two of them ruled that he offer a well-fed goat, ʿUmar then reciting this very phrase of the ayah. The Qur'anic procedure was thus lived out in the first generation.

**"An offering brought to the Kaʿbah."** Ibn Kathir notes consensus that the equivalent animal must be slaughtered in the Sacred Area and its meat divided among its poor.

**Feeding or fasting.** If no equivalent animal can be offered, the expiation becomes feeding the poor or its equivalent in fasting. Ibn ʿAbbas set out a scale: for an antelope, a sheep in Makkah — failing that, feeding six poor people, or fasting three days; for a deer, a cow — or feeding twenty, or fasting twenty days; for an ostrich or zebra, a camel — or feeding thirty, or fasting thirty days (recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir; in Ibn Jarir's narration each poor person receives a *mudd*, about four handfuls of food). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the fiqh detail practically: the animal's value is estimated (two just assessors is better; one suffices), and the offender then either buys and slaughters a sacrificial animal within the Haram for the poor, gives grain at half a *ṣāʿ* (roughly 1.62 kg) per poor person, or fasts one day for each such share — the feeding and fasting need not take place within the Haram. It adds further rulings: even wounding game obliges compensation for the loss in its value; a muḥrim may not slaughter such an animal either — if he does, it is legally carrion; and pointing out, guiding toward, or assisting in a hunt is as unlawful as hunting itself.

**Intentional or by mistake?** The ayah says "whosoever of you kills it *intentionally*." Mujahid bin Jabr held the unusual view that this means one who kills deliberately while *forgetting* he is in ihram, and that the knowing offender's case is too grave for mere expiation. Ibn Kathir calls this statement odd; the majority hold that expiation is due whether one forgot one's ihram or not. Az-Zuhri put it memorably: "The Book asserts the expiation for intentional killing, and the Sunnah included those who forget as well." Killing game is a form of waste requiring redress in either case — but only the deliberate offender bears the *sin*, not the one who erred honestly.

**"That he may taste the heaviness of his deed."** The expiation is explicitly punitive-remedial: Allah requires it so the offender feels the weight of what he did. "Allah has forgiven what is past" — the days of Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance), for the one who becomes good in Islam. "But whosoever commits it again, Allah will take retribution from him." ʿAta', asked by Ibn Jurayj, explained: whoever repeats the offense in Islam owes the expiation *and* faces Allah's retribution — yet there is no worldly punishment from the authorities, "for it is a sin between him and Allah." Saʿid bin Jubayr, ʿAta' and the majority held that the expiation recurs with every offense, first, second or third, intentional or in error. The ayah closes: "And Allah is Almighty, All-Able of Retribution." Ibn Jarir comments that Allah is invincible in His control — none can resist Him or prevent Him from exacting retribution, for all creation is His creation and His is the might and the decision.

## The sea remains open (ayah 96)

Having closed the land, ayah 96 opens the sea: "Lawful to you is water game and its use for food — for the benefit of yourselves and those who travel." Saʿid bin Al-Musayyib and Saʿid bin Jubayr explained "water game" as what is eaten fresh and "its food" as what is dried and salted. Ibn ʿAbbas read it differently: the game is what is taken from the water alive; "its food" is what the sea throws ashore dead — a view reported likewise from Abu Bakr As-Siddiq, Zayd bin Thabit and other Companions and early scholars. "Those who travel" are the seafarers, according to ʿIkrimah, or — as others said — inland travelers provisioned with salted fish.

Two hadith illuminate this generosity of the sea. Imam Malik recorded from Jabir bin ʿAbdullah the famous expedition of three hundred men under Abu ʿUbaydah bin Al-Jarrah, sent by Allah's Messenger ﷺ toward the coast: their food dwindled to a single date per man per day, and when even that ran out, they found on the shore a fish like a small mountain and ate from it for eighteen days — a she-camel later passed under the arch of its two ribs without touching them. This hadith is in the Two Sahihs. And when a man asked whether seafarers short of fresh water could make wudu' with seawater, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ replied, "Its water is pure and its dead are lawful" — recorded by Malik from Abu Hurayrah, and by Ash-Shafiʿi and Ahmad bin Hanbal along with the Four Sunan compilers, and graded Sahih by Al-Bukhari, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Hibban.

Then the boundary is restated: "but forbidden is land game as long as you are in a state of ihram." Ibn Kathir spells out the consequence: game killed by a muḥrim is like a dead (unslaughtered) animal — unlawful to eat for muḥrim and non-muḥrim alike, and the expiation is due even for a mistaken kill, with sin added for a deliberate one.

**May a pilgrim ever eat game?** Yes — with a precise condition preserved in two hadith of the Two Sahihs. As-Saʿb bin Jaththamah gifted a zebra to the Prophet ﷺ at Waddan or Abwa', and the Prophet ﷺ returned it; seeing the disappointment on his face, he said, "We only gave it back to you because we are in a state of ihram" — for he understood it had been hunted *for* him. But when Abu Qatadah, himself not in ihram, hunted a zebra and offered it to companions who were, they hesitated and asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He asked, "Did any of you point at it or help kill it?" They said no. He said, "Then eat" — and ate from it himself.
