Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same rule from the very letter of the ayah: Allah said *lā taqtulū* ("do not kill"), not *lā ta'kulū* ("do not eat") — so a muḥrim may eat halal game hunted outside ihram and outside the Haram, provided he neither pointed it out, assisted, nor had it hunted for him.

## "And have taqwa of Allah, to Whom you shall be gathered"

The passage ends where all law in this surah ends: "And have Taqwa of Allah to Whom you shall be gathered back." Drawing on At-Tabari (whose summary the translators of Ibn Kathir supply here, since Ibn Kathir's own commentary breaks off), the meaning is: fear Allah and beware of His might by obeying what He commands and avoiding what He forbids in these ayat, for to Him is your return and destination, and with Him is the reward of the obedient and the reckoning of the defiant.

That final clause explains the whole passage. These are rules almost impossible to police — a bird taken quietly in a desert camp, a hint given to a hunting companion. Their enforcement rests not on courts (ʿAta' said the authorities impose no punishment even for a repeat offense) but on the certainty of the gathering before Allah, Who — as ayah 94 said at the outset — is testing "who fears Him in the unseen." For the pilgrim, ihram becomes a school of exactly that fear: hands stayed from what they could easily seize, because Allah is watching where no one else is.

passages.title: The Ka'bah as a sanctuary of well-being
passages.tafsir:
# The Ka'bah as a Sanctuary of Well-Being (5:97–99)

This passage steps back from the legal rulings that precede it and lifts the reader's gaze to the Ka'bah itself: Allah declares that He has made the Sacred House — together with the sacred month, the sacrificial animals, and their garlands — the very support on which people's stability and safety rest. The passage then turns that observation into a lesson about Allah's knowledge (end of ayah 97), balances hope and fear in His attributes (ayah 98), and closes by defining the Prophet's ﷺ role: to convey the message, while judgement belongs to Allah alone (ayah 99). What holds the three ayat together is a single movement — from a visible, earthly proof of Allah's care and power to the unseen realities it is meant to teach.

**A note on the sources.** For these particular ayat, the printed Tafsir of Ibn Kathir carries an editorial admission: in all existing copies, Ibn Kathir explained ayah 96 but left ayat 97–99 without comment, so the editors supplied a summary from Ibn Jarir at-Tabari, "the Imam of Tafsir." The classical commentary below from that source is therefore at-Tabari's, as summarized within Ibn Kathir's tafsir.

## Why "the Ka'bah, the Sacred House"?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens with the words themselves. In Arabic, *Ka'bah* is simply the name for a square structure — and it was not unique. An Arab tribe, Khath'am, had built another house bearing the same name, al-Ka'bah al-Yamaniyah. So the Qur'an adds the defining title *al-Bayt al-Haram*, "the Sacred House," to distinguish the House of Allah from any pretender to the name. At-Tabari adds that "Haram" — sacred, inviolable — is not limited to the building: the sanctity covers the entire sacred boundary around Makkah, within which Allah prohibited hunting its game and cutting its trees or grass.

The word to sit with is **qiyāman** — rendered "a sanctuary of well-being" in the translation above, and "an asylum of security and benefits for mankind" in the translation of the ayah given in Ibn Kathir's tafsir; at-Tabari's own summarized commentary speaks of an "asylum of safety." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *qiyām* and *qiwām* are verbal nouns referring to *that on which the stability and survival of something depends* — the thing that holds another thing up. So the ayah is saying something stronger than "the Ka'bah is a safe place": the Ka'bah and its adjuncts are the cause and source of people's constancy, survival, and tranquility. And *al-nās*, "the people," is general: in context it embraces the people of Makkah and of Arabia especially, but ultimately human beings of the whole world.

## How a house kept the peace when nothing else could

At-Tabari's explanation is striking in its realism. Allah made the Ka'bah an asylum of safety *for a people who had no chief* — no ruler to prevent the strong from transgressing against the weak, the evil from the good-doers, the oppressors from the oppressed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same picture at length: peace is normally kept by government and law, but Jahiliyyah Arabia had no formal government and no general law. Its politics were tribal; one tribe could attack another's life, property, and honour at will, so no one ever truly enjoyed security. Into that lawlessness, Allah — with His perfect power — made the Sacred House in Makkah stand in the place of a strong government. He impressed its reverence so deeply on people's hearts that, as at-Tabari puts it, these sacred symbols functioned "just like the chief who is obeyed by his followers, and who upholds harmony and public safety."

The commentary gives an unforgettable measure of that awe: in an age proverbial for tribal vendetta, a son who met the killer of his own father inside the Haram would lower his gaze and walk away.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān illustrates the same reverence from the Prophet's ﷺ own life. In the sixth year of Hijrah, he and a group of his Companions entered the state of iḥrām (the pilgrim's consecration) for ʿUmrah and set out for the Sacred House. Stopping at Hudaybiyah, near the limits of the Haram, he sent ʿUthman al-Ghani (may Allah be pleased with him) with some companions to assure the chiefs of Makkah that the Muslims had come not to fight but to perform ʿUmrah. When the Makkans' representative came, the Prophet ﷺ recognised him as an upholder of the sanctities of the House and ordered that the marked sacrificial animals be brought before him. Seeing them, the man conceded that such people should never be barred from the House of Allah. Even in the hearts of the Muslims' enemies, the signs of pilgrimage commanded protection.

## The four supports

Ayah 97 names not one sanctuary but four, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān titles its commentary accordingly — "Four Sources of Tranquility":

- **The Ka'bah, the Sacred House** — the anchor of the whole system.
- **The sacred month (al-shahr al-ḥarām).** Because the word is singular, most commentators take it as Dhul-Hijjah, the month of the Hajj rites; others hold that the singular denotes the category, embracing all the sacred months. During these months the whole of Arabia treated fighting and killing as forbidden — even outside the Haram — and some had included Rajab among them.
- **The hady** — an animal being taken for sacrifice in the Haram. Arab custom was never to obstruct anyone travelling with such animals; the offerings themselves became a passport of peace.
- **The qalā'id** — plural of *qilādah*, a garland. A pilgrim would hang a garland on his sacrificial animal's neck (and such signs marked the pilgrim himself) so that everyone would know: this person is bound for Hajj — do not molest him. Even the worst men of the age would not harm someone bearing these signs.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the last three are really adjuncts of the first: reverence for the sacred month, the offerings, and the garlands is part of the reverence of the House itself. And at-Tabari notes the transformation Islam wrought: these symbols, sacred already in Jahiliyyah and the means by which people's affairs were guided and protected, "with Islam became the symbols of their Hajj, their rituals, and the direction of the prayer."

## The mainstay of the world

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the meaning of *qiyāman lil-nās* further, under the heading "Baytullah is the Mainstay of the Universe." As long as people across the world keep turning toward the House in their prayer, and the Hajj continues to be performed by those on whom it is obligatory, the world will keep going and remain safe; were that reverence ever to cease — a year in which no one performed Hajj or faced the House in prayer — the world itself would face mass punishment. The commentary cites the respected master of tafsir ʿAṭāʾ (as related in al-Bahr al-Muhit) for this idea that the House is the pillar of the world's continuance. And it answers the natural question — *what possible connection is there between the universe's order and a building?* — with humility: we do not know the reality of the link between magnet and iron either, yet the attraction is real. This connection belongs to the realm of the spirit, knowable only because the Creator has told us; but the House being the cause of peace for Makkah and Arabia is a matter of plain, long-observed history.

The commentators differed over the precise sense of "stability for people": some said it means the House and the Haram were made a place of peace for everyone; others, that it refers to Makkah's sustenance — for what does not grow there keeps reaching its people from all over the world by Allah's grace; still others, that it points to the esteem in which the custodians of the House were held. Imam al-Razi resolves the difference beautifully: there is no contradiction, for Allah has made the House the source of betterment, prosperity, and success — material and spiritual, in this life and as a road to the Hereafter — for all peoples, with a particular share of its outward and inward blessings for Arabia and Makkah.

## "That you may know" — the point of it all

Ayah 97 does not end with the sanctuary; it ends with knowledge: *that you may know that Allah has knowledge of all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth.* At-Tabari draws the connection: the One who set up these symbols that secure your life and livelihood — visible proof of wisdom working for your benefit — is the same One who knows everything in the heavens and the earth that serves your immediate or eventual good. And His knowledge is not abstract: none of your deeds ever escapes His observation, and He will count them, rewarding good with good and requiting evil in kind. The sanctuary you can see is an argument for the reckoning you cannot.

## The two-edged reminder and the Messenger's task

Ayah 98 then holds up both faces of that reckoning at once: *Know that Allah is severe in punishment and that Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.* At-Tabari links it directly to what preceded: the Lord who knows your deeds, public and secret, is severe toward those who defy Him — yet He pardons those who obey and repent, "more Merciful than to punish them for the sins that they repented from." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the pairing as a statement about the law itself: the boundaries of ḥalāl and ḥarām rest on perfect wisdom, so following them brings nothing but good, while flouting them invites ruin — and even then, Allah does not punish instantly; the doors of His forgiveness stay open for those who repent and feel ashamed of what they have done. Fear and hope are given in a single breath, and neither is allowed to cancel the other.

Ayah 99 seals the passage: *The Messenger's duty is but to convey.* The Prophet ﷺ is charged with delivering Allah's injunctions — no more. Whether people then believe or disbelieve, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the profit and the loss are theirs alone; their rejection brings no loss to the Messenger. And at-Tabari completes the thought with the ayah's second half: Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal — what the tongue announces and what the heart hides, "be it of faith, disbelief, certainty, doubt or hypocrisy." Allah cannot be deceived. In His Hand alone are reward and punishment, and He alone is worthy to be feared, obeyed, and never disobeyed.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with a settled orientation. The Ka'bah is not merely a destination but a standing sign — proof, witnessed across centuries, that Allah actively upholds human security and sustenance, and therefore that His commands of lawful and unlawful proceed from the same wisdom and care. The response it asks for is the one the ayat themselves name: honour what Allah has made sacred, take His knowledge of your open and hidden deeds seriously, hold fear of His punishment together with hope in His forgiveness — and understand that once the message has reached you, the outcome of accepting or refusing it rests with no one but yourself.

passages.title: Good and evil are not equal; needless questions
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat teach two attitudes that make a person fit to receive Allah's law. First (ayah 100): judge things by their quality, not their quantity — the pure and the impure can never be equal, however impressive the sheer bulk of the impure looks. Second (ayat 101–102): receive what Allah has legislated with gratitude and restraint, and do not pester revelation with needless questions, for a community before this one asked such questions and became disbelievers on their account. What holds the passage together is a single idea: sound religion is not about *more* — more possessions, more rulings, more questions — but about what is pure, and about contentment with what Allah has given.

## Ayah 100: the pure and the impure can never be equal

The verse turns on two Arabic words. **Al-khabīth** and **al-ṭayyib** are antonyms: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *ṭayyib* refers to what is best and purest in anything, and *khabīth* to what is most condemned and evil. The majority of commentators, it notes, take *khabīth* here to mean the ḥarām (forbidden, impure) and *ṭayyib* the ḥalāl (lawful, pure) — and because the words are general, the verse covers all three domains at once: wealth that is lawful or unlawful, deeds and morals that are virtuous or vicious, and human beings themselves who are good or bad.

Ibn Kathir compresses the verse's message into one line: **the little permissible is better than the abundant evil.** And the address "so have taqwā of Allah, O men of understanding (*ulū al-albāb*)" is pointed: it is those with sound minds who are told to abandon the impermissible and let the permissible be sufficient for them, "in order that you may be successful" — in this life and the Hereafter.

**Why "even though the abundance of the bad may please you"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on this clause. Onlookers are sometimes awed by how widespread evil and impure things are — they seem to be "winning the day" — and people begin to take those very things to be good just because they have spread everywhere. The Qur'an names this for what it is: a disease of human knowledge and consciousness, not evidence of truth. Look honestly at the world, Maʿārif observes, and in almost every comparison — belief against disbelief, honesty against debauchery, justice against oppression, knowledge against ignorance — you will find more of the worse thing. So numerical abundance can never be an absolute proof that something is good or true; a hand-count of fifty-one against forty-nine cannot become the touchstone of right. (Maʿārif is careful to add the caveat: Islam does allow majority opinion a role in resolving practical disputes — such as choosing a leader when no authority exists to decide — but that is a peace-keeping device, never a mechanism that turns what the majority adopts into what is ḥalāl and true.)

**Two stories the commentators attach to this verse.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports narrations that when liquor and its trade were prohibited, a former liquor dealer asked the Prophet ﷺ whether the savings from that business could be spent in some good cause. The Prophet ﷺ answered that if he spent it on jihad or Hajj or the like, it would not be worth even the weight of a mosquito's tiny feather — for Allah accepts only what is pure and lawful. And centuries later the verse was lived out again: citing Ibn Abi Hatim, Al-Durr Al-Manthur (as related in Maʿārif) reports that when ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, the rightly-guided caliph of the Tābiʿīn era, stopped the impermissible taxes of his predecessors and returned wrongly-taken properties, the treasury emptied. A governor wrote complaining about the collapse in revenue. The caliph answered him with this very verse — "The bad and the good are not equal, even though you are attracted by the profusion of the bad" — and told him: those before you filled the treasury with injustice; you match it with justice, let the treasury stand reduced, and do not care. Ḥalāl wealth and ḥarām wealth, Maʿārif adds, are not equal even in this world: the real benefit, comfort and blessing that come through the lawful never come through the unlawful.

## Ayat 101–102: leave what Allah has left unsaid

Ayah 101 then addresses the believers directly: "Do not ask about matters which, if made clear to you, may cause you trouble." This ayah, Ibn Kathir explains, refers to good conduct that Allah is teaching His believing servants — forbidding them from asking about useless things, since the answers, if given, might prove troublesome for them and difficult on their ears.

**The day of questions.** The occasion behind the verse is preserved vividly. Al-Bukhari recorded from Anas bin Malik that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave a speech unlike anything Anas had heard before, saying: "If you but know what I know, you will laugh little and cry a lot." The Companions covered their faces and the sound of crying came from their chests. A man asked, "Who is my father?" and the Prophet ﷺ named him — and the ayah "Ask not about things…" was later revealed. Muslim, Ahmad, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i also recorded this hadith. In the fuller account recorded in the Two Sahihs, people had questioned the Messenger ﷺ until he became angry; he ascended the minbar and said, "You will not ask me about anything today but I will explain it to you." The Companions feared it was the commencement of a momentous event; Anas looked right and left and saw only people covering their faces, crying. An argumentative man, said to be the son of someone other than his true father, asked, "Who is my father?" — and was told, "Your father is Hudhafah." Then ʿUmar, seeing the anger on the Prophet's ﷺ face, stood and said: "We accept Allah as our Lord, Islam as our religion and Muhammad ﷺ as our Messenger, I seek refuge with Allah from the evil of the Fitan (trials in life and religion)." The Prophet ﷺ said, "I have never witnessed both goodness and evil like I have today. Paradise and the Fire were shown to me and I saw them before that wall." Al-Bukhari also recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas that some people used to question the Messenger ﷺ to mock him — one asking "Who is my father?", another, having lost his camel, "Where is my camel?" — and Allah sent down this ayah about them.

**The Hajj question.** A second occasion concerns law rather than mockery. Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAli — At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah also recorded it — that when the verse of Hajj (3:97) was revealed, people asked the Prophet ﷺ, "Is it required every year?" He stayed silent; they asked again, and a third time, until he said: **"No, and had I said 'yes', it would have become obligated, and had it become obligated, you would not be able to bear it."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same background as narrated in Sahih Muslim, naming the questioner as al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis, and adds the Prophet's ﷺ instruction that followed: things about which I give you no command, leave them as they are; communities before you were damned through this very proliferation of questioning — their needless enquiries turned optional things into obligations, which they then disobeyed.

This reveals something remarkable about the moment in which these Companions lived: while the Qur'an was still descending, a question could actually *draw down* legislation — which is why the verse says, "if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be made plain to you." Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet's ﷺ words recorded in the Sahih: **"Leave me as I have left you, those before you were destroyed because of many questions and disputing with their Prophets."** Another hadith Ibn Kathir cites warns that the worst criminal among the Muslims is he who asks if a matter is unlawful, and it becomes unlawful because of his asking about it. And an authentic hadith he quotes maps out the whole terrain of the law: "Allah, the Most Honored, has ordained some obligations, so do not ignore them; has set some limits, so do not trespass them; has prohibited some things, so do not commit them; and has left some things without rulings, out of mercy for you, not that He forgot them, so do not ask about them." Divine silence, in other words, is not a gap in the religion; it is deliberate spaciousness, a mercy. Meanwhile "Allah has forgiven that" (ayah 101) reassures the Companions about their past questioning: what went before is pardoned, "and Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Forbearing."

**Ayah 102: the warning of history.** "Some people before you asked such questions, then became disbelievers on their account." Ibn Kathir explains the mechanism: earlier communities asked, were answered, and then refused to believe the answers — because they had asked not to gain guidance but to mock and defy. The rulings were made plain to them and benefited them nothing. The question itself was never the point; the heart behind it was.

## After revelation ended — does this still apply?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a subtle inference from the clause "while the Qur'an is being revealed": by tying disclosure to the period of revelation, the verse quietly signals that after the Qur'an's completion, prophethood (*nubuwwah*) and revelation (*waḥy*) would be discontinued — no new injunctions would descend, and no one's secret would be disclosed from heaven. Yet the prohibition on needless questioning does not lapse with revelation, because a second reason for it remains: it wastes time, one's own and other people's. The Prophet ﷺ said that one of the qualities making someone a good Muslim is that he leaves what is unnecessary. Maʿārif applies this frankly: those who busy themselves investigating things like the name of the mother of Mūsā (peace be upon him) or the precise dimensions of the Ark of Nūḥ (peace be upon him) are absorbed in what has no effect on conduct — and, it observes, such people are mostly unaware of the basics of their own religion, because indulging the wasteful invariably deprives one of the necessary. One important boundary: the vast juristic literature in which scholars answered hypothetical legal questions does *not* fall under this censure — later generations genuinely needed those answers, so that work was provision, not idle curiosity.

## Living these ayat

The two halves of the passage converge on a single discipline of the heart. From ayah 100: stop being impressed by volume — of wealth, of numbers, of crowds — and weigh everything by purity instead; let a small ḥalāl income, a minority position that is true, be enough for you. From ayat 101–102: receive the religion as it was given — do the commanded, avoid the forbidden, and treat Allah's silences as the mercy they are, rather than interrogating them into burdens. Both are summed up in the verse's own closing address: this is what taqwā looks like for "men of understanding" — and it is the road, ayah 100 promises, to success in this life and the Hereafter.

passages.title: Pagan livestock superstitions and blind imitation
passages.tafsir:
# Superstition, Blind Imitation, and Where Responsibility Ends (5:103–105)

This passage dismantles two things at once: the invented livestock rituals of pre-Islamic Arabia, and the mentality that kept them alive — "this is what we found our fathers doing." It then closes with a word of comfort and clarity for the believers: once you have held to guidance and done your duty, the stubbornness of those who refuse it cannot harm you. The three ayat form one movement: a false religion exposed (103), the excuse behind it refuted (104), and the believer's own responsibility defined (105).

## Ayah 103: the four animals Allah never sanctified

The pagans of Arabia had built an elaborate system of taboos around their own livestock, dedicating certain animals to the idols and then forbidding themselves the very benefits — milk, meat, wool, riding — that Allah had made lawful. Ayah 103 names four categories and sweeps them all away with the words *mā jaʿala Allāhu* — "Allah has never ordained…"

Commentators differed in explaining the four terms, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests it is possible that each word was applied to a different situation. It limits itself to the explanation of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, precisely because it appears in the Sahih of al-Bukhari:

- **Baḥīrah** — a female camel whose milk was dedicated to the idols; no one was allowed to milk her.
- **Sāʾibah** — a female camel let loose for free pasture for the idols; nothing could be carried on her.
- **Waṣīlah** — a female camel set free for the idols because she gave birth to a she-camel in her first delivery and then another she-camel in her second — two females without a male between them.
- **Ḥām** — a male camel freed from work for the idols after it had finished a number of matings assigned to it; such a camel was called a Ḥāmī.

Ibn Kathir records further reports from other narrators whose explanations differ. Ibn ʿAbbās (through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah) described the Baḥīrah as a camel that had delivered five times: if the fifth was a male they slaughtered it for the men only, excluding the women; if a female, they slit her ears and proclaimed, "This is a Baḥīrah" — no one allowed to milk her. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said the Sāʾibah was a camel that bore ten females in a row, after which no one could ride, shear, or milk her — except for a guest. Abū Rawq and as-Suddī add that a man who succeeded in some venture, recovered from illness, or grew in wealth would set an animal free for the idols in gratitude. On the Ḥām, al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that a stud camel that performed ten matings would be called a Ḥām and set free — and in another report, through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as the male camel whose offspring had produced offspring of their own: they would proclaim, "This camel has ḥamā (protected) its back," and thereafter carry nothing on him, cut none of his wool, and let him graze and drink wherever he pleased. Ibn Wahb heard Imam Malik describe the Ḥām as a stud camel who, having finished his assigned matings, would have peacock feathers placed on him and be turned loose. Ibn Kathir notes that still other opinions were mentioned in explanation of the ayah.

Two features of the system deserve notice, because the Qurʼān's rebuke lands on both. First, the animals were consecrated *to idols* — pure shirk (associating partners with Allah). Second, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses, these people were seizing the office of the Law-Giver: declaring lawful things forbidden by their own opinion, restricting what Allah had permitted, and — the "cruel joke," in its words — imagining that these polytheistic customs would earn them Allah's pleasure and nearness. Notice also the recurring discrimination in the reports: meat from these animals given "to the men only and not the women." An invented religion serves the interests of its inventors.

## The man who started it all

Ibn Kathir traces this whole system to a single historical figure. Abū Hurayrah reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I saw ʿAmr bin ʿĀmir al-Khuzāʿī pulling his intestines behind him in the Fire, and he was the first to start the practice of Sāʾibah." Muslim and an-Nasāʾī recorded this hadith. Imam Ahmad recorded a similar report from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, in which the Prophet ﷺ identified him as "the first to start the practice of Sāʾibah and worshipping idols."

Ibn Kathir explains who this was: ʿAmr, son of Luḥayy ibn Qamʿah, a chief of Khuzāʿah — the tribe that had custodianship of the Kaʿbah after Jurhum and before Quraysh. He was the first to change the religion of Ibrāhīm in Makkah, bringing idol-worship into the Hijaz, calling people to sacrifice to idols, and instituting these animal rituals along with the other rites of Jāhiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance). The lesson is sobering: one influential man innovates, generations canonize it as sacred ancestral religion — and the Prophet ﷺ saw him being punished in the Fire.

## From the Sunnah: "all the wealth Allah has given you is lawful for you"

Ibn Abī Ḥātim collected a hadith on this subject — transmitted from Abū Isḥāq as-Subayʿī, from al-Aḥwaṣ al-Jushamī, from his father Mālik bin Naḍlah — in which Mālik related that he came to the Prophet ﷺ wearing old clothes. The Prophet ﷺ asked whether he had property; he said yes — camels, sheep, horses, slaves. The Prophet ﷺ said, "If Allah gives you wealth, then let it show on you." Then he asked whether Mālik's camels were born with whole ears, and whether he would take a knife and cut the ears of some, saying "This is a Baḥīrah," and tear the ears of others, saying "This is sacred." When Mālik said yes, he ﷺ said: "Then do not do that, for all the wealth that Allah has given you is allowed for you" — and then recited this very ayah. Imam Ahmad also recorded this hadith through another chain.

The hadith turns the ayah from history into instruction. The animals are born whole — *Allah's* making — and the knife that mutilates the ear is the human hand imposing a false sanctity on what Allah left lawful.

## Ayat 103–104: the lie, and the excuse that shields it

Allah then says: "But those who disbelieve invent lies against Allah, and most of them have no understanding." Ibn Kathir explains: Allah never legislated these rituals and does not count them as obedience. The idolaters made them into acts of worship by which they hoped to draw near to Allah — but they will never bring them near; these innovations only harm their authors.

When such people are called "to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," their whole defense is one sentence: "Enough for us is that which we found our fathers following." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the background from al-Durr al-Manthūr (from Ibn Abī Ḥātim): when someone accepted Islam, his people would shame him for implying his forefathers had been wrong — as if loyalty to ancestors outweighed loyalty to truth. This verse came down about that compounded error.

The Qurʼān's reply is a single devastating question: "even though their fathers had no knowledge whatsoever and no guidance?" Ibn Kathir draws out the edge of it: if the fathers neither understood nor found the way, then whoever follows them is more ignorant and more astray than they were.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the fathers-argument "the master argument of Shayṭān," which has felled millions of otherwise sensible people, and extracts from the ayah a complete principle for whom to follow. It is entirely reasonable for the one who does not know to follow the one who does — the uninitiated following the experienced, the ignorant following the learned; this, it notes, is the reality behind following the Mujtahid Imams, who know the religion and practice it. What is senseless is abandoning the standards of knowledge, reason, and guidance and following someone simply because he came first — or because he draws a crowd. The commentary is blunt about majorities too: the mass of people is never the wisest or most virtuous portion of it, so numbers can never be the criterion of truth. From ayah 105's opening it derives two tests for any leader worth following: **ʿilm** (knowledge — knowing the destination and the way to it) and **ihtidāʾ** (guidance — actually traveling that way himself). Ancestry, popularity, wealth, and power all fail as criteria; following a leader who lacks knowledge and guidance is, in its phrase, "signing one's own warrant of destruction."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notices *how* the Qurʼān criticizes here. It does not say bluntly "your fathers were ignorant." It asks a question — could following them be reasonable *if* they had neither knowledge nor guidance? — a subtle, interrogative style that exposes the error without needlessly wounding the listener. That is itself a lesson in how to correct people.

## Ayah 105: "You are accountable only for yourselves" — and what that does not mean

After confronting this obstinacy, Allah turns to the believers: "O you who believe! Take care of yourselves. If you follow the right guidance, no hurt can come to you from those who are in error. The return of you all is to Allah, then He will inform you about all that you used to do."

Ibn Kathir explains the plain sense: whoever reforms himself is not harmed by the wickedness of the wicked, relatives or otherwise. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the connection to what preceded: the Muslims grieved over people who clung to these customs, and this ayah comforts them — you have conveyed the truth and done your duty; if some insist on error, their straying brings no loss upon you.

But the ayah has a famous misreading, and the sources take pains to correct it. Some took it to mean: mind your own conduct and leave others alone — no need to command good or forbid evil. Ibn Kathir records from Imam Ahmad that Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq stood up, praised Allah, and said: "O people! You read this ayah and you explain it the wrong way. I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'If the people witness evil and do not change it, then Allah is about to send His punishment to encompass them.'" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes this narration is also in Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, with Abu Dawud's wording speaking of people who see an oppressor and fail to stop him. Qays, who transmitted the khutbah, adds that he heard Abū Bakr say: "O people! Beware of lying, for lying contradicts faith."

So the ayah does not cancel *al-amr bil-maʿrūf wa'l-nahy ʿani'l-munkar* — bidding the fair and forbidding the unfair — which the Qurʼān elsewhere makes a defining duty of this community. When doubts arose at its revelation, the Prophet ﷺ himself clarified that it does not contradict that duty. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, as reported in al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, read it precisely this way: keep doing everything your religion obligates — including jihad and bidding the fair — and *then* the straying of others cannot harm you. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the condition in the ayah itself — *idhā ihtadaytum*, "if you are on the right path" — settles the matter, since one who has abandoned the duty of enjoining good is not on the right path in the first place.

Al-Durr al-Manthūr preserves a scene with ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar that shows the balance lived out. People told him of a bitter dispute in which parties were branding each other polytheists, and he replied: Do you think I am going to tell you to go and fight them? Never! Go, speak to them softly. If they listen, good. If not, stop worrying about them and take care of your own selves — and he recited this very ayah.

## Maʿrūf and munkar — and where honest disagreement stands outside them

Since the duty turns on these two words, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses to define them. *Maʿrūf* comes from *maʿrifah*, to know and recognize; *munkar* from *inkār*, to fail to recognize or to deny — the Qurʼān itself pairs them: "they recognize the blessing of Allah, then they deny it" (16:83). Hence al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's definition in Mufradāt al-Qurʼān: maʿrūf is what reason (ʿaql) and revelation (sharʿ) know to be good; munkar is what they treat as strange and bad.

The choice of these words — rather than simply "obedience and sin" — carries, the commentary suggests, a refinement: matters of legitimate ijtihād (scholarly reasoning where the Qurʼān and Sunnah leave room for interpretation) fall outside the scope of "forbidding the unfair." Where competent Mujtahid Imams reached different bona fide conclusions, neither view is religiously censurable; both sides stand within the maʿrūf. The Companions and the generation after them differed in ijtihād, debated and questioned one another's reasoning — but never called one another sinners over it. (Mufti Taqi Usmani's note adds the necessary caveat: this immunity belongs only to qualified mujtahids, not to anyone airing conjectures.) Writings that spread hatred over such issues, the commentary concludes, are not "bidding the fair" at all.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with a clear division of labor. Do not sanctify what Allah has not sanctified — enjoy His lawful gifts, and let His blessing show on you rather than surrendering it to superstition. Test every leader and every inherited custom against knowledge and guidance, never against "this is what we found our people doing." Speak against wrong — softly, as Ibn ʿUmar counseled, and wisely, as the Qurʼān's own gentle question models — because silence in the face of evil invites a punishment that engulfs everyone. And then rest: "The return of you all is to Allah, then He will inform you about all that you used to do." Your account is your own; having held to guidance and done your duty, no one else's straying can harm you.

passages.title: Witnessing a dying person's bequest
passages.tafsir:
This passage lays down a detailed legal procedure for witnessing the bequest of a person on the point of death, especially when death strikes far from home. The three ayat run as one connected passage: ayah 106 sets out who may witness a dying person's will and how their honesty is secured by a solemn oath; ayah 107 provides the remedy if those witnesses turn out to have betrayed the trust; and ayah 108 explains the wisdom behind the whole mechanism. Ibn Kathir opens his commentary by calling it "a glorious ruling from Allah."

## The story behind the revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the occasion that brought these ayat down. A Muslim named Budayl travelled to Syria on business in the company of Tamim and ʿAdiyy, who were at that time Christians. In Syria, Budayl fell ill. He quietly wrote out a list of his belongings and placed it in his baggage without telling his companions. When his sickness grew serious, he called the two men, made his will before them, and asked them to deliver everything to his heirs.

They did deliver the belongings — but first they removed a silver bowl worked with gold. When the heirs found the dead man's own inventory in his baggage, they noticed the missing bowl and asked the two executors whether Budayl had sold anything or spent unusually during his illness. The answer was no. The case came before the Prophet ﷺ. Since the heirs had no witnesses, the two Christians were put on oath; they declared that they had neither betrayed the trust nor hidden anything, and the verdict went in their favour.

Some time later the truth surfaced: the two had sold the bowl to a goldsmith in Makkah for a thousand dirhams. Confronted, they now claimed they had bought it from the deceased — but they could produce no witnesses to any such sale. The heirs appealed again to the Prophet ﷺ. This time the situation was reversed: the executors' own admission that the bowl had passed through their hands showed their earlier testimony to be false, and the oath passed to the other side. Two of the closest relatives of the deceased gave a sworn statement that the bowl was owned by Budayl and that the two men had lied in their oath, and the price of the bowl was handed over to the heirs.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the verses against this case step by step, matching each stage of the dispute to the wording of the passage.

## Ayah 106: the witnesses and the oath

The ayah instructs the believers that when death approaches, the will should be made before **two just witnesses "from among you"** — that is, Muslims, as Ibn Kathir explains. Then comes the concession: **"or two others from outside"** — non-Muslims, meaning the People of the Book according to Ibn ʿAbbas (as recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim). Ibn Kathir notes the two conditions that permit this: being on a journey, and the calamity of death striking with no Muslims present. He cites Sharih Al-Qadi, as recorded by Ibn Jarir: the testimony of Jews and Christians is not allowed except while travelling, and even then only to witness the dictation of a will.

If doubt later arises about the witnesses' honesty — as it did in Budayl's case — the ayah says: **"Detain them both after the Salah"** and put them on oath. Which prayer? Al-ʿAwfi reports from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is the ʿAsr prayer, and the same is reported from Saʿid bin Jubayr, Ibrahim an-Nakhaʿi, Qatadah, ʿIkrimah and Muhammad bin Sirin; az-Zuhri said simply after a congregational Muslim prayer. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Qurtubi) explains why ʿAsr in particular: the People of the Book held that hour in esteem, and telling a lie at that time was particularly prohibited among them.

The wording of the oath itself is spelled out in the ayah, and every phrase carries weight. *"We wish not for any worldly gain in this"* — no price of this fleeting world will buy our testimony. *"Even though he be our near relative"* — kinship will not bend the truth. And most striking: *"We shall not hide the testimony of Allah."* Ibn Kathir pauses on this phrase — the testimony is attributed to **Allah** Himself, as a way of honouring it and magnifying its significance. To distort, alter or conceal it is to tamper with something that belongs to Allah, "for then indeed we should be of the sinful."

## Ayah 107: when the witnesses betray the trust

If it is then **discovered that the two witnesses "had been guilty of sin"** — that they cheated or stole from the estate, as Ibn Kathir puts it — the oath transfers to the other side. Two of the nearest rightful heirs stand in their place and swear by Allah: *"Our testimony is truer than theirs, and we have not trespassed."* In Budayl's case this was exactly what happened: the executors' claim of purchase had no witnesses, so the oath was given to the heirs that no such sale had taken place to the best of their knowledge, and judgment went to them.

Ibn Kathir observes that here **preference is given to the heirs' oath**, and he draws a parallel to the oath taken by the relatives of a murder victim in defence of his honour — a subject, he notes, discussed in the chapters on oaths in the books of Ahkam (legal rulings).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the underlying courtroom logic: the claimant (*muddaʿī*, plaintiff) must produce evidence first; if he cannot, the respondent (*muddaʿā ʿalayh*) is put on oath and wins. But when the respondents' own oath is exposed as false — as when the two Christians admitted the bowl had been in their hands — the balance flips, and the oath returns to the wronged party.

## Ayah 108: the wisdom of the procedure

The closing ayah states why this design works: **"That should make it closer (to the fact) that their testimony would be in its true nature."** Ibn Kathir explains the double deterrent. First, the solemnity of swearing by Allah — whom even the People of the Book glorify and revere — may itself move a witness to tell the truth. Second, the fear of exposure: a lying witness knows that if suspicion arises, *"other oaths would be admitted after their oaths"* — the heirs will swear in their place, the fraud will be uncovered publicly, and the heirs will recover what was concealed.

The passage then closes the legal machinery with a spiritual seal: **"Have Taqwa of Allah and listen"** — be conscious of Allah in all your affairs and obey, as Ibn Kathir glosses it — "and Allah guides not the rebellious people," those who refuse His obedience and His law.

## What the scholars drew from these ayat

**The witness of non-Muslims.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that Imam Abu Hanifah deduced from *"or two others not from you"* that the testimony of non-Muslims on behalf of one another is permissible: if their witness was once accepted even in a Muslim's case, it is accepted all the more between themselves. The commentary holds that the acceptance of non-Muslim witnesses *for Muslims* was later abrogated by the verse "And have two witnesses from among your men" (2:282), while their testimony for each other remains valid. In support of Imam Abu Hanifah's position, Maʿārif cites (from Jassas) a hadith report of a Jewish man brought before the Prophet ﷺ for adultery, his face smeared with black soot by his people; after hearing the testimony of the witnesses, the Prophet ﷺ ordered the punishment of stoning — testimony given by non-Muslims, and acted upon.

**Detention for a right.** From the word *tahbisūnahumā* ("you shall detain them both"), Qurtubi — as cited in Maʿārif — derived that a person who genuinely owes something to another may be detained until the right is recovered.

**Solemnising the oath (taghlīz).** Choosing a sacred time or place for an oath — after ʿAsr, in the mosque — is permissible as a way of making it weightier, but it is not legally compulsory; Maʿārif notes it depends on the judge's discretion.

**The executor (wasiyy).** Maʿārif also defines the *wasiyy*: the person with whom the dying person entrusts his property to be delivered to others. There may be one or several. That the wasiyy be a just Muslim is better, but not a strict requirement — whether the will is made at home or on a journey.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a subtle point about the placement of this passage: the preceding ayat dealt with religious duties, and now the Qurʼān turns to worldly affairs — a reminder that the same Lord who, in His mercy, secures His servants' Hereafter also cares for their sustenance and their rights in this world. The practical instruction is direct: do not leave your final wishes to memory and goodwill. Have your will witnessed — by upright people — so that your heirs are protected and disputes can be resolved after you are gone. And for anyone ever called to witness or to swear: the ayah has already written your oath for you. No worldly price, no tie of kinship, justifies bending testimony — because testimony, in the Qurʼān's own words, belongs to Allah.

passages.title: The Day of gathering and Allah's favours upon Jesus
passages.tafsir:
# The Day of Gathering and Allah's Favours upon Jesus (5:109–111)

As Sūrat al-Māʾidah moves toward its closing stages, the scene shifts suddenly from law to the Last Day. These three ayat open a window onto the Day of Resurrection: Allah gathers all the messengers and asks them how their nations responded to them (ayah 109), then turns to ʿĪsā (Jesus), son of Maryam — peace be upon them — recounting favour after favour that He bestowed upon him (ayah 110), down to the faith He put in the hearts of ʿĪsā's disciples (ayah 111). What holds the passage together is a single courtroom scene: first the messengers in general, then one Messenger in particular whose community went astray concerning him — and every favour listed affirms that he was Allah's servant, empowered only \"by My permission,\" never a god.

## Why the Last Day appears here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the placement. The sūrah has just laid down a run of injunctions, with inducements to practise them and warnings against opposing them. Now, in the Qurʼān's characteristic style, the reader is reminded of the frightening happenings of the Day of Qiyāmah (Resurrection), \"so that obedience is promoted and antagonism is checked.\" And toward the closing stages of the sūrah, it returns to its long dialogue with the People of the Book — this time to establish facts about ʿĪsā عليه السلام which affirm that he was a servant of Allah and negate the error of ascribing divinity to him. The setting of that address, remarkably, is not this world but the plain of the Last Day itself.

## Ayah 109: the first question — and a stunning answer

\"The Day Allah will gather the messengers and say: What was the response you received?\" Ibn Kathir notes that Allah states He will question the Messengers about how their nations answered their teachings, and cites parallel ayat: \"Then surely We shall question those to whom it was sent, and verily We shall question the Messengers\" (7:6), and \"So, by your Lord, We shall certainly call all of them to account, for all that they used to do\" (15:92–93).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why the prophets are singled out. The whole of humanity will be assembled, but the *first* question will be put to the prophets themselves — so that the entire creation may see that on that Day no one, not even the highest and dearest of Allah, is exempt from reckoning. And though the question is addressed to the prophets, it is really aimed at their communities: the prophets will be the first witnesses to what their nations did. For the sinners this is shattering — the very prophets whose intercession they were hoping for are now being asked to account for their communities' conduct. Who, they will wonder, is left to intercede?

Then comes the messengers' reply, one of the most arresting sentences in the Qurʼān: **\"We have no knowledge; surely You, only You, are the Knower of all that is hidden.\"** How can messengers who lived among their people, saw their belief and their hostility, say they have no knowledge? The sources give two complementary answers:

**1. The terror of the Day.** According to Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and as-Suddī — as Ibn Kathir records, with Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also recording it — this reply comes from the horror of that Day: the messengers will become afraid and say, \"We have no knowledge.\"

**2. Adab before the All-Knowing.** Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah, explained it as a response of respect before the Lord, Most Honoured: \"We have no knowledge beyond what we know — and even that, You have more knowledge of it than us.\" Our knowledge grasped only people's visible behaviour, never the secrets of their hearts; next to Allah's encompassing knowledge, it is as if we have no knowledge at all — \"only You are ʿAllām al-Ghuyūb,\" the Knower of all that is hidden.

**ʿIlm versus ẓann.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a precise resolution, citing Imam Rāzī's answer as it appears in Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ. There is a difference between *ʿilm* — perfect certitude — and *ẓann* — well-founded opinion. Even a prophet sitting beside a man can testify to his faith only by ẓann, because real īmān is a secret of the heart which no one can know with certainty without divine revelation. Every community had hypocrites who outwardly professed faith while their hearts were empty. In this world, religious law rightly judges by the outward — the Holy Prophet ﷺ said that we judge on the basis of outward deeds while Allah is Himself the custodian of the secrets of the hearts. But the Day of Resurrection is not a world of opinion and conjecture; it is the day realities are unfolded, when — as Maʿārif cites from Sūrah Yā-Sīn — \"That Day We shall set a seal on their mouths while their hands will speak to Us, and their feet bear witness to all that they did\" (36:65). In a court where only certitude counts, the prophets' answer \"We have no knowledge\" is exactly right: they lack the *certain* knowledge the question demands, and they refer it to the One who possesses it.

**The mercy hidden in their silence.** Maʿārif notices something tender here. The prophets did have well-founded opinions about their communities' obedience and disobedience; they could have reported at least the outward record. Instead they said nothing against their people, resigning everything to the divine knowledge. Prophets are deeply affectionate toward their people and toward Allah's creation; having a legitimate excuse — the lack of certain knowledge — they used it to avoid saying anything adverse against their communities.

**Living under this Day.** Maʿārif draws the practical lesson: if even Allah's noble messengers stand in awe on the grandstands of reckoning, think of what awaits the rest of us — so we should begin preparing now, while this little life is still in our hands. In a hadith of Tirmidhi, the Holy Prophet ﷺ said that no son of Adam will move a step on the Day of Qiyāmah until he is asked five questions: about his life, in what he used it up; about his youth, in what he spent it; about his wealth, from where he earned it and where he spent it; and what he did with what he knew. Maʿārif marvels at the mercy in this: Allah sets the test and, through His Prophet ﷺ, tells us the questions in advance. Whoever still fails after being shown the examination paper — who could be more deprived?

## Ayah 110: \"O ʿĪsā, son of Maryam — remember My favour\"

The scene narrows to one Messenger. Ibn Kathir notes a subtlety of wording: although this address will take place on the Day of Resurrection, Allah speaks of it in the past tense — indicating that it is a foregone matter that will certainly occur. He adds that the ayah contains secrets of the Unseen which Allah revealed to His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ.

Allah then recounts His favours to ʿĪsā one by one, and Ibn Kathir unfolds each:

- **\"My favour to you\"** — I created you from your mother without male intervention, and made you a sign and clear proof of My perfect power over all things.
- **\"And to your mother\"** — I made you testify to her chastity, absolving her of the sin that the unjust, ignorant liars accused her of.
- **\"When I supported you with Rūḥ al-Qudus\"** — the angel Jibrīl. Allah made him a Prophet calling to Allah from the cradle onward: as an infant he declared his mother free of any immorality and proclaimed that he worshipped Allah.
- **\"You spoke to the people in the cradle and in maturity\"** — meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, you *called people to Allah* in childhood and in maturity; the word *tukallim* here means \"invited,\" since an adult merely speaking is nothing strange in itself. The miracle in the cradle was the speech; the wonder in maturity was the mission.
- **\"When I taught you the Book and the Ḥikmah\"** — the power of writing and understanding — **\"and the Tawrāh\"** — which had been revealed to Mūsā, son of ʿImrān, who spoke to Allah directly — **\"and the Injīl.\"**
- **The clay bird, the healing of the blind and the lepers, the raising of the dead** — each explicitly *\"by My permission.\"* You shaped the clay as a bird and blew into it, and it became a flying bird with a soul by Allah's permission; you called the dead and they rose from their graves by Allah's leave, power, intent and will.
- **\"When I restrained the Children of Israel from you\"** — when you brought them the clear proofs, they rejected you, called you a magician (\"This is nothing but evident magic\"), and tried to kill you by crucifixion; \"but I saved you, raised you to Me, purified you from their vulgarity and protected you from their harm.\"

That drumbeat — *by My permission, by My permission* — is the theology of the passage. Every miracle attributed to ʿĪsā was Allah's act through him; the very favours the misguided seized on as proof of his divinity are recited back as proof of his servanthood.

**\"In the cradle — and in *kahl* (middle age).\"** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on this phrase. Speaking in the cradle is self-evidently a miracle; but why mention speaking in middle age, which every adult does? Because, Maʿārif answers, ʿĪsā عليه السلام was raised from the earth *before reaching middle age*. For him to speak to people on earth as a middle-aged man is possible only when he returns to this world — which is the collective belief of the Muslims, established, as Maʿārif says, by clear statements of the Qurʼān and Sunnah. So the ayah quietly contains two miracles: the infant who spoke, and the returning ʿĪsā who will speak again.

**Two audiences, one admonition.** Maʿārif observes that the passage sets the *blessings* (ayah 110) beside the *scene of answerability* — the particular question that will be put to ʿĪsā عليه السلام on the Day of Resurrection, which the sūrah recounts in the verses that follow this passage. By this juxtaposition both wings of Banī Isrāʼīl are addressed: the recounting of blessings rebukes those who insulted, accused and harassed him, while the questioning warns those who ascribed to him divinity or divine sonship. The purpose is to display this scene to Banī Isrāʼīl and to all creation: the one honoured with the titles Rūḥullāh (the Spirit of Allah) and Kalimatullāh (the Word of Allah) will himself hasten, on the plain of the Ḥashr (the Gathering), to plead his being free of what his followers ascribed to him.

## Ayah 111: the disciples — a favour upon ʿĪsā

The final favour: \"And when I inspired (awḥaytu) the Ḥawāriyyīn (the disciples) to believe in Me and My Messenger.\" Ibn Kathir explains that this too is a reminder of Allah's favour *upon ʿĪsā* — that Allah made disciples and companions for him.

The word *awḥaytu* here does not mean prophetic revelation. Ibn Kathir notes it means \"inspired,\" as in Allah's words to the mother of Mūsā, \"And We inspired the mother of Mūsā: Suckle him\" (28:7), and to the bee, \"And your Lord inspired the bee: Take habitations in the mountains…\" (16:68–69). Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said of the Ḥawāriyyūn, \"Allah inspired them,\" and as-Suddī said, \"He put it in their hearts.\"

And the disciples' response seals the passage: **\"We believe — and bear witness that we are Muslims.\"** They answered the inspiration with faith in Allah and His Messenger, and bore witness to it with the word *Muslims* — those who submit to Allah.

## Taking it to heart

The passage asks two things of its reader. First, awe: if the messengers themselves will stand afraid before the questioning, and no one moves a step until asked about his life, youth, wealth and knowledge, then preparation for that Day belongs to *today*. Second, clarity about ʿĪsā عليه السلام: love him as the Qurʼān presents him — miraculously born, divinely aided, mighty in miracles *by Allah's permission*, protected, raised, and returning — a beloved servant and Messenger of Allah, nothing less and nothing more.

passages.title: The disciples request the heavenly table
passages.tafsir:
# The Disciples Request the Heavenly Table (5:112–115)

This passage tells the story that gives the whole sūrah its name: the disciples of ʿĪsā (Jesus), peace be upon him, ask for a *māʾidah* — a table spread with food — to be sent down from heaven, ʿĪsā turns their request into a prayer, and Allah answers with a promise joined to a solemn warning. The four ayat form a single conversation in four voices: the disciples ask (112), they explain themselves (113), ʿĪsā supplicates (114), and Allah responds (115). Ibn Kathir opens his commentary by noting exactly this: *"This is the story of the Māʾidah, the name of which this Sūrah bears, Sūrat Al-Māʾidah,"* and he counts it among the favours Allah granted His servant and Messenger ʿĪsā — accepting his request and sending the table down "as clear proof and unequivocal evidence."

## The request and the gentle rebuke (ayah 112)

The *ḥawāriyyūn* — the disciples, ʿĪsā's close followers — ask: "Can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?" Ibn Kathir explains the key word: **the Māʾidah is the table that has food on it.** He also relays why some scholars said they asked at all: the disciples were poor and deprived, and they wanted a table of food they could eat from every day, so that they would be *more able to perform the acts of worship*. On this reading, the request is not idle curiosity but need — though need expressed in a way that reaches for the miraculous.

ʿĪsā's answer is striking: "Have taqwā of Allah, if you are indeed believers." *Taqwā* is the fear and consciousness of Allah that restrains a person from what displeases Him. Ibn Kathir unpacks the reply: *do not ask for this, for it may become a trial for you — trust in Allah for your provisions, if you are truly believers.* A miracle demanded is a dangerous thing, because once granted it leaves no room for excuse.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the standing lesson from this verse under the heading "A True Believer Should Not Demand Miracles": it does not befit a faith-bearing servant of Allah to test Him with such requests. Rather than demand the supernatural, the believer should seek things like sustenance through the sources Allah has naturally appointed for him. That is the discipline ʿĪsā was teaching his disciples in one sentence.

## The disciples explain themselves (ayah 113)

The disciples do not retract; they clarify. Their answer stacks four motives, and Ibn Kathir walks through each:

- **"We wish to eat thereof"** — the plain human need: we need to eat from it.
- **"and that our hearts be reassured"** — their faith would be strengthened *when we witness it descending from heaven as sustenance for us*.
- **"and to know that you have indeed told us the truth"** — their certainty in ʿĪsā's message would increase, and their knowledge with it.
- **"and that we ourselves be its witnesses"** — they would testify that it is a sign from Allah, proof that ʿĪsā is a Prophet, and attest to the truth of what he brought.

Notice the movement: from the stomach, to the heart, to knowledge, to testimony. Whatever weakness lay in the original request, the disciples frame their desire as a wish to be strengthened in faith and to become witnesses for the truth — and it is this framing that ʿĪsā carries into his prayer.

## The prayer of ʿĪsā (ayah 114)

Now ʿĪsā himself turns to Allah: "O Allah, our Lord! Send us from heaven a table spread, that there may be for us — for the first and the last of us — a festival and a sign from You; and provide us sustenance, for You are the Best of sustainers."

His duʿāʼ — his supplication — transforms the request. What the disciples asked for as food, he asks for as three things at once:

**A festival (ʿīd) "for the first and the last of us."** Ibn Kathir cites two early authorities on what this means. As-Suddī said: "We will take that day on which the table was sent down as a day of celebration, that we and those who come after us would consider sacred." Sufyān ath-Thawrī said it means "a day of prayer." Either way, the miracle is asked for not as a private meal but as something commemorated by the whole community, generation after generation.

**A sign from Allah.** Ibn Kathir explains: proving that You are able to do all things and to accept my supplication, so that the people accept what I convey to them from You. The table is to serve the mission, not merely the appetite.

**Sustenance.** "And provide us sustenance" — Ibn Kathir describes it as a delicious food from Allah that requires no effort or hardship — sealed with the beautiful acknowledgment, "You are the Best of sustainers."

## Allah's answer — and the severest warning (ayah 115)

Allah's reply grants the request and attaches a condition of unmatched gravity: "I am going to send it down to you, but if any of you after that disbelieves, then I will punish him with a torment such as I have not inflicted on anyone among the worlds." Ibn Kathir explains the disbelief meant here: denying this sign and defying its implication — and he notes the torment is unmatched "among the people of your time." He sets this verse beside similar ayat: the people of Firʿawn being driven into "the severest torment" (40:46) and the hypocrites "in the lowest depths of the Fire" (4:145). He then relays what Ibn Jarir recorded from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr: "Those who will receive the severest torment on the Day of Resurrection are three: the hypocrites, those from the people of Al-Māʾidah who disbelieved in it, and the people of Firʿawn."

Why such severity? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the principle plainly: **the better the blessing, the worse the curse of ingratitude.** When Allah's blessing is extraordinary and unique, the gratitude owed for it rises far above the ordinary — and the punishment for ingratitude becomes extraordinary and unique in turn. A people who watch food descend from heaven and then disbelieve have no veil of doubt left to excuse them.

## Did the table actually come down?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes honestly that commentators differ on whether the Māʾidah actually descended — but the majority hold that it did, and Ibn Kathir argues the same. Alongside the reports he gathers, he points to the apparent wording of ayah 115 itself, which, he says, also states that it came down: Allah says, "I am going to send it down unto you."

The reports the sources cite fill in the picture:

- **From the Sunnah:** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a hadith of **Tirmidhi**, reported from ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, that the Māʾidah did come from the heavens and included bread and meat. The same hadith relates that some of those people committed a breach of trust and stored food away for the next day — and as a result they were transformed into monkeys and swine (may Allah protect us from His wrath). The hadith also indicates that eating from it freely was permitted — as the disciples' own word *naʾkulu* ("we eat") suggests — but storing it for future use was prohibited.
- **From the early community:** Ibn Kathir relays that Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that the angels brought the table down containing seven fish and seven pieces of bread, and placed it before them, "so the last group of people ate as the first group did." And Ibn Jarir recorded from Isḥāq bin ʿAbdullāh that they ate from it as much as they wished — until some of them stole food from it, saying "it might not come down tomorrow," whereupon the table ascended.

The details differ between reports, but their shared testimony, as Ibn Kathir concludes, is that the table was sent down to the Children of Israel in the time of ʿĪsā, as a result of Allah accepting his supplication.

## What the passage asks of us

Three threads run through these four ayat and tie them together.

**Trust the appointed means before asking for the miraculous.** ʿĪsā's first word to his disciples was taqwā — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the believer should not test Allah, but seek his sustenance through the means Allah has naturally provided.

**When you do ask, ask the way ʿĪsā asked.** His prayer models adab (etiquette) with Allah: he addresses Him as "O Allah, our Lord," asks that the gift become worship — a festival, a day of prayer, a sign — and closes by praising Him as "the Best of sustainers."

**Received blessings create obligations.** The table came with a covenant attached. The greater and clearer the favour, the heavier the ingratitude that spurns it — a warning sealed in Allah's own words, and illustrated in the fate of those who hoarded from the very table heaven had spread for them.

passages.title: Jesus disavows worship of himself; the final verdict
passages.tafsir:
# The Final Conversation: Jesus Disavows Worship of Himself

This passage closes Sūrah al-Māʼidah with a scene from the Day of Resurrection: Allah questions ʿĪsā (Jesus), son of Maryam, peace be upon him, before the very people who worshipped him — and the prophet they deified publicly declares his own servitude. What binds ayat 116–120 together is a single courtroom drama with a verdict at its end: the question (116), the answer (117–118), the judgment in favour of the truthful (119), and the closing declaration of Allah's absolute sovereignty (120). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the linkage: the earlier sections of the sūrah described the reckoning of that Day — its questions and answers — and now comes \"the outcome of the probe and reckoning of that fateful day.\"

## A question Allah already knows the answer to

In ayah 116, Allah asks ʿĪsā: \"Did you say unto men: 'Worship me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?'\" The commentators are careful to remove any misunderstanding here. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, drawing on Ibn Kathir, explains that Allah alone has full knowledge of everything — He is not asking because He does not know. The purpose of the question is to admonish those who call themselves Christians: the one they took as a god will himself confess his servitude, quite contrary to the belief they held, and declare himself free of their accusations. Ibn Kathir puts it directly: this exchange takes place *in the presence of those who worshipped ʿĪsā and his mother*, and it is \"a threat and a warning to Christians, chastising them in public,\" as Qatadah and others said. Qatadah connected it to the verdict in ayah 119: \"This is a Day on which the truthful will profit from their truth.\"

Notice that the question mentions worship of ʿĪsā *and his mother* — the passage confronts not only the deification of Jesus but the elevation of Maryam to an object of worship alongside Allah.

## An answer taught by Allah Himself

ʿĪsā's reply opens with *subḥānaka* — \"Glory be to You!\" — glorifying Allah above the very suggestion before answering it. Ibn Kathir observes that this reply \"contains Allah's direction for ʿĪsā to utter the perfect answer.\" Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Abu Hurayrah that ʿĪsā \"will be taught his argument in reply to what Allah will ask him,\" and Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah taught ʿĪsā to say: \"Glory be to You! It was not for me to say what I had no right (to say).\"

The answer then rests everything on Allah's perfect knowledge: \"Had I said such a thing, You would surely have known it.\" Ibn Kathir explains: had I said it, You, my Lord, would have known it, for nothing escapes Your knowledge — rather, I never said these words, nor did the thought even cross my mind. Hence: \"You know what is in my inner self though I do not know what is in Yours; truly, You, only You, are the Knower of all that is hidden and unseen\" — *ʿAllām al-Ghuyūb*, the Knower of every hidden thing.

In ayah 117, ʿĪsā states exactly what he did preach: \"Never did I say to them aught except what You commanded me to say: 'Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.'\" His entire message was the message of every prophet — worship Allah alone — and he explicitly places himself under the same Lordship as his followers: *my* Lord and *your* Lord. He then draws a precise boundary around his own responsibility: \"I was a witness over them while I dwelled amongst them, but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them.\" A prophet answers for his time among his people; what they invented after him is beyond his charge — and nothing was ever beyond Allah's watch.

## \"When You took me\" — does this verse teach that Jesus died?

The phrase *falammā tawaffaytanī* (\"when You took me\") has been used by some to deny ʿĪsā's ascension to the heavens and assert that he died a natural death. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses this directly and calls it an unsound inference: the time of this conversation is the Day of Qiyāmah, and by then — after he has descended from the heavens — ʿĪsā will indeed have died his natural and real death. So his words on that Day, \"when You took me in full,\" are entirely consistent with his having been raised alive. (Maʿārif refers the reader to its detailed discussion under 3:55, \"I am to take you in full and lift you towards Me.\")

Maʿārif then relates, as reported by Ibn Kathir on the authority of a narration from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, that the Prophet ﷺ described the scene: on the Day of Qiyāmah the prophets and their communities will be summoned; ʿĪsā will be called; Allah will remind him of His blessings upon him and upon his mother, and then ask, \"Did you say to the people: take me and my mother as gods beside Allah?\" ʿĪsā will deny it. Then the Christians themselves will be questioned. They will say, \"Yes, this is what he had ordered us to do\" — and after that they will be driven towards Hell. The false claim collapses in the presence of the one it was falsely attached to.

## The Prophet ﷺ will say the same words

One of the most sobering elements Ibn Kathir brings for this passage turns the warning towards this Ummah. Abu Dawud At-Tayalisi recorded — and Al-Bukhari also recorded this hadith in the explanation of this very ayah — that Ibn ʿAbbās said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood and addressed the people: \"O people! You will be gathered to Allah barefooted, naked and uncircumcised — 'As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it' [21:104]. The first among the creation to be covered with clothes on the Day of Resurrection will be Ibrāhīm. Some men from my Ummah will be brought and taken to the left (to the Fire), and I will yell, 'They are my followers!' It will be said, 'You do not know what they innovated after you.' So I will say just as the righteous servant (ʿĪsā) said: 'I was a witness over them while I dwelled amongst them… If You punish them, they are Your servants, and if You forgive them, verily You, only You are the Almighty, the All-Wise.' It will then be said, 'These people kept reverting back on their heels after you left them.'\"

The lesson cuts deep: the words ʿĪsā speaks about those who corrupted his message are words our own Prophet ﷺ will speak about people of his own Ummah who innovated after him. No community is immune from drifting after its prophet departs.

## \"If You punish them… and if You forgive them\" — why these two Names?

Ayah 118 ends not with \"the Most-Forgiving, the Very-Merciful,\" as one might expect after mention of forgiveness, but with *al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm* — the Almighty, the All-Wise. The commentators dwell on this choice.

Ibn Kathir says the ayah expresses that all matters refer back to Allah: \"He does what He wills and none can question Him about what He does, while He will question them.\" It also lays bare the crime of those who invented a lie against Allah and His Messenger, \"making a rival, wife and son for Allah\" — Allah is glorified far above what they attribute to Him. Ibn Kathir concludes that this ayah \"has tremendous value and delivers unique news.\"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (from the notes of Shabbir Ahmad Usmani) explains the wording precisely. Allah does not bring undue hardship on His servants; if punishment comes, it will be only just, right and wise. And if He forgives, it is not because He is unable to do otherwise — He is Mighty, fully capable, from whose grasp no wrong-doer can escape; and being Wise, He would not let a wrong-doer simply walk away for no reason. So the verdict on the wrong-doers will be absolutely wise and masterly. And there is a further subtlety: this speech occurs at the Maḥshar — the gathering of Resurrection — where no intercession for disbelievers and no appeal of mercy on their behalf will be entertained. That is why ʿĪsā does not invoke *Ghafūr Raḥīm*. Contrast this with Ibrāhīm, who prayed *during his life in this world*: \"Whoever has disobeyed me — then You are the Most-Forgiving, the Very-Merciful\" (14:36). In the world, the door of repentance is open and Allah may yet grant a person the ability to return to the truth; on that Day, the time for it has passed. The same prophetic etiquette, in two different moments, chooses two different Names — each perfectly fitted to its hour.

## The night the Prophet ﷺ repeated this one verse

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that Ibn Kathir reports a narration from Abu Dharr: the Prophet ﷺ once spent a whole night reciting this one single verse — \"If You punish them, they are Your slaves…\" When morning came, Abu Dharr said to him: O Messenger of Allah, you kept reciting just this verse; you made your rukūʿ with it and you made your sujūd with it, right up to the break of dawn. He said: \"I prayed to my Rabb to bless me with the station of intercession (shafāʿah), which He granted. Inshallah, it is going to be for one who has never associated anyone with Allah.\" According to another narration, after reciting the verse he raised his hands facing the heaven and said, *Allāhumma ummatī* — \"O Allah, mercy — mercy on my people\" — and wept. Allah sent Jibrāʼīl to ask why he wept, and then sent him back with the answer: He will please His Prophet soon in his concern for his people and will not let him be unhappy.

Here the passage's severity and its mercy meet: the verse that seals the fate of those who committed shirk is the very verse through which the Prophet ﷺ pleaded all night for his people — and the intercession granted is reserved for those who never associated anything with Allah. Tawḥīd, pure worship of Allah alone, is the thread on which everything in this scene hangs.

## The verdict: the Day when truth profits the truthful

Ayah 119 is Allah's answer to ʿĪsā after he disowns those who lied about Allah and refers their end to his Lord's will: \"This is a Day on which the truthful will profit from their truth.\" Ad-Dahhak reports Ibn ʿAbbās explaining it as: \"This is the Day when Tawḥīd will benefit those who believed in it.\" The truth in question is, first of all, the truth of worshipping Allah alone.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the word *ṣidq* (truthfulness) itself. Ordinarily, \"truth\" describes speech that matches reality. But in the Qurʼān and Sunnah, ṣidq and its opposite *kidhb* (falsehood) are broader — they cover deeds as well as words. Maʿārif cites a hadith from Mishkat: whoever adorns himself with what he has not been given — claiming a quality or deed not truly his — is \"as if he has put on two garbs of a lie.\" And another hadith in Mishkat describes the truthful servant in terms of action: one who performs Ṣalāh well openly *and* performs it well in private — of such a person Allah says, \"This is My servant, in truth.\" Truthfulness, then, is a life whose inner and outer match — the exact opposite of the false claim exposed in this passage.

For the truthful: \"Gardens under which rivers flow, abiding therein forever\" — and, Ibn Kathir adds, they will never be removed from them. Then comes something greater than the Gardens: \"Allah is pleased with them and they with Him.\" Ibn Kathir connects this with 9:72 — \"the greatest bliss is the good pleasure of Allah\" — and Maʿārif relates the hadith that after admitting the true believers into Jannah, Allah will say: the real blessing is that I am pleased with you, and now I shall never be displeased with you. Hence \"that is the great success\" — as Ibn Kathir says, the success beyond which there is no greater; and as Maʿārif puts it, when the Master and Creator Himself is pleased with you, what else could it be? Ibn Kathir notes the Qurʼān's own commentary on such a prize: \"For the like of this let the workers work\" (37:61) and \"for this let all those strive who want to strive\" (83:26).

## The closing word: all dominion is Allah's

Ayah 120 seals the sūrah: \"To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and all that is therein, and He is able to do all things.\" Ibn Kathir explains: He created everything, owns everything, controls the affairs of everything; everything and everyone is in His domain and under His power and will. \"There is none like Him, nor is there rival, ancestor, son, or wife for Him, nor a lord or god besides Him.\" After a scene in which the claim of a divine son is publicly dismantled by the son of Maryam himself, this final ayah states the positive truth that claim had violated — and it is a fitting last word in more ways than one. Ibn Kathir relates, with his chain of transmission, that Ibn Wahb said he heard Huyay bin ʿAbdullah saying that Abu ʿAbdur-Rahman Al-Habli said that ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr said: \"The last revealed Sūrah was Sūrat al-Māʼidah.\"

## Living it

The passage asks something concrete of the believer. Guard Tawḥīd absolutely — it is the truth that profits on that Day, and the intercession of the Prophet ﷺ is for the one who never associated anything with Allah. Be truthful in deed as well as word: worship well in private as in public, and claim nothing you have not been given. And remember that communities can drift after their prophets — ʿĪsā's followers did, and the Prophet ﷺ warned that some of his own would too — so the believer's task is to hold to what the Messenger actually brought, not what is invented after him.
